saga.name: The Contested Isle: the Hibernian Tribunal

covenants.name: Circulus Ruber
covenants.notes:
History. Two Tytalus and two Merinita magae came to Ireland in 778 to look for the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé. They found an island at war with itself and crowded with faeries, which pleased the Tytalus and the Merinita respectively, and the customs they set became the Peripheral Code: the Tytalus nurtured strife and self-reliance, the Merinita the island's faeries and its mythic past. After a year in the Brú na Bóinne they moved to the quiet Burren, raised a tower by magic on the cliffs and declared they would hold it for a year. Local wizards and their mundane kin fought hard to drive them out; allies from the Rhine and Iberia joined them, and by the end of the decade eight magi lived here. The covenant is named for the red wards a local ward-maker drew round them.

Over the centuries it stood aside from what quarrels it could and joined those it had to: mundane wars it avoided where it might; faeries, druids and hedge wizards troubled it often; the Ostmen's rune wizards fought it to several draws; and in the Schism War a Fomóir fleet attacked, leaving scars on the tower and the land. It has ignored the English invaders as of no lasting account, though the magi who came in their wake may prove otherwise.

The tower. A round tower 120 feet high and 60 across, made with an augmented Conjuring the Mystic Tower, with room for twelve magi and their staff; the magi live above, the servants on the lower floors. Each year the newest member paints a red ring round the tower's middle, halfway up.

Culture. Clinging to a romantic idea of the past, its magi refuse to touch the Peripheral Code and stress the Tribunal's warlike, individual spirit. They urge magi to found covenants and have helped some; they champion the macgnímartha and their raids on other covenants' cathaigh; and they push quarrelling magi into Wizard War, even lending enchanted items and magic weapons to the fighters. Yet they are also Hibernia's guardians, protecting sacred mounds and other places the Tribunal values, supporting both Mercer Houses with hospitality, and giving up their own time readily to the Tribunal's business. It once lodged a travelling provincial king and two hundred followers on magically made food that did not nourish them.

Magi: eight, including the Praeco Milvia and the senior Quaesitor Visioturpis, and Conán Derg, the eldest magus of Hibernia; the book names no others.

The cathach.

Story seed: Hermetic Hospitality. Circulus Ruber lodges a provincial king and two hundred followers overnight with magically made food and shelter, but conjured food does not nourish, and by morning the whole company is starving. The king demands two hundred cows, which the covenant will not pay, and the characters are asked to find another way to appease him.
covenants.summary:
The first covenant of Ireland, founded in 780, and still the largest and the loudest in its own praise: a round tower on Hag's Head, on the Cliffs of Moher, that is home to the Praeco and the senior Quaesitor. Its device is a hastily drawn red circle. Its cathach is a magic cauldron its founders found, long believed to be the Dagda's.

It leads the traditionalists of the Ordo Hiberniae: it admires Hermetic scholarship and invention but will not hear of changing the Tribunal's ways, and foreign magi who visit often feel they have gone back in time, which is just what Circulus Ruber wants. It sees itself as the Tribunal's leader and model.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: the book names none
Wealth: cattle, as tradition demands; the covenant never meets its wealth needs any other way
Library: unnamed (see its library record)
Duty: it makes all the arrangements for each Tribunal at Tara, raising the temporary camp by magic
Boon: Magical Fortress (a great tower raised with an enlarged Conjuring the Mystic Tower)
Boon: Prestige (the Tribunal's first and leading covenant)
Boon: Famous Resident (the Praeco, Milvia)
Hook: Monster (the Cailleach of Hag's Head, kept out only by the Aegis)
Hook: Hermetic Politics (leader of the Ordo Hiberniae against the English reformers)
Hook: Dark Secret (the cauldron's true nature and power)
Tension: its love of feud and Wizard War against its duty to protect Hibernia
covenants.secrets:
The cauldron is not the Dagda's, which gives food and drink without end, but the Cauldron of Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid, a notorious giant who lived beneath a lake. Legend says that cauldron passed between Irish and Welsh kings and was broken in a war between them; either the tale is wrong, or this is another vessel with the same powers.
It brings a dead warrior back to fight for one more day, if his head and spine are whole: he cannot speak, and for the next 24 hours he fights for whoever put him in. It will not raise the same corpse twice. The magi keep this from the Tribunal.

covenants.name: Cliffheart
covenants.notes:
History. Three Merinita magi founded it once their covenant, Warbler's Way (Cosán Ceolaire), fell in the Schism War. Most of House Merinita stayed out of that war, but these three fought, because House Diedne had allied with the Munster Tuatha Dé; after the last battle at Clontarf they moved to Cape Clear. Two centuries of questioning have never shown why the Tuatha Dé took Diedne's side, and since it could happen again, with Teach Duínn so close and Donn's past what it is, the magi keep dealing with them. The founders have gone to death or Final Twilight, and their filii carry on.

The ráth. A simple ráth round a dozen huts on a steep hill over the Cove of the Black Stream on the island's north shore, where supplies are landed in secret. The Shrouded Glen hides it, less well than in a forest but well enough. Inside the palisade are the magi's huts and laboratories, the servants' huts, a meeting hall and the sheepfold. The steward Maynard handles every mundane matter, playing a madman who lives among the birds, and warns people that the standing stones are haunted; visiting magi look for the dirt track to the stones or for the hermit among the gulls and barnacle geese.

The cathach. One of three standing stones outside the ráth is a Diedne magus turned into an obelisk. A hand-wide hole runs through it, which the magi say is a mortal wound: they renew the spell every year, since if it lapsed he would die at once. Faisgia keeps the spell up and moves the stone to each Tribunal with Rego Terram magic. Some say the three Diedne who fell at Clontarf were never found, and Cliffheart claims one though it did not fight there.

Culture. Four of the six magi study faeries, collecting, fighting, questioning and entertaining them; the other two seldom leave their sancta. Faeries hate disorder, so the grounds, the library included, are kept a deliberate mess, and though the Aegis would stop nearly any faerie, the magi take many precautions besides: they never cut hair or beard; wear iron rings on both little fingers and necklaces of horses' back teeth; smash eggshells so small faeries cannot live in them; keep cats and dogs out; set each hut's front and back doors in line so a faerie walks straight through; never dig inside the ráth or trim its bushes and trees; sprinkle stale urine on every threshold; and never begin lab work or a journey on a Friday.

The magi: Faisgia, the leader; the Merinita Ruaidrí Mór (Rego), Áine Dhubh, Black Ann (Herbam), and the warlike Coscrach Cam; and the Bonisagus Palantus and the Verditius Styrbjórn, who rarely leave their laboratories.
covenants.summary:
A ráth of a dozen huts on Cape Clear Island, off Ireland's southern tip, whose magi study faeries and have grown fearful of them; its device is three doves flying in a ring, and its cathach a Diedne magus turned into a standing stone. Founded after Clontarf by Merinita survivors of Warbler's Way.

Staunchly of the Ordo Hiberniae: it will not accept English magi, uses every lawful means to stop them founding covenants, and is working out how to cast spells in Irish instead of Latin. Its magi keep their Oath and the Peripheral Code; they are anxious recluses, not criminals or troublemakers.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: the book names none
Library: untidy on purpose (see its library record)
Research: Palantus's spells in Irish, built from faeries' true speech
Boon: Island (Cape Clear Island)
Boon: Seclusion (few visitors, hidden by The Shrouded Glen: Perception against 9 to find)
Boon: Ringwork (a simple ráth and palisade)
Hook: Monastery (the monks on the southern half of the island)
Hook: Hermetic Politics (against the English magi; Ashenrise especially)
Hook: Rival (the faeries it fears, with Teach Duínn and Donn not far off)
Tension: the Marriage Stones, lovers who seek them out and monks who forbid them

covenants.name: Elk's Run
covenants.notes:
History. Oswald of Bonisagus and Lugardis of Guernicus came in 1159 with cattle, silver, vis sources the Tribunal did not know of and the giant antlers for a cathach, claimed a remote valley and began building a round tower in the old style. Native magi of several covenants soon came demanding to see the cathach. Oswald said the antlers came from a true Irish elk, seven feet tall, which he had hunted and killed in the Faerie realm by acting out an ancient story, a deed done before only by the Fir Bolg heroes who hunted the beasts out of Ireland. Since such antlers turn up in bogs, few believed him. The Irish saw a Stonehenge magus and a Quaesitor come to impose English rule on the Order as the English were doing on the kings, too near Connacht to be trusted with the Treaty.

So they disputed the newcomers' right to the vis of the region, claiming it for other covenants by ancient custom (though Hibernian tradition gives such a claim no footing), reciting their lineages, old pacts and treaties with supernatural beings and local wizards. Without vis there could be no covenant. Oswald, a tiny man with a mop of white hair, offered a wager: all the land and vis he could ride round before sunset would be his. The Irish, taking it for a joke, agreed, and a wise maga added that he must cast no spell. He threw down the antlers, which rose as a giant elk; he rode it into the mountains over fallen trees, crumbling scree and flooding rivers, and came back with the last light as the beast turned back to antlers. Many of the Irish laughed and allowed his right; some were furious at the trick. Since then many young magi on their macgnímartha, and some older ones, have raided for the cathach, but none has held it long enough to end the covenant.

The cathach. The antlers of an Irish elk, an extinct beast bigger than any living. Nobody knows what else they can do; Oswald has brought the elk to life and ridden it three times, each time to defend the covenant.

The covenant. Three towers in the old style, a small feast hall, a good stone scriptorium that holds the library, a hamlet, pasture and fields, all within the Aegis; it claims great tracts of mountain, lake and forest beyond, and all the vis in them.

The library and the Cow and Calf rule. Elk's Run lives for research and above all for collecting books. Oswald spent long years copying in the Archbishop of Armagh's fine library, where he learnt the Ars Notoria, and swaps texts with religious houses throughout Hibernia. The Cow and Calf rule is strictly kept here: anyone may make a copy of a book, but the copy may leave only in exchange for a text of like worth. Many books are copied here and sent to covenants across Mythic Europe as gifts or trades.

Lately the other magi have grown warlike under constant raiding and have bound themselves to English nobles; Lugardis has warned them more than once that this may count as interfering with mundanes, but the feeling is that the covenant must lean on the English to survive.

Covenfolk. The locals are Cenél Áeda na hEchtge, a branch of the Uí Fiachrach Aidhne, the ancient royal house of Connacht, in two great families: the Uí Sheachnasaigh, who serve the covenant, and the Ua Cathail, who resent the English magi's help to their rivals and may soon complain to the Tribunal. Other covenants might back them, though Lugardis works against it and it seems unlikely, since meddling with mundanes that brings ruin on sodales is itself a crime under the Code.

Magi: three, with two apprentices, both Oswald's; the second, native born, was given him at the last Tribunal at Lugardis's urging. The magi agree less and less on what to do.

The book puts the founding in 1159 in this chapter and just after the Grand Tribunal of 1195 in its history; the pack follows 1159.

What the magi do not admit.
covenants.summary:
A young covenant of three towers in a remote valley of the Slieve Aughty, west of Lough Derg, close to the border of forbidden Connacht, founded in 1159 by Oswald of Bonisagus and Lugardis of Guernicus. Its device, and its cathach, is a magnificent pair of giant elk antlers.

It means to revive the learning, hospitality and scholarship of Ireland's golden age of covenants, and keeps a great library, but it is the English covenant, of the English Council's party: raided by Irish clansmen and by Irish magi after its cathach, it has turned more and more to English nobles for help.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: the sources across the mountains, loughs and forests Oswald rode round before sunset; the book does not list them
Library: very large; mundane books, laboratory texts and rare magical volumes, among them the Ars Notoria (see its library record)
Boon: Prestige (Oswald's name for generosity and scholarship across Mythic Europe)
Boon: Local Ally (the Uí Sheachnasaigh, its covenfolk, and English nobles)
Hook: Tribunal Border (on the edge of Connacht, closed to magi by the Treaty)
Hook: Rival (the Ua Cathail, and Irish magi on their macgnímartha after the cathach)
Hook: Mundane Politics (its ties to English nobles; the Ua Cathail's coming complaint)
Tension: Igneous Drake's killings and Wizard Wars against Lugardis's diplomacy
Tension: Oswald may leave Ireland with the library if politics turn against him
covenants.secrets:
Oswald has used acts and gifts of magic to help Irish and English nobles and clerics in return for books, which could plainly be judged interfering with mundanes; he does not see how far he has compromised himself.
Igneous Drake kills raiders, Ua Cathail bandits and hedge wizards who stray out of Connacht, and wages Wizard War on Irish magi he thinks have slighted the covenant, believing Hibernia enforces no law among magi.

covenants.name: Leth Moga
covenants.notes:
History. Leth Moga and Leth Cuinn were made in 898, out of Hibernia's first meeting as a Tribunal of its own. The Redcap Imag, wife of Cloyne's abbot Cian Ua Cathain, offered land and leadership and was given the southern house: he led the dozen monks and the monastery's people, she ran the House. After the monastic chroniclers' example she began the Red Book of Cloyne, the Tribunal's Hermetic history, and her successors have kept it up.

The Red Book was open to all until Fergal mac Cuircc, leader after the Schism War, recorded the war faithfully and then shut the book on it, saying the magi had to forget; from then only Redcaps could read it. In the twelfth century magi argued that its eye-witness records would be useful evidence at law. Fergal's son-in-law and successor Diarmait agreed that each Redcap's own testimony should be available, but held that the book, inherited from Fergal as his own, lay under his sanctum marker; the Tribunal agreed, and several magi still resent it.

The House. A large wooden house and a little-used barn on the southern edge of the monastery. The barn, draughty and cold on a Magic aura of 1, serves well enough as a laboratory; with no Gifted Redcap in residence, Diarmait rents it to other magi. Guest magi recast a weak Aegis of the Hearth round house and barn each year. The House's valuables, its records, stored vis and magic items, are kept behind locked doors in the caves under the village, out of the monks' way; Diarmait knows the tunnels far better than the abbot.

Culture. Monks and Redcaps keep apart but on good terms, and the Redcaps mix freely with the villagers. Every Redcap here is kin to Imag through the female line, so with the abbot's household and the married Redcaps' families the House is hardly secret. All have been initiated into the Art of Memory, and after witnessing an event each must write it into the Red Book, a chore but not a heavy one. Apprentices who skip the macgnímartha sometimes come here for shelter, board and the libraries in return for copying and other service.

Its Redcaps: six, none Gifted, Diarmait and his filius Gopstan, Ercc Cam and his filius Luathan, and the tearful Rónán and his filia Áine. Their worry is their ageing leader: by custom his filius follows him, but that is in doubt, and since leadership is not the Tribunal's business, the Redcaps must settle it.

The book gives no season; Autumn is assumed, for an old leader and an open succession.

Story seed: The Missing Book. Leth Moga is poorly defended, and one morning the Red Book is gone from the scriptorium. Diarmait assumes a youth in the macgnímartha took it, as they take cathaigh, and asks the characters to get it back; a trail leads to the woods around the Killarney lakes.
covenants.summary:
The southern Mercer House, sister to Leth Cuinn, serving every covenant south of the Eiscir Riada from the village monastery of Cloyne in Desmond. It is not a covenant at law: it keeps no cathach, needs no cattle, and stands because it serves the Tribunal, guarded by many rulings of the Peripheral Code. The book gives it no device.

Where the northern Redcaps train as warriors, Leth Moga's are the Tribunal's eye-witnesses and keep its history, above all in the Red Book of Cloyne. It takes no side between the Ordo Hiberniae and the English magi, though who may read the Red Book is a sore point with both.
covenants.what_matters:
Income: its barn laboratory, rented to visiting magi for one pawn of vis a season
Vis: stored behind locked doors in the caves beneath Cloyne; the book gives no amount
Library: the Red Book of Cloyne (Diarmait's own, under his sanctum marker)
Services: Redcaps as witnesses and recorders at Hermetic gatherings, each trained in the Art of Memory
Hook: Mercer House
Hook: Monastery (Cloyne's monks, on good terms)
Boon: Hidden Resources (records, vis and magic items in the tunnels under the village)
Hook: Hermetic Politics (magi who want the Red Book opened)
Tension: who succeeds Diarmait, Gopstan or Luathan
covenants.secrets: The trail is false. The thief is an older magus who wants an inglorious episode cut from the annals, and hopes to slip the book back while the characters search the woods.

covenants.name: Ashenrise
covenants.notes:
History. Helles and Pollices fled to Ireland after Moles Magna fell, having heard that the Angevins had settled it; they found it scarcely settled and its old customs alive, and took up reforming its law as a worthy challenge. For their cathach they chose Rhiannon, who had been buried among her Uí Riain kin in Ossory rather than at Qui Sonant. They attacked the chieftain's ráth during the fighting between Raymond le Gros and the Uí Riain and carried her remains away. Joined by three sodales from Stonehenge, they showed the corpse at the Tribunal of 1186 and declared their covenant. The hall was in uproar and Wizard War was declared on them; some said a corpse was no magical treasure, but the Praeco Conán Derg ruled that the raw vis grown in the bones made it a fit cathach. They held it for the year, hard as it was, and were recognized in 1187.

The cathach. Rhiannon had a Christian burial, so her ghost lies beyond Hermetic magic. The magi have enchanted the body against rot and to caper and dance at a word, and left the raw vis in its bones untouched. It stands half a mile west of the covenant's western tower, outside the Aegis, looking toward Connacht and Munster.

Culture. The magi try to live as civilized continental magi: each pursues his own speciality, debate is lively, and they hunt, hawk and give lavish feasts with song and dance. Their neighbours harry them with Wizard Wars and raids on the cathach; they guard Rhiannon doggedly and usually wage their wars passively, keeping out of the aggressor's way. They keep the Hibernian Code to the letter until they can change it, and have sworn no oaths and broken no law, but they raid no cathaigh and send no apprentice on the macgnímartha, and they want both customs gone.

Covenfolk. Beyond the sanctums it is an ordinary English castle of the colony, served by a few imported settlers. The magi deal openly with mundanes, though most must work through agents because of the Gift.

Magi. Helles, Pollices and Dyfrgi, a Welsh Bjornaer with a wolf heartbeast, remain of the founders; Tug, Dorján and Konstanczia came later from the Stonehenge Tribunal. Tug, the only one the covenant would take in, may be the man to open talks with Cliffheart, if Ashenrise ever wants peace.

Founded 1186, at the Tribunal where the cathach was shown; recognized 1187 after the year's defence. Season: Spring.
covenants.summary: A covenant of continental magi, refugees of Moles Magna, the fallen covenant of the Normandy Tribunal, who mean to rise from its ashes to a leading place in Hibernia and to drag its Peripheral Code, which they think barbarous, into the thirteenth century. They live as guests in an English castle in the Liberty of Carlow. Its device is a scroll crossed with a sword. Its cathach is the corpse of Rhiannon Uí Riain, once Prima of House Merinita, enchanted to dance. It leans to the English Council: Helles leads the reform debate at every Tribunal, so far with little to show for it. It is at odds with most covenants, Lámbaird and Cliffheart above all.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: the raw vis grown in Rhiannon's bones, left in them on purpose (the cathach itself)
Income: the hospitality of Ralph fitz Stephen, whose castle it is
Library: unnamed; Helles's glosses of Hermetic law and the books the magi brought from Normandy and Stonehenge
Boon: Courtyard Castle (a square castle with four corner towers)
Boon: Local Ally (Ralph fitz Stephen, four knights and fifteen men-at-arms)
Hook: Hermetic Politics (reform motions, and high crimes charged against its magi at every Tribunal)
Hook: Rival (Lámbaird and Cliffheart, who press it with Wizard Wars and cathach raids)
Hook: Infamous (a dead Prima's corpse made a dancing trophy)
Tension: the Uí Riain and the Déise túatha resent every English lord on the Barrow
covenants.secrets:
The Uí Riain rising was the magi's invention: they used minstrels to convince Raymond le Gros that his vassals meant to rebel, and his campaign gave them their chance at the grave.
Dorján and Konstanczia's sigils are held by magi in Transylvania, who direct them to help Ashenrise modernise the Tribunal.
Tug's sodales doubt his saint: he met Patrick in the Schwarzwald, a forest full of mischievous faeries, and it may have been a faerie that converted him. Tug admits he met many faeries there but swears it was the saint.

covenants.name: Lámbaird
covenants.notes:
History. While Diedne was purging Ireland's native magicians, the druid Raghallach fell in with Petrifer of House Flambeau, newly settled in Ireland, and they became friends until Raghallach learnt Petrifer was of the Order, which he believed had sanctioned the purge. He attacked in fury; Petrifer barely survived behind his Parma, admired the druid's savage magic, and once Raghallach was subdued offered him a place in the Order. Reconciled, the two made a camp in the Wicklow Mountains and sheltered any of Raghallach's tradition. Diedne would not accept druids as Flambeau; when the Tribunal would not hear her, she made Wizard War on them, and only Raghallach and two others lived to found a true cell in the House. The camp became Lámbaird, and his druidic practice became a school of war.

Lámbaird kept a deep hatred of Diedne and threw itself into the Schism War in Hibernia and the Tribunals round it. The school boomed as Flambeau magi flocked to the hills to study and to hunt Diedne, and foreigners turned the name into Lombard. At Clontarf in 1014 its magi, warned by Brian Bóramha's druid that sons of Diedne marched with his army, found the last Diedne of Hibernia on the field and destroyed them.

The cathach. A hollow false arm of silver made by a magical smith for the bard Cairpre, which served him as a living arm. In the year the covenant sought recognition, one of its magi, stung by Cairpre's satire, broke the ancient ban on harming bards and killed him; Petrifer, his own pater, slew him in Wizard War for it, and his name has been struck from the records. A covenfolk bearer wears the arm over his own left arm, a great honour: his own arm is useless inside it, for the silver moves by its own will, the murdered bard's spirit, people say. The bearer may not stray from the covenant nor live within the Aegis.

The covenant. A palisade of stakes rings it; inside there is a din of hounds barking, weapons clashing on the training fields and magi bellowing orders. The magi's two wings flank a great wooden lodge, with stables, kennels and mews behind for its many horses, dogs and hawks. It looks little like a Hermetic covenant: there is no library, the laboratories are cluttered with makeshift apparatus hard to bring so deep into the hills, and the magi ignore each other's sancta (never an outsider's) and borrow equipment without asking.

Culture. The magi live like the heads of a family, not scholars or lords; they hunt with hounds and hawks in the wooded hills, everyone eats together and does a share of the work, and the covenfolk grow up used to the Gift and speak their minds (a cook may well send a magus to the well). The magi still make the great decisions. Beasts sold are gelded, and buyers are told that by common law any offspring belong to Lámbaird anyway; sales pay for laboratory gear and the odd luxury, and the covenant feeds itself.

The School of Raghallach teaches that no defence withstands a strong enough attack. Raghallach's tradition drew power from blood and self-inflicted pain, cnámh greamú or bone-biting, which also gave House Tremere a certamen style of that name; the druidic tradition is lost, but the school has become expert at beating supernatural foes and is often asked to carry out a Wizard's March. Its magi learn to assault and dispel an enemy's Magic Resistance head-on rather than slip round it, and usually have high Penetration (Life Boost or Puissant Penetration suit them). On a hunt they watch their prey closely, steal possessions or even dig through latrine pits for arcane connections, but prefer blood from their soldiers' weapons, and use a foe's name as a sympathetic connection: they listen for it or introduce themselves first, by baptismal name, hoping for an answer. Their spells include Retrieve the Bloodied Arrow, Revoke the Protection of Bonisagus, and Revoke the Protection of (Form) and of (Realm) (in the spell catalog), built on two new Perdo Vim guidelines: dispel a Form Resistance of level up to the spell's +10 + a stress die, or the Magic Resistance of one Realm's Might up to the spell's +20 + a stress die, in each case penetrating the target's Vim resistance. Hibernia forbids enchantments of Revoke the Protection of Bonisagus without limits on who may use them or how long they last.

Magi and covenfolk. Three Flambeau magi live here, with apprentices of the two elders; there is room for more once the stores are cleared out of the spare rooms, but it seldom takes magi from outside, since nearly all were trained here. The covenfolk are Uí Broin: Cathasach Ua Broin, their young, untried chief, who defers to Dalton; and Tadg Ua Broin, their seanchaidh, schooled at the bardic school of Ceall Cluaine at Dalton's expense, who binds the clan with tradition and loyalty. Its young men train as warriors, every one eager to hunt the Normans who plundered their home.

Founded 826. Season: Summer. Aura: Magic 2 in the glen, 4 at the covenant.
covenants.summary: The arm of a bard (LAWM-beard), called Lombard by foreigners: an old covenant of House Flambeau, founded in 826 by Petrifer and the druid Raghallach, and home ever since to the School of Raghallach, a school of magical combat. Born when a Hermetic magus sheltered a native magician, it has always cast itself as guardian of the old ways, and has lately taken up the defence of the Irish against the Normans. Its device is a severed human arm, and its cathach the silver arm of the bard Cairpre. It is of the Ordo Hiberniae, and the fiercest political foe of any covenant it thinks is pursuing an English agenda; the English Council worries more about it every meeting. So far it has escaped real sanction by saying it only defends itself and its resources, but many suspect it of raiding the Normans.

links.note: its magi try, so far in vain, to breed a true mare

covenants.what_matters:
Income: horses, hounds and hawks bred and trained for Irish nobles and magi, including lines unaffected by the Gift and wolfhounds with Magic Sensitivity that smell out vis
Library: none; texts stay with whoever used them last
Boon: Veteran Fighters (the largest turb in the Tribunal, young Uí Broin warriors)
Boon: Loyal Covenfolk (the Uí Broin, who have lived among its magi since it was founded)
Boon: Secondary Income (the breeding of beasts)
Boon: Difficult Access (a blind glen with a single road)
Hook: School (the School of Raghallach, and its long-term visitors)
Hook: Wooden (a palisade and a timber lodge)
Hook: Hermetic Politics (reprimanded in 1193; the English Council's concern)
Hook: Dark Secret (its part in the hill clans' war on the English)
Tension: Dalton against Éinri of Vigil, a long feud of certamen and grog brawls
Tension: Wizard War on any magus who undercuts its monopoly of bred beasts
covenants.secrets:
Lámbaird gives the mountain clans magical help now and then against the English in the Wicklow Mountains, which the Tribunal would surely judge interference with mundanes if it were known.
So far it has left no witnesses and has not tied the Order to the raids, but its doings have been noticed: hence the reprimand of 1193.

covenants.name: The Paruchia of Nerius
covenants.notes:
History. Fedelmid of Limerick, a Hermetic magus on pilgrimage to Rome, wandered into a strange valley in the Alps and saw a run of visions of the mysterious magus-saint Nerius that shaped the rest of his life. He sought out the secrets of Holy Magic and trained an apprentice, Indrechtach, who taught a manaim of his monastery in turn. All three are Gifted; Indrechtach has no Gentle Gift and was put out of his community. Together they made a new monastery and covenant on the Saltees. Fedelmid is on excellent terms with his fellow Céli Dé, even those of the Coill Trí, but some magi think these holy men untrustworthy, even dangerous should the Anglo-Irish Church start to take notice.

The cathach. Nobody knows how Fedelmid came by the relic, given the mystery of Nerius's martyrdom. A little shrine high on Great Saltee's cliffs holds it, outside the Aegis; the islanders say it works miracles but keep quiet about them, fearing churchmen will carry it off to a mainland church.

The Hermetic Céli Dé. They take Holy Magic as their Major Virtue and Subtle Magic as a Minor Hermetic Virtue, with the Restriction that their magic cannot touch women. Their ascetic life gives them a Living Conditions modifier of 0 to aging rolls, not a magus's usual bonus. As a Divine societas their Favored Abilities are Holy Magic, Intervention, Purity and Transcendence. They do not teach True Faith: they are a few who already have it and are drawn to this path, and they accept only Gifted apprentices of that rare devotion.

The covenant. Beehive cells, a small chapel, laboratories in caves nearby and a tall library tower; a little graveyard holds earlier hermits. Each Sunday the monks cross to Great Saltee for mass in an enchanted coracle Fedelmid built. They need little vis and few laboratory texts, and welcome Hermetic visitors, whom the missing Magic aura and the diet (largely seaweed and seabirds' eggs) soon send on their way. Fedelmid and Indrechtach mean to save the Order by teaching it Holy Magic, and try to save newcomers' souls the same way. They would welcome magi of any House, though few will want to come.

Covenfolk. The islanders of Great Saltee: two farming families and three fisher brothers with wives and children, and Father Diarmaid, priest of St. Mary's, a good friend who guards his isolated flock.

Founded 1189, when the tradition joined the Order. Season: Spring.
covenants.summary: A monastic community and covenant of the Hermetic Céli Dé, a tiny tradition that joined House Ex Miscellanea in 1189: three Gifted holy men, two monks and a manaim, on Little Saltee, an island otherwise empty five miles off the Wexford coast, closely tied to the folk of Great Saltee next door. Its aura is Divine 3, not Magic. Its device is a skeletal hand shining with light, and its cathach the skeletal arm of Saint Nerius, a relic with three Faith Points. Irish by birth, its magi stand against the old pagan customs and argue for a Christian Tribunal on the continental model, so they get on better with the English reformers than with their fellow Irish magi and look for allies among newcomers.
covenants.what_matters:
Vis: little needed, and none named
Library: a tall tower on Little Saltee; Indrechtach begs leave to copy books across the Tribunal
Boon: Island
Boon: Difficult Access (treacherous tides, no good landing)
Boon: Loyal Covenfolk (the twenty-eight islanders of Great Saltee)
Hook: Missing Aura (Divine 3, no Magic aura; few visitors stay long)
Hook: Gender Imbalance (no woman may land on Little Saltee)
Hook: Hermetic Politics (its campaign for Holy Magic and a Christian Tribunal)
Tension: the Túath Buidhe of the Coill Trí, and the Fomórach, Tuatha Dé and Fir Bolg ambassadors
Tension: uneasy with much of House Ex Miscellanea and with House Merinita
covenants.secrets:
Father Diarmaid was posted to Great Saltee for a past wrong that still haunts him; anyone who threatened to reveal it could blackmail him.
Fedelmid made many enemies in the feuds of his youth, and some may try to kill him on the road before he reaches Qui Sonant to die.

covenants.name: Leth Cuinn
covenants.notes:
History. From its founding in 898 Leth Cuinn cared for martial skills. In 1029 Dáire Farranta came back after seven years away and challenged its leader, his own parens, to Wizard War; both were unGifted, and Dáire won without a spell, by feats of speed and swordplay out of legend, the clesrada. He exiled the other Redcaps and filled the house with his kin, among them Úathach, the faerie woman who had taught him. He made it a house of the Cult of Heroes, House Mercere's society that seeks to bring back the heroes of old by training exceptional people as champions, heroes and perhaps demigods; his heirs still rule it. Dáire Farranta also killed the péist of Lough Neagh.

Úathach of the Glen. The name means 'spectre'. She has not aged a day since she came with Dáire Farranta: a faerie of great power, one of the few Tuatha Dé still active in Hibernia, a granddaughter of the battle gods Nuadha and Badhbh, and the daughter of Scáthach, Cú Chulainn's teacher, and his lover in the tales. She feeds on the vigour young warriors spend learning and practising war. She is severe, hatchet-nosed, her dark hair streaked grey and drawn back tight; she always wears leather armour and is never without nine javelins or more, a staff-sling and a thrusting spear, and her right forefinger is badly set, broken, they say, by Cú Chulainn when they first met. She is ritually married to Dáire Cú, a union more than symbolic since his mortal wife died. She has no stat block.

Culture. All the Redcaps and most of the sizable turb practise the clesrada, which take constant hard training in weapons and athletics; at Tribunal its people are known for superb fitness and for showing it off. Its Redcaps also train grogs and companions the covenants send, and Dáire an Chogaidh can make a fighting force of raw recruits in months.

The clesrada. The clesa ('feats', singular cles) were the Ulster heroes' displays on the battlefield, the exercise ground and in the king's hall, part weapon-play, part juggling, part magic. Lugh was held to have invented them, hence Ildánach, 'skilled in every art'; Cú Chulainn mastered all of them, one known only to him and to his son Connla, whom he taught it. Scáthach, daughter of Nuadha, taught them on Skye with her sons Cúar, Cet and Cruife; Cú Chulainn studied there a year and a day. Úathach alone teaches them now.

Each cles is a separate Initiation (Ease Factor 15; Úathach's Presence + Organization Lore: Clesrada is 12): a quest tied in symbol to the feat, then a geas, a Prohibition Flaw linked to the feat that is in effect the charm that works it; break it and the cles is gone. Every script takes the geas as an Ordeal and none counts an earlier Ordeal, so the unGifted can be Initiated. Úathach also lays a geas, outside the Initiation, on every Initiate never to Initiate anyone else, on pain of losing every cles. Her sample script, the Ubullchless by Quest and Ordeal (+6): the Initiate leaves with an apple pip after a rite, and within a year and a day returns with an enchanted apple freely given by the supernatural creature that owned it (+3), then accepts the geas she whispers (+3), most often about apples or apple trees.

Using clesa. A cles may be used as often as wished, at no cost unless its text says so, by a stress roll of an Ability; a botch always costs a Fatigue level. They are Faerie powers, each roll like a 15th-level spell with Penetration 0 plus the Penetration bonus, so magic that affects spells, an Aegis included, can touch them, but they act on the user, like Aimed spells, and need not penetrate a foe's resistance; while one works the user counts as magical. Several clesa of the same Ability may be chained into one action, each rolled in turn until one fails, with nothing else that round, an Attack included: a Redcap may run down a horse with the Profit of Speed, leap onto it with the Salmon Leap and keep his feet with the Rope Feat in one round. The troupe may invent more. With the Rope Feat, Perfect Balance adds its +6.

Athletics. Baí Brasse, the Profit of Speed (Qik): hurry at three times and run at six times walking pace for a round. Cless Caitt, the Cat Feat (Dex): a standing long jump of up to eight times one's height, less Encumbrance. Ich-n-Erred, the Hero's Salmon Leap (Str): a standing high jump of up to four times one's height, less half Encumbrance. Ochtarchless, the Eight-Men Feat (Sta): +5 Strength to lift or bear a weight, held while the rolls keep succeeding. Rothchless, the Wheel Feat (Str): hurl what one could not normally throw, such as a chariot wheel, its Load as its damage. Tétchless, the Rope Feat (Dex, Ease Factor 3 and up for unstable, moving or sloping footing): balance on anything smaller than a foot, and soften falls.

Concentration. Cless for Análaib, the Breath Feat (Sta): hold one's breath for minutes, or +3 to a precise task after three rounds of preparing. Corpchless, the Body Feat (Dex, 6, 9 or 12): dislocate joints to slip shackles or squeeze through small gaps, and +3 to break a grapple. Sáebchless Díberge, the Wild Feat of Contortion (Qik): bend the body unnaturally for +3 to trips, disarms and the like, or to resist them. Siaburchles, the Phantom Feat (Qik): give no defence and let a blow pass through a body made partly insubstantial, never two rounds running.

Single Weapon (or Great Weapon, chosen at Initiation). Béim Co Commus, the Stroke of Precision (Dex): harmless feats of exactness with a blade, such as trimming a beard in a fight. Brúd nGeme, the Crushing Roar (Sta): a hit that damages the foe's weapon, harder against fine or enchanted ones. Fáenchless, the Sloped Shield Feat (Str): with an Irish edged shield, turn a winning parry into a glancing attack. Foramchles, the Swooping Feat (Sta): a leaping swing that ruins the armour on one location.

Thrown Weapon. Cless Cletenach, the Javelin Feat (Dex): one javelin drives another for a 15-pace range increment and doubled damage. Cless Nónbair, the Nine-Men Feat (Str): up to nine javelins at one target at once. Torannchless, the Thunder Feat (Str): a sling stone to the head, with a thunderclap, that knocks the foe down. Ubullchless, the Apple Feat (Dex): juggle up to nine stones in one hand, loading a sling without pause or throwing three a round.

Magi: seven Redcaps, none Gifted: Dáire Cú, five of his sons and daughters (Dáire an Chogaidh the eldest, Elen Bhodhar the youngest) and a nephew. No season is given.

Story seed: A Rival School. Some Redcaps resent that only Leth Cuinn teaches the clesa, and mean to quest into Arcadia for one or all of Scáthach's sons to found a rival school. Characters refused initiation may be recruited by them, or friends of the Mercer House asked to stop them.
covenants.summary:
The northern Mercer House, on the north-eastern shore of Lough Neagh where the Slighe Mhidhluachra bends west for Doire. Like Leth Moga, its southern partner, it is not a covenant at law: it has no cathach and needs no cattle, for the Peripheral Code itself guarantees it, and it bears no device the book records. Its Redcaps serve the covenants of the northern half of the Tribunal, chiefly on three High Roads: an tSlighe Mhór, the Slighe Assail and the Slighe Mhidhluachra.

Where Leth Moga keeps records, Leth Cuinn is warlike: it trains warriors and heroic Redcaps, and since 1029 it has been an outpost of the Cult of Heroes, run by Dáire Farranta's descendants and home to Úathach, the only living teacher of the clesrada. It is built like a king's hall, a bold gesture in the Earl of Ulster's lands, hidden from chance discovery by The Shrouded Glen; on the parade ground before it up to a dozen men at a time drill at gymnastics, weapons and feats of strength and endurance.

Leaning: Irish in sentiment. House Mercere is neutral by custom, but its leader despises the English-friendly bookishness of Leth Moga, and his heir, Dáire an Chogaidh, hates the English and has even voted at Tribunal.
covenants.what_matters:
Income: the Peripheral Code's guarantee and the Tribunal's covenants, which pay for Initiation into the clesrada
Services: Initiation into the clesrada for Redcaps, grogs and companions; the training of covenants' warriors
Price of Initiation: longevity rituals for the Tribunal's Redcaps, three years' casting of the Aegis of the Hearth and The Shrouded Glen (Leth Cuinn gives the vis and the casting tablets), or enchantments for its Redcaps
Library: none described; the clesrada are taught in person by Úathach
Boon: Veteran Fighters (a large turb trained in the clesrada)
Boon: Mystical Allies (Úathach, a faerie of the Tuatha Dé)
Boon: Hidden Ways (The Shrouded Glen hides the hall)
Hook: Mercer House
Hook: Superiors (House Mercere's primus may answer Dáire an Chogaidh's vote)
Hook: Rival (Leth Moga, whose leader Dáire Cú scorns)
Tension: Dáire an Chogaidh's votes against the House's neutrality
Tension: the Earl of Ulster's lands all round a king's hall

covenants.name: Qui Sonant Pro Quieto
covenants.notes:
History. Druids have always sung the giant to sleep here, and the site was already old, and already a burial ground of Ireland's magical powers, when the Order came. When those druids joined the Order a covenant formed round them, and Ireland's magi have laid their dead here from then on. The book gives no founding year. In the Schism War many magi and their heroic companions were brought here; the list of who was buried was lost after the war, though the Vitae Magna in Hibernian libraries still mention them. Some say Qui Sonant buried the three Diedne who fell at Clontarf each beside the Hermetic rival who would most have hated it.

The cathach. A finely made rope of silver hung with balls of purest gold, long enough to go three times round a body, said to be the necklace of Caer Ibormeith, wife of Aengus of the Tuatha Dé. It hangs on the arch over the courtyard gate, just outside the Aegis of the Hearth. Wound round a target, it shields it from every effect of a Magic aura; here that lifts the block on Arcane Connections, so a body wrapped in it can be used to call back its spirit.

The giant. If the songs end, or the giant is disturbed, the tales say it will wake and leave Ireland, taking its magic with it. Every apprentice trained here learns the songs by heart, as do magi who join later. Opinions differ on what it is, why it sleeps and what its waking would bring; the favourite answers today are a Fomóir or Finn MacCumhaill himself, and the truth may never be known.

The chantry. A plain stone building from which unaccompanied chant rises day and night. To a stranger it sounds like any church's, but the songs praise the heroes of myth, lull the giant and remember the dead nearby. By custom no magic is worked inside, and it is lit only by candles renewed through the day. The choir, magi and covenfolk together, is a dozen or so strong; two open cloisters join the chantry to the rest.

The Hermetic cemetery. The covenant tends the dead, burying them where the aura keeps their spirits from being summoned, and as a courtesy gives the same rites to the Coill Trí's druids, the elder races and supernatural creatures. Magi of the Ordo Hiberniae who feel death coming visit to arrange their burial, so the covenant is on good terms with nearly every covenant in Hibernia; the exceptions are mostly newcomers from abroad, who find the custom unChristian and needless and dislike honouring hedge wizards like magi. Hibernia's few Tremere keep their own House's burial customs. Irish burial has long looked odd to foreigners (Saint Ciarán of Clonmacnoise had his bones laid bare on a hillside like a stag's, perhaps a custom of the Aran Isles), and for the Ordo Hiberniae, burial here is a cultural choice: the last rites save the soul, and the spirit rests while its wisdom stays within reach.

Neutral ground. Every beast and people of Hibernia's supernatural realms honours the neutrality of Qui Sonant's lands, and the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh makes them a haven for all. Some say that but for this sanctuary every native wizard would have died in Diedne's hunt, and many a foolish Wizard War has ended in a treaty agreed here. So Qui Sonant gives an aegis token to anyone in need. Meadhbh, Praesis's fallen leader, is in sanctuary here.

Consulting the spirits. Anyone who would speak with the dead petitions the covenant, which asks the ambassador of the spirit's power, or the praeco for a magus. If they agree, the tomb is opened, the body and grave goods brought to a casting space inside, the body wound in the cathach to shield it from the aura (and its realm interaction bonuses and penalties), and a ritual invites the spirit back. Every spell of Qui Sonant is closely guarded; lab texts and casting tablets for the rites are in the inner library and are not shown to visitors.

The funerary rites. A magus's body is first fixed as an Arcane Connection to his spirit, by the ordinary laboratory action. It is laid in a cairn among whatever grave goods his covenant gives and sealed with an enchanted capstone that wards it against weather, man and beast, with a hidden trigger that suspends the ward when the body is needed; further enchantments keep the body from rotting. Qui Sonant meets any other wish a magus has.

Covenfolk. No soldiers: the covenfolk are good Irishmen, handy with an axe. All must sing in the chant, and all know Organization Lore: Order of Hermes and Latin. For all the hard weather and grim work they want for little, and on holidays the magi give feasts and gifts of clothes, shoes, tools and utensils.

Magi: seven, each owing the covenant one season's work a year. Cantarus, Master of the Songs, Finn, Lewis and Turlough are described.

Story seed: Three Diedne Bodies. No one knows what became of the three Diedne who fell at Clontarf. Cliffheart claims one as its cathach, though it fought nowhere near the battle; others say Qui Sonant buried each in the grave of a Hermetic rival, and none had Christian burial. Hibernia has no law against digging into its Diedne past, and a Seeker who wants to question a Diedne ghost may ask the characters' help.

Story seed: The Body of a Ghost. Envoys of a covenant ask to speak with a member buried some fifty years ago, but the summoning fails: someone has destroyed the spirit. Did someone at Qui Sonant break that trust, and what are they hiding?
covenants.summary:
A covenant on a ridge high in the Cuailnge mountains, where legend says the giant Finn MacCumhaill is cursed to sleep for as long as song is heard above him; its magi see that the songs never stop. It is also the last resting place of Ireland's magi, hedge wizards and even faeries and magical beasts, and a great chantry where magi and covenfolk sing without end for the souls of the fallen.

Its device is a silver rope hung with balls of gold along its length; its cathach is the necklace it pictures, the huge gold and silver necklace of Caer Ibormeith. Leaning: the Ordo Hiberniae, and neutral ground for all; the English newcomers find its customs unChristian.

Low stone buildings stand outside a large walled manor round a cobbled courtyard, holding sanctums, libraries and the chantry; the craftsmen's workshops lie outside the wall.
covenants.what_matters:
Services: burial of magi, hedge wizards, faeries and magical beasts, with tombs that keep the body whole
Services: summoning the spirits of the buried, by leave of the praeco or the spirit's ambassador
Services: aegis tokens for all in need, and neutral ground for ending Wizard Wars
Library: the inner library of funerary rites and summonings, closed to visitors
Duty: each magus gives the covenant a season a year (estates, research into the dead, leading the songs)
Boon: Aura (Magic 7)
Boon: Prestige (neutral ground recognised by every power of Ireland)
Boon: Difficult Access (treacherous mountain tracks)
Hook: Ceremonies (the songs must never stop)
Hook: Sanctuary (Meadhbh of Praesis and any in need)
Hook: Monster (the giant sleeping under the ridge)
Hook: Harsh winters
Tension: Cantarus has no heir he trusts, and Finn assumes he is it
Tension: Lewis's exiled rival Peter is about to widen their feud
Tension: the English call the aegis tokens reckless, an opening for the Infernal
covenants.secrets:
Turlough of Criamon, who keeps the cemetery and the spirits, wants more from the dead than summoning them, and hides his growing interest from his sodales; any help he gets must come from outside, and he would trade his favour with the Coill Trí for it.
Should a magus appear who would commit himself to the covenant, Cantarus would happily pass Finn over and make that magus Master of the Songs.

covenants.name: Vigil
covenants.notes:
History. House Diedne founded the first Vigil in the Sperrin foothills, winning its standing by hunting down the great black pig whose ditches later guarded old Ulster from the south and taking its tusks. Viking rune-smiths from Dublin raided it in 830; it recovered and for a time helped other covenants against those invaders, until Ireland's Diedne, Vigil among them, withdrew from the Tribunal's affairs in 851. With the Diedne gone from Ireland's defence, a band of Merinita sacked Vigil, carried the tusks to the far north and raised a fortress there, the new Vigil, with a great unseen tower from whose top all Ireland could be seen, and used it to find and cut off the rune wizards and their Vikings. The book gives no year for the refounding.

Fighting the vengeful Diedne and the rune wizards at once, Vigil made alliances with the faeries and beasts of the northern sea, which still guard the north coast against magical invasion; the treaties between the Order and the Coill Trí record them, and no druid outside the Order may deal with the creatures of the northern seas. In 980, unwilling to see Teamhrach fall to Olaf Cuaran, king of Dublin and Northumberland, Vigil used magic to seal a treaty of Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill with the Leinster and Ulster kings and fought beside them to rout the Norse; the Tribunal let the interference go as vital to its own sanctity.

When the Schism War came Vigil struck fast at its old enemies, taking Diedne heads as trophies, plundering their laboratories and libraries and killing their familiars. Afterwards it used the Diedne threat to prove its worth, and its magi went abroad to learn new magic for Ireland's defence; few came back, sending instead accounts of their travels, strange spells and devices won from foreign magi, while the vaults filled with curios and Vigil dined on its past. For two hundred years it has sunk into decadence and sloth, trading on a fame centuries stale, yet sure it is all that stands between Hibernia and its enemies.

The cathach. The curled tusks, six feet from root to tip, hang over a great arched gate in the covenant's wall under faerie guard, and travel to Tribunal in an ornate wooden case. They tint Faerie auras so that they pass on a Personality Trait of Protecting Ireland +3, and turn Magic auras toward magic that guards Ireland from invasion.

Culture. Vigil lives by conspicuous consumption, as its old Merinita did, who fought hard, traded vis to Verditius for arms and armour against the Vikings and the Diedne, and won more by conquest. Its magi love loud pleasures: hunting, certamen, raiding the country round, and above all baiting young magi in their macgnímartha. Yet they keep the old treaties, the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh most of all, and guard every old custom of the Tribunal fiercely. They are urged to marry for comfort, not politics, and to share their Parma Magica with their wives against The Gift; to bind a familiar and make a talisman early; visitors with neither are teased, kindly. Each spins long tales of danger, adventure and love with himself as the hero, puffing up his familiar or his talisman, and there is a purpose to it: all of Vigil's magi know the Merinita Folk Mysteries, whose magic feeds on such symbols. Máel-ruanaid is their mystagogue.

Its magi excel at music, etiquette and every pastime of the privileged. Every apprentice learns Charm Magic, and though none must stay, a bond of magic ties members together. Fiercely loyal to Ireland and Hibernia and its traditions.

Covenfolk. Vigil's excess reaches its people too: well dressed, well fed, rather too familiar at the frequent feasts. Its warriors, the Two Dozen Men of Mhálanna, are trained in the clesrada, used to magic, armed and armoured in faerie gear forged in past wars, deadly and fiercely loyal to Vigil and above all to Gráinne. They spend most of their time keeping a Fachan king and his Fer Caille off Mhálanna.

Magi: six, and two apprentices soon to set out on their macgnímartha. Éinri, Gráinne, Máel-ruanaid and Maoilfhinnéin are described. The founding year is not given (the Merinita took the tusks soon after 851).

The drowned library, from the Infernal chapter: casting tablets and laboratory texts against Infernal sickness and foul weather, from the years when Vigil watched the north for demon-sent hardship and fought the demons behind it. The Infernal has lain quiet long enough for Vigil to sink into idleness, and the texts lie untouched in the flooded vaults under the lost fortress. Hermetic annals mention them, so a covenant struck by an Infernal winter or plague may come to Vigil asking for them.
covenants.summary:
The covenant that keeps watch over Hibernia, guarding Ireland against any who mean her people harm; or so it once did. Those days are long past, and Vigil has grown fat and idle on old glory. Its halls and homesteads, each in its own ringfort with a magus, his household and his sanctum, are spread across Cionn Mhálanna on Inis Eóghain.

Its device is a pair of huge boar's tusks curving viciously from root to tip; its cathach is the tusks themselves, those of the immense magical black pig. Leaning: the Ordo Hiberniae, traditionalist and decadent; the English are welcome in its halls so long as they keep the customs and do not try to change them.

A Merinita covenant, though a half-forgotten treaty with House Verditius lets a magus of that House claim one laboratory here.
covenants.what_matters:
Income: an endless supply of silver; Éinri's herds and bees (honey among Hibernia's best)
Library: the drowned vaults, with anti-Infernal lab texts and casting tablets, rotting and forgotten
Treasure: uncatalogued curios, magical weapons and devices from abroad in the vaults, in Gráinne's keeping
Site: Banbha's Crown, a spire in a three-level Faerie regio that sees all Ireland
Treaty: the beasts of the northern coast belong to Vigil's Order alone (Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh)
Claim: Aileach, which Vigil will defend with certamen and Wizard War
Boon: Aura (Faerie, at each hall)
Boon: Regio (Banbha's Crown)
Boon: Mystical Allies (the faeries and beasts of the northern sea)
Boon: Veteran Fighters (the Two Dozen Men of Mhálanna)
Boon: Wealth
Hook: Faerie Court (faerie kings all along the coast)
Hook: Monster (a Fachan king and his Fer Caille warriors)
Hook: Rights and Customs (the Verditius right to a laboratory)
Hook: Crumbling (the old fortress abandoned, the vaults drowned)
Tension: Éinri's feud with Dalton Ballaugh of Lámbaird
Tension: Gráinne and Guillaume of Praesis, and Maoilfhinnéin's plan for her
covenants.secrets:
The drowned vaults hold forgotten magical weapons and devices from far lands and a library against Infernal plague and winters; covenants struck by such troubles may come asking for it.
No one recorded what turned Vigil's Merinita against the Diedne; those who know how demons work may wonder.
Maoilfhinnéin expects the Ordo Hiberniae to be driven back as the native wizards once were, and has readied Inishtrahull to take the cathach and a rebuilt Vigil; he is courting Lámbaird, feeding Gráinne's overconfidence because a sacrifice may be needed, and steering the shards of her first talisman, now an Arcane Connection to her, toward Guillaume of Praesis.

covenants.name: Praesis
covenants.notes:
History. Praesis was founded where Connacht meets Meath, not long after the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh, as a meeting place for the Order and Connacht's hedge wizards. Within a century that purpose was nearly forgotten and its standing was already falling. Its druid allies, later the Pact of Oireadh, left Meadhbh when her demands outgrew their friendship.

The siege. In spring 1213 Praesis took in, warily, a foreigner from the continent, Holzner of Tytalus. He stole the cathach and fled; his sodales caught and killed him, and Meadhbh hung his head by the hair from the palisade. His parens Ballack came from the Rhine for justice and, arguing that if the Tribunal would not punish Praesis it must be taken by force, declared Wizard War and struck. Praesis held. From the eastern shore Ballack's people stripped its vis sources and killed anyone going in or out, which kept Praesis from the Tribunal of 1214, where it might have found allies. For a full year of stalemate mercenaries and several young magi on both sides died while the covenants of Hibernia argued; magic and men were evenly matched, but Ballack's nerve lasted longer. As Praesis's last allies fled, Báetáin Ua Traimair made terms: the Gáe Bulg for Meadhbh's safe passage. She took sanctuary at Qui Sonant Pro Quieto, and Ballack has held Praesis since. Not all the besiegers were foreign; some were sons of old Irish lines who saw the war as a blow against centuries of tradition. The new tower was raised by Hermetic ritual.

The cathach in 1221. Praesis did not show its cathach at the Tribunal of 1214. Ballack has now held the Gáe Bulg for years, well beyond the year a thief must keep a cathach, but whether a cathach given up as the price of a truce may be presented by the men who besieged its covenant, and whether the Wizard War that won it should be challenged, are both open questions for the next meeting; its new masters expect no trouble.

Covenfolk: barely any yet beyond the conquerors' own servants, except Guillaume's turb of Bréifne mercenaries, who serve him for good pay and plenty of food, fighting, drink and women, and whom the country round has learned to dread. Oscar von Harz, a white-haired man of giant's blood, fearless and wholly loyal to Ballack, guards the Gáe Bulg, standing on a wooden platform that looks toward Meath with the spear held out as a dare; by custom it is kept outside the Aegis of the Hearth.

Six magi live here, four of them named, and two apprentices; one is the apprentice Guillaume took with the cathach of an independent magus. The book gives no founding year: 855 is assumed, soon after the Treaty was signed in 851.

Story seed: Remember Who You Work For. A player character who has joined a cult or society is ordered to carry a message to Ballack, who has been forgetting what he owes certain powerful, mysterious benefactors (see Ballack's Debts). Can a younger magus bring the society's authority to bear on him?
covenants.summary:
A winter covenant in a stone tower on a wooded island in Lough Ree, between Connacht and Meath. Its device is a spear made of thigh bones with a skeletal hand. Once the shining proof of friendship between the Order and the druids of Ireland, it was left to its fate by the Tribunal and taken in a year's siege by Ballack of Tytalus and the foreign magi with him; it now leans to the English. Some see in it the danger of outsiders, others proof that Hibernia must change, and its new masters must somehow drag it out of its winter.

Its cathach is the Gáe Bulg, a spear of the thigh bones of the monstrous witch Coinchenn, whom Art son of Conn killed, tipped with her clawed right hand. When it pierces a target the hand clamps on bone or gut and will not let go until the victim dies. Whoever holds it gains the Death Prophecy Virtue; each prophecy differs, but every one begins with the spear being lost. The witch was hideous and cruel, her daughter lovely and good: foreseeing that she would die on the day her daughter was won, she kept the girl close and set the heads of suitors on the stakes round her house.

The tower is cold and bare; from almost every window the ruined laboratories of the siege can be seen. A council meets weekly to track where Meadhbh and her friends are and what they intend, and to keep the defences ready in case they come back. Holzner's head still hangs from the palisade where Meadhbh put it. For two seasons Guillaume has been telling the others of promising sites his spies have found over the Connacht border, and the shifting crowd of foreign magi newly come to Hibernia who stay here is looking west with growing interest.

The country round shuns it: the villages of both shores serve it only grudgingly, and anyone tied to Praesis counts as Infamous, with a bad Reputation of 4. Mundanes will not help, and the Coill Trí warn hedge wizards against it.
covenants.what_matters:
Cathach: the Gáe Bulg, held by Ballack's Praesis since the siege
Vis: the covenant's own sources round the island and the lake, stripped bare by Ballack's besiegers and slow to recover
Vis (contested): sources over the Connacht border that Guillaume's Bréifne mercenaries seek out and raid
Income: none yet; Ballack lives on vis and casting tablets borrowed from distant benefactors, and needs the covenant to pay its way soon
Right: by the Treaty, its members may enter Connacht in pursuit of Hermetic justice, at Manannán mac Lir's express request, or to find bees for their hives
Library: no books are named; what the fire and the siege left is unknown
Boon: Island (a wooded island in Lough Ree, beyond Voice range of both shores)
Boon: Regio (Minor) (the tower and the spear stand in a warded regio)
Boon: Veteran Fighters (Guillaume's turb of Bréifne mercenaries)
Hook: Infamous (the villages of Lough Ree fear its people)
Hook: Indebted (Major) (Ballack's debts of vis and favours)
Hook: Crumbling (the ruins of the old tower and laboratories)
Hook: Death Prophecies (the Gáe Bulg)
Hook: Rival (Major) (Meadhbh and the magi who fled with her)
Hook: Hermetic Politics (the extended Wizard War, and whether the Gáe Bulg may be shown in 1221)
Tension: Báetáin shares the tower with Guillaume, who burnt the people he grew up among
Tension: Guillaume's raids into Connacht could break the Treaty for everyone
covenants.secrets:
The tower and the spear stand in a regio, out of mortal sight, warded and guarded by magic: the platform the world sees is not where the spear truly is.
Oscar has seen his own death through the Gáe Bulg. No one knows what he saw; since taking the spear he has been studying the legends of the Fir Bolg.
Ballack's distant benefactors are a powerful cult or society he does not belong to but took help from; they may soon send someone to remind him of what he owes.

tribunals.name: The Hibernian Tribunal
tribunals.summary:
The Tribunal of the whole island of Ireland, on the western rim of Mythic Europe: five provinces, Connacht, Leinster, Munster, Ulster and Meath at the centre, where tribal kingdoms under hereditary Irish kings share the land with English lords who have seized much of it since the invasion of 1169 and 1170. The Order came in 778 and was ruled from Britannia for a time, then left in 898 to stand on its own; its Code took shape in the ninth century and has barely changed since. Hibernia has no domus magna, and most of the Order thinks it backward and odd.

A Tribunal of conflict. Tytalus and Merinita magi founded it, and its customs reward rivalry: Wizard War is easy to declare, certamen is common, grogs raid rival covenants, and a covenant that cannot hold its land is thought unworthy of it. The art is to dominate, not to kill. The deepest split is between the native magi, who call themselves the Ordo Hiberniae, and the continental newcomers they call the English, who have come over the last fifty years to claim land and reform the Code. The fall of Praesis to the English in a year-long Wizard War is the question every magus now turns on.

Covenants and their cathaigh. A covenant is recognised by the Praeco once it has held land, cattle and a cathach, a storied magical trophy it took rather than made, for a year, and its name is entered at Leth Moga. It votes only while it brings the cathach to the meeting. There are nine covenants and two Mercer Houses, Leth Moga in the south and Leth Cuinn in the north, which are not covenants at law. A magus who lives outside a covenant is a vagrant with no vote. Dozens of covenants have fallen over the centuries, so a new one can rarely be sited with fewer than a dozen ruins within a day's ride.

The meeting. Every seven years the magi gather on Meath's Hill of Tara, Cnoc na Teamhrach, in the great ráth round the Lia Fáil. The last meeting was in 1214, which Praesis, under siege, could not attend, so the next is in 1221; the book gives no season, so summer is assumed. Circulus Ruber arranges each one and raises a camp by magic for the seven days and nights it lasts: hearths smoking, banners, servants and familiars everywhere, a fire pit and food kept by each covenant, bards wandering between them and fine weather held by spells. Covenants bring all the consortes and custodes they can, to look strong. Business is done in Latin, but Irish is what is heard between sessions. Indrechtach of the Paruchia, a Hermetic member of the Céli Dé, opens and closes the meeting with prayers and blessings.

The Sacred Council. Before the meeting opens, the Praeco, the Presiding Quaesitor and invited magi meet the embassies of the hedge wizards, the faeries and the magical beasts, hear their quarrels, and confirm each faction's ambassador. Those ambassadors hold a voting sigil for the meeting and their votes count as any magus's: Fothaid for the Fir Bolg, Ainid for the Fomórach, the Eagle King for the beasts of magic, Mug Ruith for the Tuatha Dé, and an ambassador the Coill Trí choose. House Merinita speaks for faeries who send no one. The English have argued against these votes at every meeting since they came.

The English Council. The magi not born to Hibernia meet on their own at the start of each meeting to agree a common line, usually on reforming the Code, and lately on the aggression of Lámbaird. They find agreement hard and lack a leader able to see past Praesis.

Customs. Bees matter to an Irish covenant, each covenant's honey tastes of its own place, and the magi trade jars of it at every meeting, which the continental magi find quaint. The Ordo Hiberniae wear patchwork mantles by rank: an apprentice one colour, one in the macgnímartha three, a magus five, a covenant's head six and the Praeco seven; the newcomers dress as at home. Irish magi call House Ex Miscellanea the Younger House, since it was the last formed, and its newly arrived members dislike it. Irish glosses in Hermetic books cost a reader who has no Irish the usual +1 for quality. The Ordo loves Vitae Magorum, lives of great magi written as Order of Hermes Lore, and the Hermetic Computus, Artes Liberales tractatus for reckoning durations, moons and laboratory work. Vis is left where it lies until it is needed, so few covenants keep much in store, and many sources are made casting places.

The macgnímartha. Between apprenticeship and the Oath a young Irish magus spends a year or so on 'youthful exploits', away from the parens and outside the Code, without the Parma Magica. Most test themselves against faeries, some against mundanes or other magi, and what they steal from covenants is usually ransomed back. The treaty with the Coill Trí is silent about them, so they often slip into Connacht. Each comes back with a Reputation of 1 for how they behaved, and some choose a year of service at Leth Moga instead.

The officers. The Praeco is Milvia of House Bonisagus, of Circulus Ruber, aged 164, who has held the office for the last four meetings; Visioturpis of House Guernicus, Hibernia's oldest Quaesitor, also of Circulus Ruber, presides. Conán Derg of Merinita, the eldest magus, gave up the office in 1186 after losing an arm. Hibernia keeps few hoplites: every covenant is expected to defend itself and lend its strength to the Tribunal.

Stories. The book frames the saga as change coming to Hibernia: the English magi mean to remake the Tribunal and the Ordo Hiberniae means to keep it, and the characters may drive the change, soften it or fight it. Under way in 1220 are Guillaume's push into Connacht from Praesis, the test of the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh at Tara in 1221, and the English reform motions. Others wait for the storyguide to begin them: Maoilfhinnéin's plot against Gráinne, Ballack's debts, Donn's army, the Gaileoin infernalists, the giant under Qui Sonant, Áillen burning Tara, the Conspiracy of Mellifont and the Pact of Oireadh's Parma. Four private feuds run between magi, and the book's smaller story seeds sit on the places and covenants they use.

cases.title: The extended Wizard War against Praesis
cases.brought_by: (not yet brought: magi of the Ordo Hiberniae and others)
cases.charge: Ballack besieged Praesis for a year under the Hibernian rule that a Wizard War runs on until death, surrender or treaty, and took it when Báetáin gave up the cathach for Meadhbh's safe conduct. For most of the English it was the first such War they had seen. Opinion is divided on whether to lodge a formal challenge, and the Tribunal may be asked whether the War was lawfully waged and whether Meadhbh, in sanctuary at Qui Sonant, has any claim left.

cases.title: May Praesis's new masters show the Gáe Bulg?
cases.charge: Praesis did not attend the meeting of 1214, being under siege, and did not show its cathach. Its new masters have held the Gáe Bulg since about 1215, longer than the year a thief must keep a cathach to claim a covenant's resources, and expect no trouble presenting it; but it came to them by a bargain at the end of the siege, not by holding it against the old masters, and those who back Meadhbh may say Praesis has no right to sit.

cases.title: The test of the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh
cases.brought_by: English magi, with some Irish magi who covet Connacht
cases.charge: Successive Tribunals have treated the Treaty as binding without ever putting it to the vote, and any move to question it is shouted down. The English say hedge wizards are given rights here that no other Tribunal would allow and that mock a Code made for Hermetic magi; some Irish magi have long eyed Connacht too. The day it is formally tested is close.

cases.title: Reforming the Peripheral Code
cases.brought_by: Helles of Tytalus (Ashenrise), for the English Council
cases.charge: Helles moves at every meeting to bring the Code up to date: general laws in place of private treaties, an end to the Treaty's privileges, and continental practice on vis and Wizard War. He has made little headway. In return the Irish magi lay charges of High Crimes against him and his sodales at every meeting, which he spends his seasons glossing the Code to answer.

cases.title: The ambassadors' votes
cases.against: The ambassadors of the Sacred Council
cases.charge: Since they arrived the English have argued at every meeting that giving the votes of faeries, giants and beasts the same weight as a magus's is unlawful and beneath the Order.

cases.title: Lámbaird and the Normans
cases.brought_by: (not yet brought: English magi suspect it)
cases.charge:
The English Council is growing worried by Lámbaird's open hostility, and its raids against English interests are suspected. The Tribunal reprimanded it in 1193 but found nothing to sanction.

Secrets
Lámbaird's magi do lend magic to the Wicklow clans resisting the English, and leave no witnesses. If proved, it is plain interference with mundanes.

cases.title: The Ua Cathail against Elk's Run
cases.brought_by: The Ua Cathail of the Cenél Áeda na hEchtge (expected)
cases.charge: The Ua Cathail resent the English magi of Elk's Run and the help they give their rivals the Uí Sheachnasaigh, who serve the covenant, and may soon complain to the Tribunal of interference. Lugardis is working against it. The other covenants may take the complaint up, though that is unlikely: the charge would need to show that the magi's meddling put their sodales in danger.

cases.title: Guillaume's raids into Connacht
cases.brought_by: (not yet brought: the Coill Trí, through their ambassador)
cases.charge: Guillaume has not crossed into Connacht himself, but for two seasons his Bréifne mercenaries have been finding and stripping vis sources there while he briefs Praesis's foreign guests on what his spies have found. The Treaty makes the Coill Trí masters of their own places and promises them justice.

cases.title: Igneous Drake's killings
cases.brought_by: (not yet brought: the Coill Trí, or the Irish covenants)
cases.charge: Igneous burns raiders caught inside his ring of fire, macgnímartha among them, along with Ua Cathail bandits and any hedge wizard who annoys him outside Connacht, thinking the Tribunal enforces no law between magi. Killing a hedge wizard without declaring War is assaulting the Order's allies, and he has lately begun declaring War on Irish magi he thinks have slighted Elk's Run.

cases.title: Faolán in Connacht
cases.brought_by: (not yet brought: the Tribunal, once it learns where he is)
cases.charge: Faolán fled into Connacht before Praesis fell and has stayed far beyond the three nights the Treaty allows a magus, which no member of the Coill Trí can waive. He thinks himself nearer to the druids than to the Order. When the Tribunal finds out, it will want him fetched back.

cases.title: A Redcap who votes
cases.against: Dáire an Chogaidh of Mercere (Leth Cuinn)
cases.charge: Dáire an Chogaidh, heir to Leth Cuinn, hates all things English since fighting de Courcy in his macgnímartha, and has voted at Tribunal, against his House's custom of neutrality. It has made him famous, and his House's Primus is said to be preparing an answer.

cases.title: Who maimed Conán Derg?
cases.charge: Two months after the meeting of 1186, Conán Derg was set upon while walking alone near Connacht and had his right arm cut off at the shoulder. He would not have it regrown, saying a leader must be whole, and gave up the office of Praeco. Some magi think Faisgia waylaid him, since it happened where she often travels; he neither confirms nor denies it, and she laughs at the idea.

cases.title: Access to the Red Book of Cloyne
cases.brought_by: Magi who want its records as evidence
cases.charge: The Tribunal upheld Diarmait's claim that the Red Book is his own, under his sanctum marker, though the Redcaps' testimony may be called. Several magi still dislike the ruling. Diarmait himself now thinks the book should be seen, though never copied, so a motion to open it may find him willing.

rulings.title: The Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh
rulings.says: At its first meeting as a Tribunal of its own, Hibernia made the Treaty with the hedge wizards of Connacht binding, with every private treaty then standing between a druid and a magus. Most of the Code is made of treaties like it: particular bargains between named parties, not general rules, so a Munster case of 1134 need not decide a like case in 1220. The English call this unworkable and ask for change at every meeting. Its clauses are on the Treaties list.

rulings.title: Treaties
rulings.says: Anyone with the right to be heard at Tribunal may make a treaty: a magus, a covenant, the Order, the Tuatha Dé, the Coill Trí and so on. A treaty may be for a time, for ever, or until a stated condition frees the parties. The parties reach it themselves with a Quaesitor's help, and the Tribunal's part is to see that they agree. No treaty may break the Code or bind a magus against the Oath. A hedge wizard who wants a treaty or a hearing needs the Coill Trí to sponsor him, and faeries and beasts treat only through their ambassador.

rulings.title: Founding a covenant
rulings.says: Any magus may found a covenant by proving land, wealth and a cathach: a place to live that the magi have defended for a year, cattle (Ireland's old measure of wealth), and the trophy. Once all three have been held a year the covenant asks the Praeco to recognise it, its name and lands are written down at Leth Moga, and the Redcaps begin to call. Others may try to take the cathach in that year, and if they do the covenant cannot form; they must keep to the Code and may harm no resident without Wizard War.

rulings.title: The cathach
rulings.says: A cathach must answer to Intellego Vim as magical, though not necessarily Hermetic; it must have been taken, from the land, the magic realm or another magus, and how it was won becomes part of the covenant's story; it must be storied, legendary itself or made by a famous hand; and it must be shown at each meeting and be kept outside the Aegis of the Hearth between them. The custom goes back to the four founders of Circulus Ruber, who swore to hold their land and its treasures for a year. Great families keep cathaigh too.

rulings.title: Holding another's cathach
rulings.says: A magus found with a cathach another covenant justly claims is treated as if caught in a sanctum and loses his immunity, and the same holds for its cattle. A thief who means to claim the robbed covenant's resources must keep the cathach a year against all comers.
