Stealing every cathach could leave the meeting without a quorum, though magi without one can still be heard through allies who kept theirs.

rulings.title: Representation and votes
rulings.says: No magus is represented without his covenant, and no covenant without its cathach, which must be carried to the meeting and kept on show. A magus whose covenant shows it has one vote and may lend it as a proxy as elsewhere.

rulings.title: Residency and vagrants
rulings.says: A magus is resident, and votes, only through a recognised covenant. One outside any covenant is a vagrant, however long he has lived in Ireland: no Redcaps call, he has no voice, his property has no protection, and he may be exiled. Many solitary magi live so all the same; to vote, one must found a covenant of one, with land, cattle and a cathach.

rulings.title: No chapter houses or vassals
rulings.says: Hibernia recognises neither chapter houses nor liege and vassal covenants. A magus who would leave his covenant must join or found another, or give up the Tribunal's protection.

rulings.title: A covenant's lands
rulings.says: A covenant's lawful lands are its vis sources: all those a magus can walk round between sunrise and sunset, using no spell or enchanted device to go faster. Raiding them is depriving a magus of his magical power. Everything outside is common land: a covenant may mark a source there with its symbol, but must defend it itself, and certamen is often fought over such sources.

rulings.title: Forfeiting immunity
rulings.says: Slaying a magus outside Wizard War is a High Crime, with the usual defences. A magus forfeits his immunity by trying to take an apprentice from a covenant, taking a cathach, entering a sanctum, attacking a familiar, or raiding a covenant's protected vis.

rulings.title: Declaring Wizard War
rulings.says: War is declared in person, in public and before witnesses, though not necessarily to its target, and it starts a month later; no letter of warning is needed. A declaration kept from its target on purpose has been ruled void. One declaration may name several enemies, and draw in the allies of either side, as in a war on 'Meadhbh and all who hold to the Gáe Bulg'.

rulings.title: Extended Wizard War
rulings.says: No pause is required between months of War, and the Code presumes a War extended unless it is shown otherwise, so it lasts until one side dies, yields or makes a treaty. Most such Wars sink into raids and theft, fought by grogs and hired men, until someone calls a truce; submission is the aim more often than death.

rulings.title: Certamen
rulings.says: The aggressor names the Technique and the defender the Form, as the Definitive Edition already has it; the Hibernian custom is that neither may veto the other's choice, and nothing limits who may challenge, when, or how often. Refusing a challenge shames a magus as anywhere, but using vis in a duel carries no stigma.

rulings.title: The ambassadors
rulings.says: The Tribunal holds itself the magical authority over all Ireland, so each recognised supernatural faction may send a voting ambassador, confirmed at the Sacred Council and given a sigil for the meeting; its vote counts as any magus's. The Tuatha Dé confirm theirs at the Council; the Fomórach and the Fir Bolg send royal kin; other faeries may send one or be spoken for by House Merinita; beasts of magic who speak and understand men may choose one, or a magus stands for them. The Infernal has never tested this right.

rulings.title: Speaking creatures
rulings.says: A creature that speaks any human tongue counts as a man and may be represented at Tribunal: no covenant should harm it or take from its territory without leave or a fair return. Even the Ordo Hiberniae keeps this loosely.

rulings.title: Allies of the Order
rulings.says: The Fomórach, the Tuatha Dé, the Fir Bolg and, by the Treaty, the Coill Trí are the Order's allies, and must be warned of Wizard War as a magus would be, so they can make terms first. A hedge wizard too must be declared on before he is attacked; killing one without it is assaulting the Order's allies. Magi who declared War on 'all hedge wizards' have been talked into letting it lapse.

rulings.title: The rights of hedge wizards
rulings.says: A hedge wizard may claim one protected vis source; any others he uses are common land. Redcaps must carry the Order's messages to the Coill Trí as to any covenant, but visits to single hedge wizards are a courtesy. A hedge wizard may ask a covenant to take him in, and is then expected to swear the Oath and join the Younger House.

rulings.title: Mundane interference
rulings.says: Hibernia's Quaesitors take the Transitionalist view: in so small a Tribunal, with magi born among the people and kings long used to asking druids for counsel, dealings with mundanes cannot be helped. A charge of interference must show that the Order was put in danger.

rulings.title: Guarding the auras
rulings.says: Magic and Faerie auras, often tied to great events of Irish history, are in the Order's keeping. Defending one against mundanes who would spoil or destroy it, or punishing them for it, is not interference, and the Tribunal backs a strong hand. Drawing vis out of an aura is frowned on as bad husbandry.

rulings.title: Scrying
rulings.says: A scrying charge carries a heavy burden: without clear signs of magical spying found by a trustworthy witness, the Tribunal requires that the knowledge could not have been had without magic. Most magi accept some scrying as unavoidable and settle it privately.

rulings.title: The Presiding Quaesitor's veto
rulings.says: The Presiding Quaesitor may set aside a decision only when it plainly conflicts with any reasonable reading of the Oath or the Code, which leaves Hibernia room to read the Code in its own way. Magvillus has reviewed the Hibernian Code many times, before and after the English came, and each time found its oddities lawful.

rulings.title: Apprentices and the macgnímartha
rulings.says: One in the macgnímartha is outside the Code and no longer the parens's charge. A Bonisagus who wants another's apprentice must claim the child at a Tribunal, when the Coill Trí or the parens first present them or at a later meeting, before the macgnímartha begins.

rulings.title: Exile
rulings.says: In place of casting a magus out of his House or the Order, Hibernia exiles him: he must leave the island or be Marched. An exile may ask to return if a resident magus will stand surety and plead for him; the Tribunal decides by free vote. A magus who flees overseas while under judgment has exiled himself, and must come back by the next meeting or be cast out of the Order.

rulings.title: Sanctions, naidm and ráth
rulings.says: Like Irish law, which avoids putting men to death, the Tribunal seldom calls a March or takes a familiar or talisman; it wants redress for the injured and better conduct, through fines, duties, restrictions and exile. A naidm is named to see the penalty paid, and those close to the offender, his covenant, parens and filii, stand surety (ráth), paying or suffering in his place if he defaults. A fine is rarely raw vis: more often the injured party is given use of the offender's vis source for a term.

rulings.title: Trafficking with demons
rulings.says: The only crime the Tribunal answers with a March as a matter of course. When the Oath's call to slay a magus is invoked, it is carried out in earnest, though Hibernian justice stops at the shore.

rulings.title: Censuring creatures and the Coill Trí
rulings.says: A faerie or beast that sets the mundane world against the Order is punished as the case deserves: faeries have been chained, beasts driven from their haunts for a time or put to a covenant's service, and once a creature was bound into servitude, a sanction few want repeated. Members of the Coill Trí, who have no Code, are judged case by case and may be made to serve, pay vis each season for a year, or keep out of a district, and their ambassador must see the judgment met.

rulings.title: The Mercer Houses
rulings.says: Leth Moga and Leth Cuinn are not covenants: they keep no cathach, need no cattle, and stand because they serve the Tribunal, under many rulings of the Code that guarantee them.

rulings.title: The Red Book of Cloyne
rulings.says: When magi asked in the twelfth century to use the Red Book as testimony, Diarmait of Leth Moga agreed that each Redcap's own witness may be called, but the book, which he inherited from his parens, is his own and lies under his sanctum marker. The Tribunal upheld this, and several magi resent it.

rulings.title: Revoke the Protection of Bonisagus
rulings.says: Enchanting the effect into a device that anyone may use, or whose effect never runs out, is forbidden, lest it fall into the wrong hands. Casting the spell on a conscious magus outside Wizard War or a March may be taken as the first step of a killing.

rulings.title: The Battle of Teamhrach
rulings.says: Vigil was not punished for magically securing an alliance of Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill with the kings of Leinster and Ulster against Olaf Cuaran of Dublin, nor for fighting beside them to drive the Norse from Tara: keeping Teamhrach from the northmen was held vital to the Tribunal's sanctity, though it was plain interference.

rulings.title: Ashenrise's cathach
rulings.says: While the hall was in uproar and magi were declaring War on the newcomers, the Praeco Conán Derg accepted the dug-up corpse of Rhiannon, a former Prima of Merinita, as Ashenrise's cathach: against those who said it was no magical treasure, he ruled that the raw vis grown in its bones made it one.

rulings.title: Lámbaird reprimanded
rulings.says: Lámbaird's magi, suspected of helping the Wicklow clans against the English by magic, were reprimanded by the Tribunal but not sanctioned, since nothing tied the Order to the raids.

rulings.title: The Grand Tribunal and Damisona
rulings.says: At Durenmar the Grand Tribunal heard a long debate on whether Hibernia needed a Code modelled on Stonehenge's, against those who held a Tribunal free to set its own. Those whose apprentices, in their macgnímartha, had attacked Damisona of Jerbiton's party in 1190 and killed three grogs were found guilty only of a Low Crime, to Stonehenge's outrage.

diary.title: Patrick's mission
diary.details: The old tales tell of five peoples who took Ireland one after another (Cessair's, Partholón's, Nemed's, the Fir Bolg and the Tuatha Dé) before the Sons of Míl, the Gaels, won it for good and the Tuatha Dé went under the hills. Palladius's mission had already failed when Patrick, once a slave of Irish raiders, comes back to preach. He goes round the island from Leinster to Connacht, Ulster, Meath and Munster, outdoes the druids in a contest of wonders and drives them out, banishes the snakes and turns the people Christian; he lies today in Down Cathedral. (The book says only the fifth century, and that the sources disagree; 432 is the year tradition gives.)

diary.title: Patrick baptises Eóghan at Aileach
diary.details: At Aileach, Patrick baptises Eóghan son of Niall, from whom the Cenél nEóghain of Tír Eóghain descend.

diary.title: Brigid's abbey at Kildare; the Uí Enechglaiss driven to Arklow
diary.details: In the last years of the century Saint Brigid founds a double house of monks and nuns at Cill Dara and lights the fire that has burned there ever since. In Meath the ruling Uí Enechglaiss are driven south to Arklow, and the Uí Mael Sechlainn, the southern Uí Néill, take the land and give Ireland several high-kings. Saint Aebh's monastery is founded at Antrim about the same time. (The book says only the late fifth century.)

diary.title: Ciarán dies at Clonmacnoise
diary.details: Saint Ciarán, a founder of many monasteries, dies of the yellow plague at Clonmacnoise, his greatest house. (The book puts it early in the sixth century; the plague of Justinian came in the 540s.)

diary.title: Comgall founds Bangor
diary.details: Saint Comgall founds the abbey of Beannchor Mór, around which the town of Bangor grows.

diary.title: Ruadán curses Tara
diary.details: Saint Ruadán, wronged by King Diarmait, foretells that the king will die in his own hall at Tara; the high-kings' seat begins its long decline. (The book says only the sixth century.)

diary.title: The Battle of Tola
diary.details: The Ulaidh beat the Osraighe at Tola, the first of the defeats that wear down the kingdom of Ossory.

diary.title: Four magi come treasure-hunting
diary.details:
Two Tytalus and two Merinita magae come looking for the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé. With a local ward-maker they dig a cauldron out of a mound at the Brú na Bóinne and take it for the Dagda's. The high-king sends his druid and a warband against the grave robbers; the five hold a barrow against three days of assaults, and, true to their leader's boast, stay on the mound for a whole year.

Secrets
The cauldron is not the Dagda's but the Cauldron of Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid, which raises a dead warrior to fight for one more day.

diary.title: Circulus Ruber founded
diary.details: The four magae move to the Burren and raise a tower by magic on Hag's Head, among the Cliffs of Moher, vowing to hold it for a year. Local wizards and their kin fight hard to be rid of them, but with allies from the Rhine and Iberia the newcomers hold, and at the Tribunal of this year the covenant is founded, named for the red wards their helper drew. By the decade's end eight magi live there.

diary.title: Diedne comes to Ireland
diary.details: Diedne arrives seeking the druids for her House, and the chief druid Sechnassach, offended by a choice of joining or dying, sends her away. She leaves with threats he does not take seriously.

diary.title: The first Ostmen raids
diary.details: Norse and Danish raiders begin to fall on the monasteries without warning, at first only in spring and summer. Within a generation they stay, turning the coastal trading posts into the towns of Dublin, Waterford, Wexford, Cork and Limerick, and they bring rune wizards with them. (The book says only the late eighth century.)

diary.title: Diedne's pogrom begins
diary.details: Twenty-seven Diedne magi land near Wexford and split into three bands of nine to hunt the druids, offering each the same choice; most choose death. Quendalon (Cuin-dallán), an Ulsterman of House Merinita, comes home from the Rhine to save what he can: some of the old wizards he takes into his House, others he hides in Connacht. Meanwhile the Diedne found covenants of their own and dig in. In the midst of the purge the druid Raghallach meets Petrifer of House Flambeau, attacks him on learning he is a magus, and is won over to the Order instead.

diary.title: Qui Sonant Pro Quieto founded
diary.details: The druids who sing the giant to sleep in the Cuailnge mountains, at a place already old and already a burial ground for Ireland's magical powers, join the Order, and the covenant grows up around them. Ever since, Hibernia's magi have been laid to rest there. (The book gives no year, only that the druids joined the Order after the magi came.)

diary.title: Diedne and Pralix quarrel at Lough Cuan
diary.details: Pralix, chasing followers of Damhan-Allaidh, meets Diedne on the shore of Lough Cuan. Diedne expects help with her purge; Pralix wants to recruit the druids without forcing them. Their argument becomes an illegal Wizard War that neither ever charges, and Nendrum monastery on Machaoi island is left in ruins, no one knows by which of them. About twenty of Ireland's stronger native wizards fight for Pralix against Damhan-Allaidh, and the survivors join her new order, the root of House Ex Miscellanea.

diary.title: Diedne boasts the druids are gone
diary.details: After almost fifteen years of killing, Diedne tells the Tribunal that not one druid is left in Ireland. It is an exaggeration, but the old tradition is broken. (The history chapter counts seventeen years of pogrom from 793.)

diary.title: Lámbaird founded
diary.details: Petrifer and Raghallach of House Flambeau turn their camp in the Wicklow Mountains, a refuge for Raghallach's tradition, into the covenant of Lámbaird. Diedne's complaints at Tribunal fail, so she makes Wizard War on the druids in House Flambeau; only Raghallach and two others live to found the school of magical combat that bears his name.

diary.title: Rune wizards raid the Diedne Vigil
diary.details: Runesmiths from Dublin raid Vigil, then a Diedne covenant in the Sperrin foothills whose magi won their standing by killing the great black pig and keeping its tusks. Vigil recovers and helps defend other covenants against the northmen's wizards.

diary.title: The Order of Odin
diary.details: At the Grand Tribunal, Hibernia's magi name the Ostmen's wizards "the Order of Odin." Unsure of their strength, the Order looks for peace: Máel-tuili of House Merinita meets the Dublin rune wizards and offers a large tribute, but they fall on his party and kill most of it, Máel-tuili among them. Skirmishes with rune wizards, raids on native druids and certamen in reprisal become the custom of the age.

diary.title: The high-king's embassy
diary.details: Cormacan the Learned, Chief Bard of Ireland, brings an embassy from the high-king: his subjects, hedge wizards, complain of the Order's harassment. The Mercere Fedelmid Ua Heirméais is chosen to treat for the Order, and since Diedne's pogrom has shown that the Irish would rather die than join, he looks for another way. (The book names the high-king Congalach Cnogba, who in history reigned a century later.)

diary.title: Diedne withdraws; the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh
diary.details: On the brink of open war over peace with the Coill Trí, Primus Obregon declares that the Diedne will no longer shield their unworthy sodales, and Hibernia's Diedne shut themselves in their covenants. In their absence the other magi sign the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh. The Diedne never accept it and keep entering Connacht, so hedge wizards seek out magi as personal protectors, one to one, on the model of amici.

diary.title: Merinita take Vigil north
diary.details: With House Diedne gone from the Tribunal's affairs, a band of Merinita magi sacks the Diedne Vigil and carries the boar's tusks to the far north, where they raise a new fortress and an unseen tower from which all Ireland can be watched, to hunt the rune wizards and their warriors. Fighting the Diedne and the northmen at once, Vigil makes pacts with the faeries and beasts of the northern sea that guard the coast to this day. (The book says only after 851.)

diary.title: Praesis founded
diary.details: Praesis is raised on an island in Lough Ree, on the border of Connacht and Meath, as a meeting place between the Order and the Coill Trí. Within a century its purpose is mostly forgotten and its standing on the wane. (The book says only soon after the Treaty.)

diary.title: Hibernia made part of Britannia
diary.details: At the Grand Tribunal Hibernia's magi complain of raiders from England and Scotland, and are told their treaty with the hedge wizards is illegal. Ireland is joined to England and Scotland in the new Britannian Tribunal under its Peripheral Code, and the Irish plea that the Treaty alone keeps the native traditions alive is refused.

diary.title: The Hibernian Tribunal; the Treaty ratified
diary.details: Following the Tytalus lead, the Irish magi leave the Britannian Tribunal. The first Hibernian Tribunal ratifies the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh and holds every private treaty between magus and hedge wizard binding; those who flouted them are brought to heel. The hedge wizards of Connacht are gathered into the Comman Cosán Chían, soon called the Coill Trí, and those who quarrel with magi over resources are helped, or pushed, to move there. The same meeting gives rise to the two Mercer Houses: the Redcap Imag, wife of the abbot of Cloyne, is granted the southern house of Leth Moga and begins the Red Book of Cloyne, and Leth Cuinn is founded on Lough Neagh. Treaties, trophies and lawful raiding enter the Code as an outlet for the island's violence.

diary.title: Clonmacnoise's stone cathedral
diary.details: The high-king builds the stone cathedral at Clonmacnoise.

diary.title: Mathgamain slain
diary.details: Mathgamain mac Cennétig, who won Cashel and Limerick for the Dál gCais, is killed, leaving his brother Brian Bóramha sole king of Munster.

diary.title: The Battle of Teamhrach
diary.details: Olaf Cuaran, king of Dublin and Northumberland, threatens Tara. Vigil magically binds the kings of Leinster and Ulster in a pact with Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill, then fights beside his army to rout the northmen and open the way to Dublin. The Tribunal lets this interference go unpunished, holding Tara's sanctity at stake.

diary.title: A pestilence out of Tír Chonaill
diary.details: Another of the great plagues born in Tír Chonaill sweeps Ireland, and the annals tell of demons dancing among the dead.

diary.title: Brian Bóramha high-king
diary.details: Having beaten Munster's and Leinster's ruling clans, Brian marches into Ulster and the Uí Néill high-king gives up the title to him. Druids and hedge wizards of Munster march with his army, and the magi watch him so closely that the Schism War takes them by surprise.

diary.title: The Schism War: the Widow's Throat falls
diary.details: Of the Tribunal's six Diedne covenants, three prove empty, their magi fled abroad or gathered in the other three, and the Hibernian magi split their forces against them. The Diedne have allies ready: Salmon's Eye in Munster has Donn, and the Widow's Throat in Ulster has a Fomóir fleet, five ships of which sail up the Shannon while five fall on Circulus Ruber. The magi regroup to save Circulus Ruber and beat the fleet at sea, then destroy the Widow's Throat; two months later their first attack on Lugh's Retreat, at the Shannon's source in the Dartry Mountains, fails. Vigil strikes its old enemies hard, taking heads, libraries and familiars, and Lámbaird draws Flambeau from abroad to fight, earning the name "Lombard." (The book gives no years for these battles, only that they come before Clontarf.)

diary.title: The Schism War: Warbler's Way and Salmon's Eye
diary.details: The Munster Diedne and Donn's host destroy Warbler's Way, a Merinita covenant in the woods by Lough Leane. The magi unite to answer, raze Salmon's Eye and drive Donn back to his island. So many dead are brought to Qui Sonant in these years that the record of who lies there is lost. (The book gives no year.)

diary.title: The Third Battle of Moytirra
diary.details: Two years after the first assault the magi move on Lugh's Retreat again, joined this time by the druids and hedge wizards of Connacht, whom Mercere messengers had warned. Together they destroy it, killing Fomóir and Diedne alike. The poets call it the Third Battle of Moytirra. (The book gives no year.)

diary.title: Clontarf
diary.details:
Brian Bóramha marches on the Ostmen of Dublin. His dwarf druid, Muírcheartach mac Lía, warns Lámbaird's magi that druids calling themselves sons of Diedne ride with the army, and the Flambeau go to the battle. On Good Friday, while Irish and Ostmen fight at Clontarf, they hunt the Diedne down in a short and blazing duel that ends the House in Hibernia. The Ostmen are beaten for good, but Brian dies on the field and his army goes home too weak to rule the island. No one knows what became of the three Diedne bodies: Cliffheart says one is its cathach, and some say Qui Sonant buried each beside a rival.

Secrets
Cliffheart's cathach is a Diedne magus turned to a standing stone, alive only while the spell holds; the magi renew it every year, since its ending would kill him at once.

diary.title: Cliffheart founded
diary.details: Three Merinita survivors of Warbler's Way, who fought the Diedne for their alliance with Munster's Tuatha Dé, settle on Cape Clear Island and found Cliffheart. (The book says only after Clontarf.)

diary.title: The Red Book closed
diary.details: Fergal mac Cuircc of Leth Moga, having set down the Schism War in the Red Book of Cloyne, closes it to all but Redcaps so that the magi may forget their war; he goes on recording. (The book says only after the Schism War.)

diary.title: The Ostmen thrown out of Cork
diary.details: Raiding Ostmen winter at Cork; an Uí Briain and mac Cárthaigh army storms the walls while its druids blast the earthworks with lightning, and Cork becomes the one Irish town to cast the Ostmen out.

diary.title: Dáire Farranta takes Leth Cuinn
diary.details: Back after seven years away, Dáire Farranta challenges his parens, the leader of Leth Cuinn, to Wizard War and wins with no spell cast, by feats of the clesrada. He exiles the other Redcaps, fills the house with his own kin and the faerie Úathach who taught him, and makes it an outpost of the Cult of Heroes, which his descendants still run.

diary.title: The Rogh Rámhach
diary.details: A plague called the Rogh Rámhach is said to kill a quarter of Ireland.

diary.title: The Scuab a Fánait foretold
diary.details: A pestilence is prophesied to come out of the north of Tír Chonaill. It never does.

diary.title: Aileach broken
diary.details: The King of Munster breaks the power of Aileach in Tír Eóghain.

diary.title: Dún Bhun na Gaillimhe built
diary.details: Tairrdelbach Uí Conchobhair builds a fort above Loch Lurgain as a naval base; Munster's kings destroy it in 1132 and again in 1149.

diary.title: Malachy archbishop of Armagh; Kildare's abbess deposed
diary.details: Máel Máedóc, later Saint Malachy, becomes Archbishop of Armagh and sets about reforming a lax church. Diarmait Mac Murchada removes the abbess of Kildare and gives the post to his niece.

diary.title: Cong Abbey rebuilt
diary.details: Cong Abbey, burned early in the century, is rebuilt. (The book says about 1135.)

diary.title: Malachy goes to Down
diary.details: Malachy resigns Armagh to become Bishop of Down, ruling from Bangor and bringing Augustinian canons to Downpatrick.

diary.title: Mellifont founded
diary.details: Malachy founds Mellifont, near Drogheda, on land from the King of Meath; it becomes mother of most of Ireland's Cistercian houses. He also founds the Augustinian abbey of Saint Mary at Trim.

diary.title: Newry and Cahir
diary.details: Cistercians rebuild the old monastery at Newry, and a town grows up around it. Conchovor Uí Briain builds Cahir castle.

diary.title: Malachy dies; Baltinglass founded
diary.details: Saint Malachy dies. Diarmait mac Murchadha founds a Cistercian house at Baltinglass with monks from Mellifont, and the place is called the Valley of Salvation.

diary.title: The Synod of Kells; Derbforgaill taken
diary.details: The Synod of Kells ratifies Malachy's reforms and divides Ireland into thirty-six sees under four archbishops, at Armagh, Cashel, Dublin and Tuam; Kildare's abbess is put under the bishop. Diarmait Mac Murchada, King of Leinster, carries off Derbforgaill, wife of Tighearnán Ua Ruairc of Bréifne, the Irish Helen, who is content to stay with him.

diary.title: A King of Meath deposed by Mellifont
diary.details: At the abbot of Mellifont's urging, a synod excommunicates and exiles Donnchadh Ua Maeleachlainn, King of Meath, and makes his brother Diarmaid king.

diary.title: Laudabiliter
diary.details: Pope Adrian's bull Laudabiliter, later read as granting Henry II the right to take Ireland and reform its church.

diary.title: Elk's Run founded
diary.details: Oswald of Bonisagus and Lugardis of Guernicus arrive from abroad with cattle, silver, unknown vis sources and the antlers of a giant elk, and claim a valley in the Slieve Aughty. Irish magi challenge the cathach and the vis; Oswald wagers for all he can ride round before sunset without a spell, throws down the antlers, and rides the living elk they become over the mountains until dusk. Elk's Run is founded. (The history chapter places it just after the Grand Tribunal of 1195; this pack follows the Munster chapter's 1159.)

diary.title: Derry's Great Church; the Nun's Church
diary.details: Tempull Mór is finished at Doire. Derbforgaill endows the Nun's Church at Clonmacnoise. Domnall Mac Giolla Phádraig founds a Benedictine house for Saint Nicholas's relics where Jerpoint now stands; it fails.

diary.title: The Mac Diarmaids turn the druids away
diary.details: From this year the Mac Diarmaids, patrons of Boyle, keep no druid at their court.

diary.title: A castle at Tuam
diary.details: The Uí Conchobhair build a castle at Tuam to tighten their hold on Connacht.

diary.title: Diarmait exiled
diary.details: Tighearnán Ua Ruairc invades Leinster, Ossory rises, and Diarmait Mac Murchada loses his throne and flees to England. Henry II will not invade for him, so he hires English mercenaries, while the new high-king, Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, takes Leinster.

diary.title: A gathering at Tlachtga; Christchurch Augustinian
diary.details: Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair musters a great host at the Hill of Tlachtga, but Tlachtga does not show herself. Lorcán Ua Túathal makes Christchurch in Dublin an Augustinian priory.

diary.title: The English land
diary.details: Diarmait and Robert FitzStephen besiege Wexford, which the Bishop of Ferns persuades to open its gates, and win the Pass of Achad-ur from the Osraighe with a Norman cavalry charge.

diary.title: Strongbow
diary.details: Strongbow, Earl of Pembroke, invades Leinster, puts Diarmait back on his throne and marries his daughter Aoife. The conquest stirs the Order's interest in Hibernia for the first time in a long while, House Tremere first among them.

diary.title: Diarmait dies; Henry II comes
diary.details: Diarmait dies and Strongbow takes Leinster, against Brehon law. Henry II comes to bring his vassal to heel, takes Dublin, Wexford and Wicklow for the crown, receives the Irish kings' tribute and has a synod called at Cashel. The English close the abbey of Kildare when its last abbess dies. Tighearnán Ua Ruairc parleys with Hugh de Lacy on Tlachtga and is killed, by murder or mishap. (History puts his death in 1172.)

diary.title: Meath granted to Hugh de Lacy
diary.details: The last King of Meath is deposed and his kingdom granted to Hugh de Lacy; the Uí Mael Sechlainn settle near Clonmacnoise. Henry II sails for France from Wexford, leaving its mills to the Templars. Bishop Tuathal Ua Connachtaig of Kells swears fealty to Henry, to much anger.

diary.title: Limerick burned
diary.details: Domnall Mór Uí Briain burns Limerick rather than let the English have it.

diary.title: The Treaty of Windsor
diary.details: Ruaidhri Uí Conchobhair, unable to stop the English, seeks the Fir Bolg kings on Árainn Mhór, who give him Fionntan's counsel. On 6 October he signs the Treaty of Windsor, owning Henry as ruler of Ireland and keeping Connacht for a yearly tribute still paid.

diary.title: De Courcy takes Ulster
diary.details: John de Courcy, granted Ulster if he can win it, marches with twenty-two knights and some three hundred men and takes Down by surprise on 1 February. The King of Ulster, laid low by Macha's Birth-Pangs, returns with an army a week later and is routed, and de Courcy soon holds all the land east of the Bann. He sacks the abbey of Erenagh and builds castles at Belfast and Carrickfergus. Cork, held back from the English by mac Cárthaigh, is granted to Robert FitzStephen and Milo de Cogan, who take it by force.

diary.title: Inch, Dundrum and Jerpoint
diary.details: De Courcy founds the Cistercian abbey on Iniscourcy in penance for Erenagh and builds Dundrum castle. Donogh O'Donoghoe, king of the Osraighe, founds Jerpoint Abbey. Work begins on Clonfert's cathedral, where a magical mason's arch draws beasts of every realm to watch.

diary.title: The Temple House at Ballymote
diary.details: The Templars build Connacht's only Temple House near Ballymote, close to the Bréifne border.

diary.title: Down's cathedral priory
diary.details: De Courcy founds a Benedictine cathedral priory at Downpatrick with monks from Chester.

diary.title: Tuam's cathedral burns
diary.details: Tuam's cathedral burns down; it has not been rebuilt.

diary.title: Prince John, Lord of Ireland; Ruaidrí abdicates
diary.details: Henry II makes his son John Lord of Ireland. John, seventeen, mocks the Irish kings who come to do him homage and pulls their beards. Gerald of Wales comes with him, and his books on the marvels of Ireland stir Stonehenge's magi to talk of reform. Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair gives up the high-kingship and retires to Cong. Aed Meith Ua Néill seizes Tír Eóghain from Aileach. Work begins on Saint Flannan's cathedral at Killaloe. Using minstrels, Helles and Pollices persuade Raymond le Gros that the Uí Riain plan rebellion and, in the fighting, take Rhiannon's body from their chief's ráth. (The book gives no year for the theft.)

diary.title: The Tribunal of 1186: Ashenrise's cathach
diary.details: Helles and Pollices, refugees from Normandy's fallen Moles Magna, with three sodales from Stonehenge, present the dancing corpse of Rhiannon, a former Prima of House Merinita, at Tara and announce their covenant, to live as guests in a FitzGerald knight's castle. The hall erupts and Wizard Wars are declared, but Conán Derg, then praeco, accepts it, ruling that the raw vis grown in its bones makes it magical enough. Hugh de Lacy dies, and Walter de Lacy will take Meath. A church council at Dublin, called at Prince John's wish, shows how far English reform means to go.

diary.title: Conán Derg maimed
diary.details: Two months after the Tribunal, walking alone on the Connacht border, Conán Derg loses his right arm to an attacker. Refusing to regrow it, he holds that a leader must be whole, gives up the office of praeco and leaves Hermetic politics. Some magi suspect Faisgia of Cliffheart, who often travels there; Conán Derg will neither confirm nor deny it, and Faisgia scorns the charge.

diary.title: Ashenrise recognised
diary.details: Helles and Pollices hold Rhiannon's corpse for a year against all comers, and Ashenrise is a covenant at law. It has pressed for reform of the Code ever since.

diary.title: The Paruchia of Nerius
diary.details: Fedelmid of Limerick, who saw visions of the magus-saint Nerius in an Alpine valley on pilgrimage to Rome, with his apprentice Indrechtach and Indrechtach's own pupil, brings a tiny tradition of the Céli Dé into House Ex Miscellanea and founds a monastery and covenant on the Saltee islands.

diary.title: Damisona attacked; Dublin burns
diary.details: Damisona of Jerbiton and her party are set upon by what seem to be young Irish magi, and three grogs die. Knowing nothing of the macgnímartha, Stonehenge cries out for something to be done about Hibernia. A great fire wrecks Dublin, and settlers from Bristol and Wales take the place of those who leave.

diary.title: The Tribunal of 1193: Lámbaird reprimanded
diary.details: Lámbaird's secret help to the Wicklow clans against the English is noticed, and the Tribunal reprimands the covenant without a sanction. Milvia of Bonisagus presides as praeco, as she has at every meeting since. Geoffrey fitz Robert founds Saint Mary's priory at Kells in Ossory.

diary.title: Limerick falls to the English; Drogheda's charter
diary.details: Domnall Mór Uí Briain dies, and the English take Limerick and most of its lands. Drogheda-in-Meath receives its charter.

diary.title: The Grand Tribunal at Durenmar
diary.details: Magi who want Hibernia reformed under a Code like Stonehenge's debate long against those who uphold a Tribunal's right to its own; Milvia leads the Hibernian delegation. The parentes of the apprentices who attacked Damisona in their macgnímartha are found guilty only of a Low Crime, to Stonehenge's fury. Traffic with the continent and appeals to Magvillus grow. William Marshal builds his castle at Kilkenny.

diary.title: De Courcy beats Tír Chonaill
diary.details: De Courcy defeats the King of Tír Chonaill and takes tribute from his land.

diary.title: Limerick chartered
diary.details: Limerick receives its charter and is given to Philip de Braose.

diary.title: Ruaidrí dies; de Courcy's revenge
diary.details: Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, the last High-King, dies at Cong and is buried at Clonmacnoise. After his brother is murdered at his court, de Courcy harries the north of Ulster and destroys Raphoe's cathedral. Archbishop John Comyns orders Saint Patrick's Cathedral built in Dublin.

diary.title: King John; Lismore's bishop returns
diary.details: John becomes King of England, to de Courcy's ruin (the book dates his accession to 1201). Desmond gives up its long sieges of Cork. When the English Bishop of Waterford, who had seized Lismore and driven out Bishop Felix, dies, Felix goes home, and the long quarrel of Waterford and Lismore begins.

diary.title: King John's Castle; Temple Melaghlin
diary.details: King John's Castle rises on King's Island in Limerick. The Uí Mael Sechlainn build Temple Melaghlin at Clonmacnoise.

diary.title: Mayo dissolved; Ossory's cathedral moved
diary.details: A papal legate dissolves the diocese of Mayo into Tuam, against its clergy's will. Bishop Felix O'Dulany moves Ossory's see to Kilkenny and begins a stone cathedral, dying the same year.

diary.title: De Courcy overthrown; Cong attacked
diary.details: Allied with Cathal Crobhdearg of Connacht, de Courcy is taken in rebellion by Hugh de Lacy, younger son of the Lord of Meath. William de Burgh attacks Cong Abbey, deep in Connacht.

diary.title: Dublin Castle; Malachy back at Lismore
diary.details: King John orders a castle built at Dublin. Bishop Malachy of Lismore, who escaped Waterford's prison and was restored by Innocent III, comes home to find his rival Robert dead.

diary.title: Hugh de Lacy, Earl of Ulster
diary.details: In May King John makes Hugh de Lacy the first Earl of Ulster, with all the lands de Courcy held.

diary.title: The Liberty of Kildare
diary.details: King John creates the Liberty of Kildare to crush the deposed Uí Dúnlainge, and summons the nobles to Naas to submit.

diary.title: Charters for Kilkenny and New Ross; Bishop David killed
diary.details: Kilkenny and New Ross receive royal charters. Malachy, driven from Lismore again by the Welsh Bishop David of Waterford and confirmed again at Rome, returns to find David murdered.

diary.title: Plague in Dublin
diary.details: A terrible plague kills many in Dublin.

diary.title: Black Monday; Swan of Ghent killed
diary.details: On Easter Monday the Ua Broin and Ua Túathal fall on English settlers at their sport outside Dublin's walls and kill three hundred. The maga Swan of Ghent dies among them. Dublin still marks the day under arms.

diary.title: Munster granted; Waterford's new bishop
diary.details: King John grants Munster to his favourites, keeping Waterford, Limerick and Cork: the lands north of Waterford to Robert le Poer, Thomond to Philip de Braose, Desmond to Robert FitzStephen and Milo de Cogan, none of whom can take them. Kerry becomes a shire. Robert II is consecrated Bishop of Waterford, seizes Malachy, and has him tortured; no court dares convict him. John de Gray, the justiciar, builds a stone castle at Athlone, now Walter de Lacy's. (The book says ten years before 1220.)

diary.title: Kilmore castle
diary.details: Walter de Lacy builds a motte and bailey at Kilmore, one of many for a push into Connacht. Geoffrey fitz Robert dies a hostage of William Marshal at Hereford.

diary.title: Holzner at Praesis
diary.details: Praesis, wary of foreigners, accepts Holzner of Tytalus from the Rhine. He tries to steal the covenant's cathach, the Gáe Bulg, and flee, and is caught and executed; Meadhbh, its leader, hangs his head by the hair from the palisade. His parens Ballack leaves the Rhine for Hibernia, persuades others that if the Tribunal will not punish Praesis they must take it by force, and declares Wizard War. (The Connacht chapter puts the theft two years after his arrival.)

diary.title: The Siege of Praesis; the Tribunal of 1214
diary.details: Repulsed by a covenant stronger than it looked, Ballack's forces camp on Lough Ree's eastern shore, strip Praesis's vis sources and kill anyone who goes in or out. The siege keeps Praesis from the Tribunal at Tara, where it might have found allies; few intervene, since the Code allows the war, and the Tribunal debates while mercenaries and young magi on both sides die. At the same meeting Oswald of Elk's Run is granted a second, Irish-born apprentice. The mac Cárthaighs massacre Uí Súilleabháin nobles at a peace feast at Raheen, and within the year Desmond falls to a war between two mac Cárthaigh brothers. Glendalough's diocese is folded into Dublin's.

diary.title: Praesis falls
diary.details:
After four seasons of stalemate Ballack's nerve outlasts the defenders'. As the last of Praesis's allies flee, Báetáin Ua Traimair trades the cathach for Meadhbh's safe passage, and Ballack takes the covenant; Meadhbh claims sanctuary at Qui Sonant. The druids of Oireadh, once Praesis's friends, had already left Meadhbh over her demands. William Marshal the younger loses his wife.

Secrets
Ballack has spent everything he had on the war and borrows vis and casting tablets from distant, powerful benefactors whose debts he is beginning to forget.

diary.title: The Conspiracy of Mellifont; King John dies
diary.details: A visitation from Cîteaux arrives to restore the Rule in Ireland, and Mellifont shuts its gates on it. Innocent III confirms the end of the diocese of Mayo. King John dies; his young son Henry III succeeds, and Waterford's bishop loses his protector, ending the Lismore quarrel for now.

diary.title: Abbot Thomas deposed; the itinerant justices
diary.details: The Cistercian general chapter deposes Thomas, abbot of Mellifont, in name only: backed by his monks and daughter houses, he stays. Itinerant justices begin riding the Liberties to hold English assizes. Dublin pays the royal tallage.

diary.title: The Chief Bard dies
diary.details: Giolla Ernain Ua Martain, Chief Bard of Ireland, dies, and no successor has been chosen. Boyle's abbey church is consecrated. Ailbe Ua Mail Mhuaidh, Bishop of Ferns, writes a life of Saint Abbán.

diary.title: William Marshal dies; Cashel goes to Rome
diary.details:
William Marshal dies, and his son William the younger takes up the regency. The Archbishop of Cashel leaves for Rome to plead the Irish clergy's case against the bar on Irish-born bishops.

Secrets
The Pope has ruled the policy against Rome's will; the archbishop will be home with the order to drop it in August 1220, and word has not yet reached Henry de Londres.

diary.title: Henry de Londres vows to quench Brigid's fire
diary.details: Archbishop Henry de Londres, viceroy in Dublin, declares he will put out Saint Brigid's sacred fire at Kildare to prove it a superstition, a blow at the Uí Dúnlainge whose patroness she is.

circulus_ruber.cathach: a magic cauldron, thought to be the Dagda's

cliffheart.cathach: a Diedne magus turned into a standing stone

elk_s_run.cathach: the antlers of a giant Irish elk, which Oswald can bring to life

ashenrise.cathach: the enchanted dancing corpse of Rhiannon, once Prima of House Merinita

l_mbaird.cathach: the silver arm of the bard Cairpre, worn by a covenfolk bearer

the_paruchia_of_nerius.cathach: the skeletal arm of Saint Nerius, a relic with three Faith Points

qui_sonant_pro_quieto.cathach: Caer Ibormeith's great gold and silver necklace

vigil.cathach: the tusks of the great black boar that dug the Black Pig's Dyke

praesis.cathach: The Gáe Bulg, a spear of the witch Coinchenn's thigh bones and clawed hand

treaties.title: The Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh
treaties.parties: The Order of Hermes in Hibernia and the Coill Trí
treaties.witness: Negotiated by Fedelmid Ua Heirméais of Mercere
treaties.ends: Never by one party alone; a clause is added when a Tribunal votes it and every ceannaire agrees
treaties.terms:
Made after High-King Congalach Cnogba's embassy of 844, brought by the Chief Bard Cormacan, on behalf of hedge wizards harried by the Order; signed in 851 once the Diedne had withdrawn, refused by the Diedne, rejected by the Grand Tribunal of 865, and made binding at Hibernia's first meeting in 898. It is named for Connacht's highest mountain, and its terms apply 'between druids and magi', not to lesser hedge wizards. Druids can change it only through a magus who proposes it for them.

1. The Order founds no covenant in Connacht, and no magus spends more than three nights running under a Connacht sky or roof.
2. The Coill Trí give the Order seven Gifted children at each Tribunal.
3. The Coill Trí have the right to be heard at Tribunal, their grievances are considered, and the Order does not deny them justice.
4. The Coill Trí are masters of their own places; the Order is master of all others.
5. The lands of Qui Sonant Pro Quieto are a safe haven for everyone.
6. Magical places outside Connacht are in the Order's protection until the Order gives that charge back.
7. The Coill Trí may use the beasts of the coast as they wish, save those of Vigil, which are the Order's alone.
8. Members of Praesis may enter Connacht for three reasons only: to pursue Hermetic justice, when Manannán mac Lir expressly asks it, and to find bees for their hives.
9. No magus or druid alone may set aside a clause: a magus invited into Connacht by a druid must still leave after three days.

treaties.title: The surrender of Praesis
treaties.parties: Ballack of Tytalus; Báetáin Ua Traimair for Praesis
treaties.ends: Fulfilled when the cathach changed hands
treaties.terms: As the last of Praesis's allies fled, Báetáin bargained with Ballack: the Gáe Bulg, Praesis's cathach, in return for safe passage for Meadhbh, who went into sanctuary at Qui Sonant. Ballack has held Praesis since.

treaties.title: Vigil's laboratory for House Verditius
treaties.ends: No end is given; the treaty is largely forgotten
treaties.terms: A member of House Verditius may claim one laboratory at Vigil, a Merinita covenant. It dates from the days when Vigil's magi traded vis to Verditius crafters.

neighbours.name: Ireland
neighbours.summary:
Mythic Ireland, the whole island and the Hibernian Tribunal's region, steeped in magic: enchanted lakes and woods, faerie hosts, hags, giants, beasts that speak, saints who take vengeance and demons. Its five provinces are Connacht in the west, Leinster in the east, Munster in the south, Ulster in the north and Meath between them; the Eiscir Riada splits it into Leth Cuinn, Conn's Half, to the north and Leth Moga, Mogha's Half, to the south, and the two Mercer Houses are named for them.

The English came in 1169 and 1170 and their settlers live mostly in the south-east; Irish kings rule the rest, and no one is strong enough to keep the peace, so lords raid one another and make and break alliances as it suits them. The Lord of Ireland is King Henry III of England, aged 14, whose regent is William Marshal the younger, his father having died in 1219.

The druids' heirs, hedge wizards of many traditions, are too many and too stubborn to be made to join the Order. Most live in Connacht, which the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh closes to covenants, and many belong to the Coill Trí, a league that mimics the Order. The elder races, the Fomórach, the Fir Bolg and the Tuatha Dé, are the Order's allies, and Ireland's history, its people say, keeps repeating: each people to come has driven the last into a corner, and the native magi fear that the English magi will drive them into Connacht in turn.

The land. Ireland is shaped like a bowl: a rim of low mountains along most of the coast round rolling plains and deep forest, threaded with rivers and spotted with lakes. It is milder and wetter than England; snow is rare and never lies more than three days, rain falls more in the west than the east (three days in five, some say), and floods can wash out the spring sowing. Apple, hazel and oak forests shelter boar, wolves, deer, foxes, badgers, hares and squirrels, and the outlaws and fiannai (bands of young nobles living wild while they wait for their inheritance, to prove themselves); many outlaws today did nothing worse than hold land an Englishman wanted, and their neighbours call them heroes. One Area Lore (Ireland) covers the whole island, four days' walk from coast to coast and eight from the northern tip to the southern; its specialties are a province, a clan's history, a line of kings, legends or old feuds.

Land and lordship. The Irish reckon land in cantreds, each in a clan chief's keeping. The English bundle cantreds into Liberties, heritable fiefs, and shires, the king's cities and their country; a lord of a Liberty keeps its rents and taxes and is freer, while a shire's keeper is the king's agent and sends him most of the money, though the trade of a city can make him the richer man.

Cattle. Cows are wealth, power and honour; raising them and lifting them from others are the heart of Irish life. Herds move to high summer pasture and low winter pasture, and are shut in roofed byres at night against the wolves. A man must keep a herd fit for his rank, so a raid costs honour as well as beasts, and getting stolen cattle back from a stronger man depends on allies. Grain is a small part of a farm's yield (oats, then wheat and rye), sown in unfenced fields that last two harvests; cattle may lawfully cross a field to reach water, and fencing them from it is a crime.

The túath. Irish society rests on the clan, a lineage claiming a heroic ancestor, and its unit is the túath, 'people', which means its land, its free and unfree clients and its slaves as well as its kin. Most túatha date from the fourth and fifth centuries; a strong leader may break away to found a new one, and a weak one is destroyed or swallowed. About 125 exist in 1220. The greatest are the five bloods: Ulster's Ua Néill, Meath's Máel Sechnaill, Connacht's Ua Conchobair, Leinster's Mac Murchadha and Munster's Ua Briain.

Ranks. The daorcheile, those without honour, are slaves, unfree farmers and the poorest free farmers; the grád flatha, those with honour, are rich free farmers, nobles, clergy and the learned professions. A bothach, unfree, takes a cow and a plot from his lord for labour and goods on terms he can never pay off; a bóaire, free, gets terms he can. Nobles rise from lesser nobles, with the fewest client farmers, through cattle lords to greater nobles; the derbfine, everyone within four generations of the chief, are the clan's core. A rí tuaithe rules one túath, a fuirig or over-king holds others as clients, a rí ruirech is king of over-kings and a rí cóicid a provincial king (an English baron, earl and duke in turn, though the Irish rank a provincial king higher). There has been no ard rí, high-king, since the English came. Judges, poets and physicians are mostly hereditary, trained as long as a university master, and a great king names an ollamh to head each. Each túath meets in its oireacht at set places and seasons to settle disputes, fines and taxes and, when needed, to choose a king from the derbfine, sometimes naming a tánaise ríg, heir apparent, in advance. A king is wed to the tribal land in a sacred rite, in some túatha to a local Tuatha Dé land goddess.

Eraic. Every free man has an honour-price, eraic, paid to him in cows for any harm to body, name, connections or goods; a slight costs a good share of it, a killing the whole. In play it is a Reputation within his túath (for example Eraic 1, Ua Riain túath). His herd should number twelve times his eraic and his blood-price is six times it, both doubled for the five bloods; lesser wrongs cost a share the troupe decides. Starting eraic follows Social Status: a slave (the Slave Flaw) and a bothach (Peasant) have none; a bóaire (Peasant and Wealthy, or Knight and Poor) has 1; a lesser noble is a Gentleman at 2 or a Knight at 3; a cattle lord (Landed Noble) has 5, 6 if also a Knight; a king (Greater Noble) has 7. Wealthy adds 1 and Poor takes 1 away, and a Poor Knight falls to bóaire. Climbing a rung takes 10 Gratitude Points (Lords of Men). The Irish have no title for a knight, but the rank is the lowest of the grád flatha.

Law and custom. The Brehon Laws are civil law, on marriage, hostages, fostering, rank and clientship; they set the share of the victim's eraic a wrong costs, and how big a man's house and herd may be, but give no king power to punish, so the wronged must collect for themselves. Only one marriage in twenty is made in church; a couple need only declare it, divorce and remarriage are easy, cousins wed, the groom pays a bride-gift, every son not born of a slave inherits, and marriage binds no alliance. Nobles give sons as hostages to a king, whose lives are forfeit if the túath breaks faith; noble children are fostered from seven to seventeen (girls to fourteen) and a foster-son is a son in all but inheritance. Every superior owes hospitality, a meal and a bed, and a monastery three nights; a mean host risks a satire, or a demon, and a lord's clients owe him cuddy, a night's feasting, when he goes on circuit.

Settlements. Villages are ráths, palisades round wooden huts, set away from rivers and roads and movable with the clan; there are nearly a thousand. Monastic ráths enclose a stone church and round tower. The Ostmen founded the only cities, Dublin, Waterford, Wexford, Cork and Limerick; the great churches (Armagh, Cashel, Kildare, Tuam and Dublin) and royal seats have turned to stone walls.

The year. Winter begins at Samhain (1 November), when on its eve ghosts and faeries are abroad and the Tuatha Dé move to their winter halls; summer begins at Bealtaine (1 May), a good day for year-long charms. Lughnasa (the Sunday nearest 1 August) is the harvest feast and Oímelg (1 February) the Feast of Saint Brighid. Ireland is wholly Christian, though: at Easter the sun dances, granting +1 to a pious Personality Trait for the week to all who see it, and on Christmas night beasts can speak until dawn, which it is very bad luck to hear.

Pastimes. Poets and musicians pass freely between Irish and English halls (love songs are in fashion), which makes a poet a fine spy, and Performance Magic is common among Hibernian wizards, though native poets resent a magus taking their part. Irish youths of every rank play hurling, which the English shun and faeries love (a good player may be stolen for a night's faerie match); Athletics covers it, and a hurley hits as a club. Horses race riderless; fidhcheall uses Etiquette, or Carouse at -2, and táiplis (backgammon) is an English lord's game.

Languages. Gaelic, with Munster, Connacht, Ulster and Leinster dialects (Meath has none of its own); Anglo-Norman French for the lords; English in many dialects for their servants; West Norse among the Ostmen of the southern ports; and Latin for the learned. A speaker of another dialect of the same tongue is at -1. Some Gaelic-speaking magi give their Houses Irish forms: Ua for the four lineages (Ua Bonaoságas), cultas for the four Mystery Cults (cultas Meriníte), and a byname for the societates (an Flambó, an t-Iarbiteon, an Taotalas, an t-Éigse Measceal); old accounts call House Diedne Deoradach, 'the banished'.

The English opposition. The English prize land and the Irish prize cattle: Irish wars took herds, not territory, while the English build stone towers to keep what they take. Irish sons share their father's land and herd, worked together for five years and then divided by the youngest; the English give everything to the eldest, and an Englishman who marries an Irish heiress expects her father's lands and title, which her kin deny. An Irish king's son has no right to the throne, which the derbfine bestows, and an over-king cannot overturn his client king's rulings, where an English king's law runs over every lord. The settlers are failing to plant French feudalism on the clans and are instead going native, 'more Irish than the Irish themselves'.

The Chief Bard. The ard-ollamh Érenn, Chief Bard of Ireland, is the high-king's own poet and king of the bards: he judges between bards and others, sets the fashions of verse and tale, and alone may strip a bard of rank; only a man whose father and grandfather were bards may hold it. The last, Giolla Ernain Ua Martain, died in 1218, and the seat has stood empty since.

The Divine in Ireland. A land haunted by angels and shaped by saints, thick with monasteries and hermits' cells; its people are devout and call on Heaven often, but treat religion practically, unlike the English churchmen now ruling much of it (see the four archdioceses for the two Churches). Over a hundred saints are honoured here; Patrick, Brigid and Columba are the island's patrons, and any Irish character may call on them and the Virgin. Irish saints take a close interest in magicians, so the Meddlesome Saint Hook (Covenants, page 23) suits a Hibernian covenant well. The old Irish church bells, shaped like hollow pears with the clapper inside, are rare now; where one is rung it drives ghosts from all within earshot, as Ward Against Spirits 15 with Penetration 15 at Voice range, measured by the bell's sound.

The Infernal in Ireland. Evil here hides in men's hearts and deeds: temptation, obsession and possession. It came early, with Partholon's jealousy (see Inis Saimera), then plague, which killed Partholon and his people save Tuan, then war, with Nemed's victories over the Fomórach paid for in his wife and sons; plague took him, the Fomórach enslaved his people for 207 years, and when they fled, a Fomórach flood left only thirty alive.

How the demons work. They prefer to stay unseen and unheard, from cunning and cowardice rather than wisdom: anything that shows itself and boasts of serving Hell is probably not a demon. Two ways are favoured: crush a man until only the dark road is left, or feed his envy and obsession until he damns himself. Love, land and rank drive men to evil, so the demons give to those who have and take from those who have little. In the clans' wars they use Obsession on claimants and Possession on their advisers, rarely Envisioning, lest the dreams betray them. Plagues and famines among beasts and farmers are a favourite tool, often sparing a church or covenant so the starving neighbours learn to hate it; churches have been plundered for it, and covenants are wise to find the source before the hungry come for their stores. Winter is the dangerous season. By Patrick's miracle no demon in Ireland may take a serpent's shape; one that can coagulate must take another form or stay unseen. Fictiles (Realms of Power: The Infernal, page 69) abound, and lesser demons rule storm, flood, fire, sickness, famine and even gates that come unlatched at night. Hedge traditions fight plague too, above all in Connacht, where the Order is absent.

Their powers, beside Obsession and Possession: Winter's Chill (2 points, Init Qik -2, Auram), used daily over all the demon sees, so that anyone with Living Conditions of 0 or less makes a daily Deprivation check (ArM5 page 180) and loses a Long-Term Fatigue level for each failure; The Plague of Ages (Corpus, Init Qik -20, 10 points), the Curse of the Unportended Plague (ArM5 page 133) on a town or village, costing the demon 10 Might that comes back at a point a season spent wholly in an Infernal aura; and A Death in the Night (Animal or Corpus, Init Qik -4, 4 points), which kills one person or beast after the demon enters its dreams by Envisioning, usually to rid the true target of a calming friend.

Devils of folklore are mostly faeries in a devil's part, or ghosts; as continental doctrine calls faeries fallen angels, more of them now play road-haunting imps, with another faerie nearby as priest or wise woman to let the traveller renew his faith, and they draw vitality from both parts. Folk charms work against demons with an Abhorrent Material or Circumstance, Compulsiveness or Protected Group weakness, and against faeries playing demons: a candle burning in the field all night keeps the cattle safe; a hagstone in the stable or over a cradle stops horses or a child being stolen and blocks Envisioning; a house shut tight bars a demon that must come by an open door or window; a branch of elder holds a demon all night counting its thorns and berries; and a pouch of salt makes a demon spend its maker's Intelligence + (Infernal or Divine) Lore in Might before it can begin to possess the wearer.

Infernal places are of three kinds: battlefields soaked in slaughter, whose malevolent auras cover the whole plain where blood fell, hold demons as worms in the soil, and have patron demons that lure enemies back with dreams of victory (Magh Slécht, Druim Leatan, Dún Bhun na Gaillimhe); auras born of human corruption; and places where Hell itself touches the world (Inis Doney).

Story seed: The High-King's Treasure. Many high-kings found faerie treasures, some of them true enchanted items made by the Tuatha Dé's Gifted craftsmen, and took them to the grave or lost them back to the Tuatha Dé, who hid them again. Since clans seldom move, a magus who wants such an item need only find its old owner's homestead and start opening barrows.

Story seed: Sometimes They Return. A child makes an abandoned faerie ráth his secret den, and after a month of play he vanishes. Its owner, a brutish swamp ogre, has come home. Was the boy eaten, flayed, or sold to another faerie? The magi must find out and save him.

neighbours.secrets: It is not recorded what turned Vigil's Merinita against the Diedne long ago; those who know how demons work may guess.

neighbours.name: Salmon's Eye (Súil Bradáin)
neighbours.summary: A Diedne covenant of Munster that took Donn, the death god of the Tuatha Dé, as its ally in the Schism War. With Donn's host it destroyed Warbler's Way; then the Hibernian magi united, beat the Munster Diedne, razed Salmon's Eye and drove Donn back to his island, Teach Duínn. The book does not say where it stood; the aura is assumed.
neighbours.secrets: Cliffheart has spent two centuries asking why the Munster Tuatha Dé sided with the Diedne and still does not know; whatever bound Donn to this place may be found in its ruins.

neighbours.name: The Widow's Throat (Scornach Baintrí)
neighbours.summary:
A large Diedne covenant of Ulster that brought a fleet of Fomóir warships into the Schism War: five sailed up the Shannon toward Lugh's Retreat while five fell on Circulus Ruber from the sea. Once the fleet at sea was beaten and Circulus Ruber relieved, the magi turned north and destroyed it. The book does not place it in Ulster; the aura is assumed.

Story seed: The Secret of Ráth Cinn-Eich. Nemed's royal fort on the slopes of Slieve Croob was dug by four Fomóir slave brothers; Diedne's covenant of the Widow's Throat later rose on its ruins and fell in the Schism War. Nobody has explored the deep Fomóir passages beneath, where treasure, Fomóir enchantments and Diedne lore may lie.

neighbours.name: Lugh's Retreat (Cúlráid Logha)
neighbours.summary: A Diedne covenant at the Hollow of Shannon, the lonely spring in the Dartry Mountains where the Shannon rises. The first Hermetic attack, two months after the fall of the Widow's Throat, failed, and Fomóir warriors from the river fleet joined its defence. Two years after that first attack the magi came back with the druids and hedge wizards of Connacht, warned by the Redcaps, and killed Diedne and Fomóir alike. Poets call it the Third Battle of Moytirra. Some Diedne escaped, to die at Clontarf in 1014. The aura is assumed.

neighbours.name: Warbler's Way (Cosán Ceolaire)
neighbours.summary: A Hermetic covenant of three Merinita in the woods round Lough Leane, destroyed by the Munster Diedne and Donn's forces about a year after the Widow's Throat fell. Its survivors fought on to Clontarf and then founded Cliffheart on Cape Clear Island. The realm and aura are assumed from its Merinita founders and the faerie woods.

neighbours.name: The Diedne Vigil
neighbours.summary: The first Vigil, a Diedne covenant in the foothills of the Sperrins, which won its standing by killing the great black pig that dug the ditches guarding old Ulster and taking its tusks. Dublin's rune wizards raided it in 830; it recovered and helped defend other covenants, until the Diedne withdrew from the Tribunal and a band of Merinita sacked it after 851 and carried the tusks to Malin Head, where the new Vigil stands. The aura is assumed.

neighbours.name: The lost covenant of Uisneach
neighbours.summary: A covenant founded on the Hill of Uisneach early in the Order's time in Ireland, for its strong aura and the Stone of Division, where oaths and treaties binding the whole Tribunal are sworn. One summer evening it vanished and left no trace; only scraps of record remain and even its name is forgotten. It seems likely another covenant will one day rise here.
neighbours.secrets: Folk tales tell of a mighty magician who wanted to rule all the others in Ireland, broke a geas, and was carried off by the Good Folk for his pride. The truth is not known.

neighbours.name: The Ordo Hiberniae
neighbours.summary:
The native Hermetic magi, as they name themselves: raised to Irish lineages that have lived and worked in Hibernia for generations, steeped in Irish legend, and judging law as much by Brehon custom as by the Code. Circulus Ruber leads the traditionalists. They see the English as a new flock of black birds, the omen that once foretold the fall of the Fir Bolg, and fear being driven into Connacht as each people before them was driven into its corner.

They are not of one mind. Some younger Irish magi, many still in their macgnímartha, have taken up the English argument that no part of Ireland should be closed to the Order and that the old treaties with hedge wizards, beasts and faeries should go, and a few joined the siege of Praesis. If the Ordo loses the Tribunal as it lost Praesis, centuries of custom could be gone within a generation.

details.rules: Magi of Irish Hermetic lineages; patchwork mantles by rank
details.wants: To keep the Code, the Treaty and the old ways, and Ireland's magic in its own keeping
details.offers: Deep lore of Irish legend, alliances with the elder races, and votes at Tara

links.note: Fierce foe of the English agenda
Irish, though for a Christian Tribunal
Former Praeco; held to the old Code

neighbours.name: The English Council
neighbours.summary:
The magi not native to Hibernia, called the English after the Stonehenge magi who first came to look, though they hail from across the continent. House Tremere took notice once England invaded around 1170, after Gerald of Wales's books and Stonehenge's reports painted the Tribunal as dangerous and archaic, and backed the first comers; over fifty years they have come to claim land and to reform the Code. They find the hedge wizards' protections and Connacht's status improper, and are as set in continental ways as the Irish are in theirs.

They meet as a council at each meeting's start to agree their stance, mostly on reform and lately on Lámbaird's aggression, but agreement is hard among so many views, and the council wants a leader who can look past Praesis. Helles of Ashenrise leads the reform debate. Some of them have now raised apprentices in Ireland, denied the macgnímartha, and in a generation the line between Irish and English may blur.

details.rules: Meets at the start of each Tribunal to agree a common line
details.wants: A Code on the continental model: general law, vis harvested when it appears, no votes for faeries and beasts, Connacht opened
details.offers: Votes, and the backing of Stonehenge and House Tremere

links.note: Taken by the English in the siege

neighbours.name: Munster
neighbours.summary:
Mumhan, the southern province of Mythic Ireland, and the first the Sons of Míl took: it fell to Éibhear Fionn, whose descendants split into many túatha. It was once three kingdoms, Desmond in the south, Thomond in the north and Ormond in the east, but much of it has been renamed and parcelled out to English lords. Irish kings keep their own privileges in their ancestral cantreds and keep English knights at bay to the east; English lords lay English law on the Irish they have subdued; the Ostmen and foreigners of the three cities, Cork, Waterford and Limerick, answer to the English in name and please themselves in fact; and outlaw bands in the forests rob Irish and English homesteads alike.

The peoples. The Eoghanachta, named for Eoghan Mór, were the strongest clan of Munster for centuries and have split into several: the Eoghanachta Caisail round Cashel, the Eoghanachta Áine round Cnoc Áine and the Eoghanachta Locha Lein round the Lakes of Killarney. The Dál gCais, the tribe of Cas, came north from the south-east to the lands by the Shannon and the Fergus that became Thomond; their chief house is the Uí Briain. The Déise, a knot of clans west of the Nore and north of Waterford, were driven out of the lands round Tara by Cormac mac Airt long ago and were vassals of the Eoghanachta; they now bow to English lords by day and make what mischief they can by night.

The English. In 1210 King John granted his favourites the province, keeping the three cities for himself: Robert le Poer had the country north of Waterford, Philip de Braose had Thomond, and Robert FitzStephen and Milo de Cogan shared Desmond. None of them made good the grant, and in 1220 their sons hold little; hostile neighbours and the lack of any great victory keep them in check. Both Desmond and Thomond have lately fought wars of succession in which every side hired English swords, and the English have crept into Desmond in the confusion, slowly, quarrelling among themselves as readily as the Irish do. In Cork and Limerick the Ostmen are beyond their lords' control, and are let raid the countryside, plundering whoever they find.

Hermetic Munster. Four Hermetic houses stand here: Circulus Ruber, the first and largest covenant of Hibernia, on Hag's Head; Cliffheart on Cape Clear Island; Elk's Run, the English covenant, in the Slieve Aughty on the Connacht border; and the Mercer House of Leth Moga at Cloyne, which serves every covenant south of the Eiscir Riada. The Munster Tuatha Dé sided with House Diedne in the Schism War, and Donn's isle of Teach Duínn lies off this coast.

Vis (each in its place): Lough Gur (five pawns of Aquam, faerie lake foam, under a full moon) and the pearls of Lén's anvil at Sídh Femen (Ignem, one night a year). Elk's Run holds the vis of the lands Oswald rode round; the book names no other source in the province.

Story seed: The Siege of Shandon Castle. Shandon's squat tower is the keystone of Cork's defences, and Diarmait mac Cárthaigh has set his lightning-hurling hedge wizards to destroy it. If they succeed, the defeated may blame the Order, Ireland's best-known wizards. Should the magi stop them?

Story seed: The Faerie Saint Flannan. Saint Flannan foresaw only deaths, but the legend has grown until a social faerie has taken his part, visiting the cathedral's architect at night. The abbot notes that the building is going a little crooked and sprouting pagan images, and that the 'saint' calls only at the architect's house.

Story seed: The Sacred Yew. The Eoghanachta once revered a yew at Cashel's heart, cut down in the Dál gCais raids. Their hedge wizards say the clan will not rise until a new one grows, and an Uí Cerbaill sorcerer can grow a yew from seed overnight. The monks keep felling his trees, and a Cashel envoy seeks a magus to stop him.

Story seed: The Ruinous Toad. Before the English came, a toad, a creature unknown in Ireland, was found on a Waterford quay, and seers called it an evil omen. Toads have multiplied since, and a French merchant is said to have brought in a venomous snake. Have the English changed something in Ireland's supernatural fabric?

links.note: the faerie poet who walks Munster with his band

neighbours.name: The Kingdom of Desmond
neighbours.summary:
Deas-Mhumhain, south Munster, the kingdom of the mac Cárthaigh kings, which vies with Thomond as the strongest Irish realm in the province and is shrinking: royal grants since the invasion have pushed its border west of the new Liberty of Cork, past the Bandon estuary and the English town of Kinsale. Five years ago Cormac Fionn rose against his brother King Diarmait; he failed, and the two patched up a peace when they saw the English pressing on the border.

Small castles ring the kingdom, some thrown up in haste by English knights, others raised by Desmond's own nobles for defence and for raiding; Donagh Uí Mathghamhna has built twelve along the south coast to keep enemies from landing. Every summer Desmond's warriors fall on one of the Ostmen towns, Youghal or Cork.

Story seed: Returning the King. The Red Book of Cloyne says Eoghan Mór did not die at Magh Léana: a faerie woman, Éadaoin, carried him into an invisible yew, healed him, and keeps him still, telling him he won and has been with her only days. The yew's reflection shows in the stream, but the regio has never been found, and failing Eoghanachta kings ask magi to bring him home.

Story seed: The Midnight Builder. The Uí Mathghamhna's twelve coastal castles, all of stone, rose so fast that some magi suspect magic. Is a magus raising castles overnight for the túath? Cliffheart, known to favour the Irish, lies close by.

neighbours.name: The Kingdom of Thomond
neighbours.summary:
Tuadhmhumhain, north Munster, the old lands of the Dál gCais and the Uí Briain, between the Shannon, the Fergus and the southern shores of Lough Derg. It is a buffer between Connacht and the Liberties of Limerick and Tipperary, and the Uí Briain have lately raided all three. The Shannon stops the English building castles here as the FitzStephens do in Desmond.

The Dál gCais credit their rise to two patrons: Saint Patrick, who met them on their first march north and is honoured at their stone church of Singeal, and Aoibheall, a faerie land-goddess whose mound, Craig Liath, stands on Lough Derg's western shore. Every king of the Dál gCais weds her in a public rite, and if he rules well she gives him foresight and prophecy, though she spends little time with him and he usually keeps a mortal queen besides. Brian Bóramha married her and some say owed his high-kingship to her sight; she warned him on the eve of Clontarf that he would die there. In 1220 others hold both sacred sites.

Some Uí Briain warriors are still buried the old way, upright and armed and facing Connacht, in nearly a hundred mounds along the northern border.

Story seed: The Stealer of Secrets. Some Uí Briain warriors lie buried upright, weapon in hand, facing Connacht, in nearly a hundred mounds along Thomond's northern border. A hedge wizard has learned to speak with them and is plundering their memories for military secrets, and the robbed ghosts wail until the countryside cannot sleep. Stop the wizard, or at least lay the ghosts.

Story seed: The King's Treasure. After the recent raid King Donnchadh buried his treasures, and when his most faithful warrior boasted he would guard them even in death, the king took him at his word and killed him. Now he has forgotten the spot and asks the characters to find it, without mentioning the ghost that waits there.

neighbours.name: The Liberty of Tipperary
neighbours.summary:
Once the Kingdom of Ormond, a borderland with Ossory on its eastern side and Desmond and Thomond on its western, thick with Eoghanachta septs. The clans lost their standing when the Dál gCais felled their sacred yew, and the English found them easy prey. King John made Theobald Walter hereditary Chief Butler of Ireland with lands in the north; William de Burgh took the middle country between Cashel and the town of Tipperary, from his castles of Kilfearkle and Athassel; and Philip de Worcester the south, with Cahir castle, built by Conchovor Uí Briain in 1142.

English holdings are islands in a rough sea. Life can be pleasant in the towns the English founded, Nenagh and Clonmel, and in those they hold, Athassel and Cahir, but the roads are perilous, and travellers between the towns go rarely or under guard, for the Déise and Eoghanachta clans gladly ambush them.

The Silvermine Mountains on the Thomond border are a ring of wooded peaks round valleys of hazel, hawthorn and rowan that could hide an army; Keeper Hill, Sliabh Coimeálta, the mountain of fosterage, stands over them all. Legend says Sadhbh, a Connacht princess spurned by her Munster husband, hid there and gave their twins to the Tuatha Dé to raise; what became of them nobody knows. Magic auras are rare in the range, which may be why no covenant has been founded in such defensible country; a careful search might still find a site.

neighbours.name: The Liberty of Waterford
neighbours.summary:
South Déisi to the Irish, the first part of Munster the English took and, lying close to Leinster, the safest of the liberties. Its bounds run up the Suir to Clonmel, west to the abbey town of Lismore, then down the Blackwater to Youghal and the sea.

Pockets of Irish resistance remain: Déisi fighters gather now and then to strike at English towns and castles, and the local lords cannot find where their war band shelters.

Story seed: The Secret Army. Déise raiders strike English towns and castles in the Liberty of Waterford, and no one can find where their full-time leaders hide. Is the stronghold magically concealed in the inland woods? Ashenrise has taken an interest and is asking Redcaps what they know.

neighbours.name: The Liberty of Limerick
neighbours.summary: Western Thomond and eastern Ormond, once the lands of the Uí Fidgenti, an Eoghanachta clan that kept them through every raid, since Irish princes take cattle and not land, and both mac Cárthaigh and Uí Briain called them to their hostings. The English take land, and have driven the Uí Fidgenti out. King John named it a liberty, but its English lords barely hold it, and the Uí Súilleabháin resist them from their castles in Kerry and west Cork.

neighbours.name: Kerry
neighbours.summary:
Carruidhe, named for the Ciarraige, the descendants of Ciar, son of Fergus mac Róich and Queen Medb. Stronger túatha drove half the clan north to the Thomond–Connacht border; those who stayed became the Uá Conchobhair, and the land was the Kingdom of Ceir, vassal to Desmond, until Henry II gave it to Robert FitzStephen and Milo de Cogan. King John made it a shire in 1210.

A country of mountains and peninsulas, where Slieve Mish sweeps down to the shore of the Dingle peninsula; remote and dangerous. The Uí Súilleabháin are its strongest túath, then the Uí Cinnéide and the Uí Donnchadha; though the mac Cárthaigh have lately weakened them, the Uí Súilleabháin still pen the English lords in their castles, lords in name only.

neighbours.name: Magh nAla
neighbours.summary:
The plain of swans: the mac Cárthaigh king's royal ráth, hidden deep in the Blackwater valley now that Cork is lost to him, and the gathering place of his hostings. Forest closes it in and it is hard to find, reached only by a few winding roads, not all of which lead there. In winter it is an ordinary ráth of a few hundred people and a thousand cattle; each spring King Diarmait calls every freeman and fighter of Desmond to war, and they come out of the woods in their hundreds.

Story seed: Seeking the Plain of Swans. Mac Cárthaigh's hidden ráth is reached only by forest roads, and one is the road of the Coitse Bodhar, the Silent Wagon, whose faerie driver runs travellers down and throws them into a faerie forest to wander. The characters may be asked to find people who went looking for Magh nAla and never arrived.

neighbours.name: The Road of the Coitse Bodhar
