neighbours.summary: One of the woodland roads toward Magh nAla, driven by the Coitse Bodhar, the Silent Wagon: a two-wheeled chariot whose driver, a malicious faerie woman, loves to ride travellers down. Those knocked off the road land in an endless faerie forest and wander there until magic fetches them out.

levels.name: The faerie forest
levels.enter: Being struck from the road by the Coitse Bodhar
levels.notes: A vast wooded regio where those thrown in wander lost.

neighbours.name: Tech Dairbhre
neighbours.summary: An island just off the Desmond coast, joined to the mainland by a thin neck of land (Dairbhre Isle). Mug Ruith lives here, the faerie who calls himself the most famous druid in Éire, court wizard to the king of the Munster Tuatha Dé and their ambassador to the Sacred Council. He flies the roth rámach, the oared wheel, in a bull's hide and a bird mask, and keeps a hoard of enchanted things: a shining chariot, a magic shield and a stone that can become a venomous eel. He often visits his daughter Tlachtga on her hill in Meath.

neighbours.name: Shandon Castle
neighbours.summary: A squat stone tower on a crag over Cork harbour, the keystone of the city's defences.

neighbours.name: The Yew of Éadaoin
neighbours.summary: A faerie regio by a stream near the battlefield of Magh Léana, known only from the Red Book of Cloyne: an invisible yew in which the faerie woman Éadaoin is said to have carried off the dying Eoghan Mór. Nobody has found it.

levels.name: Inside the yew
levels.see: The yew's reflection in the stream, so the legend says
levels.notes: Where Eoghan Mór is said to live on with Éadaoin.

neighbours.name: The River Shannon
neighbours.summary:
Abha na Sionainne, the longest river of Mythic Ireland, almost 250 miles from its spring in the Dartry Mountains to the Atlantic, and the great barrier between east and west along Connacht's border. It is named for Sionainn, a mortal woman who lifted the capstone from a faerie well of knowledge and was drowned by the flood that became the river; changed by it, she now rides the water in a little hide boat, watching all that passes.

The whole river has a Faerie aura of 1, stronger in its lonely reaches, where some pools and hidden eddies hold faerie regiones. West of the river faeries grow more dangerous: cruel solitary faeries are common, and trooping faeries do much of the harm laid at kings' doors. In one deep bend lives a bandraoi, a sea-witch who takes the shape of any fish or of a lovely woman, and drowns the fishermen she lures.

Story seed: Finding Fionntan. Ireland's first druid, Fionntan, who survived the Flood as a salmon, is said to be over four thousand years old and to live in a cave under the Shannon. Pagan once, he was converted by one Trefuilngid. Is he Divine, a man turned magical, or a faerie? The answer matters to any magus hunting the same long life.

Story seed: The Fish Wife. In a deep bend of the Shannon lives a bandraoi, a sea witch who takes any fish's shape or a lovely woman's. She lures fishermen to kiss her, becomes a great pike as they lean in, and drags them down by the face. Characters may be her victims or their rescuers.

neighbours.name: Craig Liath
neighbours.summary: The mound of Aoibheall, the Dál gCais's faerie land-goddess and the bride of their kings, on the western shore of Lough Derg; men of Connacht raided it lately. Called the prophetess of the Uí Briain for the truth of her foresight.

neighbours.name: The Burren
neighbours.summary: A plateau of limestone some hundred square miles on the coast of north-west Thomond, split by cracks (grikes) into thousands of bare pavements. The grikes are full of long grass and wild flowers, so cattle and sheep graze here, and raiders come after them, troubling the place and its many faeries, who live among the hundred or so stone tombs and cairns. Circulus Ruber's magi moved here after their year at the Brú na Bóinne.

neighbours.name: Hag's Head
neighbours.summary: Ceann na Cailleach, one of the higher Cliffs of Moher at the Burren's south-western edge, nearly 400 feet above the Atlantic, looking out to the Aran Islands and Galway Bay. Circulus Ruber's round tower stands on top. The cliffs are haunted by a Cailleach, a malicious faerie hag who would gladly pull the tower down; the Aegis keeps her off, but she torments travellers on the lonely road to the covenant, and some folk wrongly think she guards it. Fomóir raiders in the Schism War left scars on the land here.

neighbours.name: The Uí Briain Border Mounds
neighbours.summary: Nearly a hundred burial mounds along Thomond's northern border, where Uí Briain warriors lie upright, weapons in hand, facing north toward Connacht in the pagan fashion. The book gives them no aura.

neighbours.name: Sídh Femen
neighbours.summary:
The Mound of Femen, where Bodh Derg, the Dagda's son, holds court as king of the Munster Tuatha Dé: a vast hall under the earth, as full as any Irish king's, of minstrels, courtiers, herdsmen, warriors and wives. He is renowned as a judge and a reader of dreams, and other Tuatha Dé visit him often.

His smith, Lén, forges enchanted things for the Munster Tuatha Dé, and at day's end hurls his anvil onto a nearby hill, where its sparks turn to pearls. They vanish when he takes the anvil back, save on one night a year, when they stay and can be gathered as Ignem vis (claimed by no covenant).

neighbours.name: The Rock of Cashel
neighbours.summary:
Caisel, a great outcrop rising sheer from the Golden Vale, crowned with stone churches, oratories, chapter houses and cathedrals, the church capital of Munster. Conall Corc founded it as the seat of the Eoghanachta kings, and Saint Patrick crowned one of them here and blessed the rock with miracles. When the Dál gCais drove the Eoghanachta out, the Rock was given to the Church (to the bishop of Limerick, the book says), so that no lay hand could hold it and the Eoghanachta could never win back their old capital. It was fortified before it was given away; some old buildings are in ruins, the newer ones are kept in repair. The whole Rock has a Divine aura of 2.

Before the faith came, the Eoghanachta worshipped the yew, and a sacred yew stood at the heart of Cashel until Brian's brother Muircheartach cut it down in the Dál gCais raids; their hedge wizards say the clan will not rise again until a new one grows there.

neighbours.name: Cormac's Chapel
neighbours.summary: The main cathedral on the Rock of Cashel, with a Divine aura of 5.

neighbours.name: Croc Áine
neighbours.summary:
Two hills over the Munster plain near Lough Gur, home of the land-goddess Áine and the place where every royal marriage of Munster is made. Each midsummer the people light a bonfire on both summits, then carry blazing clairs, straw bundles bound to poles, round their fields and herds; those who keep the rite rightly gain +1 to their Aging Rolls.

The hill is shared in four, one part for the faerie lord of each province but Meath. Every Tuatha Dé and social faerie comes to the rite unseen among the crowd and at midnight goes into Áine's sídh to feast; folk think it ill luck to witness this and hurry to finish first. A magus who wants a word with any faerie of Munster will find it here on the solstice.

neighbours.name: Lough Gur
neighbours.summary:
A lake a few miles north-west of Croc Áine, Faerie 5, with a bad name. Once in seven years it vanishes for a night, leaving a wall of fog where the water was. Cairns ring it, and the sí gaoith, faerie whirlwinds, drag trespassers in to drown. Áine meets her husband Manannán here at times, but its worst dweller is a huge faerie eel, a dangerous solitary faerie that leaps out at night to attack visitors.

Vis: the faerie foam that washes up on the shore; a night's gathering under a full moon is five pawns of Aquam vis, tainted by Faerie, so most who walk the shore at night are magi. Claimed by no covenant.

Among the bigger cairns is one of Ireland's 365 Beds of Dermot and Grainne, the places where the eloping pair hid from Fionn mac Cumhaill for a year. The old druids held that a man who found every bed and slept in each in the proper order, through a year-long initiation, would gain supernatural powers.

neighbours.name: Dún Eochair
neighbours.summary: A ruin on the River Maigue, once the Uí Fidgenti's capital until the mac Cárthaigh drove them out; with English settlers nearby, both clans have left it. A regio over the old palace grounds hides the hall of Cú Roí, who in the Ulster tales was king of Munster, a magician, warrior and shape-changer, now a faerie-hero who misses the people who once lived here. He is most often a judge, famous for fair rulings: who is the better warrior or poet, or which course a man should take.

levels.name: The palace of Cú Roí
levels.notes: The faerie-hero's court on the old palace grounds.

neighbours.name: Scota's Grave
neighbours.summary: A ring of tall stones in a small valley grove on Slieve Mish, beside an old trail into the mountains from Tralee. Scota, an Egyptian princess and sorceress, wife of Gaedheal Glas and mother of the Gaels, came to Ireland nearly two thousand years old to avenge two sons slain in the Milesians' first war with the Tuatha Dé; she killed their killers, was cut down by Munster faeries and lies where she fell. Magic 5.

neighbours.name: Skellig Michael
neighbours.summary: Sceilig Mhichíl, Michael's Rock: a steep, barren island nine miles out, a monastery for six hundred years until Viking raids drove the monks away in the eleventh century. Their stone huts still sit on the peak above 750-foot cliffs. The whole island has a Divine aura of 3.

neighbours.name: Cape Clear Island
neighbours.summary:
An island eight miles off Ireland's southernmost shore, a mile wide and three long, pinched in two by an isthmus. A small monastic community lives on the southern half; the somewhat larger north is empty but for birds and Cliffheart, whose ráth sits on a steep hill over a little cove, the Cove of the Black Stream; both hill and cove lie in a Magic aura of 3.

Outside the ráth stand three standing stones the island folk call the Marriage Stones: they believe a couple who clasp hands through the hole in one of them will never part, and the monks try to stop the pagan practice.

neighbours.name: The Slieve Aughty
neighbours.summary:
Hills west of Lough Derg on the Munster side of the border with forbidden Connacht (the book's Slieve Aught). In a large, remote valley here stands Elk's Run, which claims wide stretches of mountain, lake and forest round about and all the vis in them. The Uí Sheachnasaigh and the Ua Cathail of Cenél Áeda na hEchtge hold the country.

In Connacht. A thickly wooded range along the Connacht-Munster border and a great refuge of magical beasts. Magi come seeking familiars, and some stray over into Connacht by accident, which has strained the Order's peace with the Coill Trí. Whoever could set a magical boundary marking the border across these hills would win the thanks of both the Tribunal and the Coill Trí. Elk's Run stands on the Munster side.

neighbours.name: Cloyne
neighbours.summary:
A village monastery in Desmond: wooden houses round a stone church and a round tower, with no palisade or wall; when danger comes, monks and villagers lock themselves in the tower. On its southern edge stand the Mercer House of Leth Moga, a large wooden house, and a seldom-used barn on a Magic aura of 1.

Natural tunnels and caves run under the village, linking several important caverns and chambers; the abbot knows some of them.

neighbours.name: Kingdom of Desmond
neighbours.summary:
King Diarmait mac Cárthaigh, of the strongest clan of the Eoghanachta Caisail. His forebears were kings of Cashel until the Dál gCais drove them west of the Blackwater, and the English have pushed them further still. The clan hates the Uí Briain and the Uí Súilleabháin of Kerry far more than the English; the Uí Briain are too strong to strike, but in 1214, at a peace feast in the village of Raheen, the mac Cárthaigh murdered several Uí Súilleabháin nobles. Within the year Diarmait and his brother Cormac Fionn were fighting each other for Desmond.

He rules from the hidden ráth of Magh nAla and summons his hosting every spring. He has set his hedge wizards, men who throw lightning, to bring down Shandon Castle, Cork's chief defence. The book records no tribute owed to the English crown.

neighbours.name: Cormac Fionn mac Cárthaigh
neighbours.summary: King Diarmait's brother, who rose against him five years ago and failed; the two made an uneasy peace when the English crept up to the border.

neighbours.name: The Uí Mathghamhna
neighbours.summary: A Desmond túath whose lord, Donagh, has raised a chain of twelve castles along the kingdom's south coast to stop enemies landing from the Atlantic. Unlike the hasty English motte and bailey forts, every one is of fortified stone, and they went up so quickly that some magi suspect magic. Cliffheart, known to favour the Irish, is not far away.

neighbours.name: Kingdom of Thomond
neighbours.summary:
King Donnchadh Cairbre Uí Briain, of the Uí Briain, the greatest house of the Dál gCais and one of the five bloods of Ireland. Their fortunes began with Brian Bóramha's brother Mathgamain, who took Cashel and Limerick and fell in 975; Brian, sole provincial king after him, grew so strong that the Uí Néill high-king gave up the high-kingship to him, and he held it from 1002 until Clontarf in 1014. Each king of the Dál gCais weds Aoibheall of Craig Liath.

Donnchadh worries more about Connacht, his old enemy, than about the English, and freely hires English soldiers from Tipperary and from the de Burgo family. A Connacht raid of the Uí Conchobhair lately burned Killaloe without breaking his power, and he is gathering mercenaries for a blow back into Connacht. Afraid after the raid, he buried his greatest treasures somewhere he has since forgotten. The book records no tribute owed to the English crown.

neighbours.name: The Uí Súilleabháin
neighbours.summary: A branch of the Eoghanachta Caisail descended from a seventh-century king of Munster; their most famous king, Fedelmid mac Crimthainn, was at once king of Munster and abbot of Cork and Clonfert. Forever at war with the mac Cárthaigh, they were badly hurt by the massacre of Raheen in 1214, but they are still the strongest túath of Kerry, rule Tralee, and keep the English lords of Kerry and Limerick shut in their castles. The book names no chief.

neighbours.name: The Déise
neighbours.summary: Clans west of the Nore and north of Waterford, once vassals of the Eoghanachta, driven from near Tara long ago when their founder Aonghus Gaífhuileach, 'bloody spear', fell out with a son of Cormac mac Airt over a woman. The southern Déise joined the Ostmen to defend Waterford against the English and lost; now they serve their English lords politely by day and make trouble by night. Déisi raiders still muster against English towns and castles from some hiding place nobody has found.

neighbours.name: The Uí Sheachnasaigh
neighbours.summary: One of the two great families of Cenél Áeda na hEchtge, a branch of the Uí Fiachrach Aidhne, the ancient royal house of Connacht. They serve Elk's Run as its covenfolk and enjoy its help, which their rivals the Ua Cathail resent.

neighbours.name: The Ua Cathail
neighbours.summary: The other great family of Cenél Áeda na hEchtge, rivals of the Uí Sheachnasaigh. They resent the English magi of Elk's Run for helping their rivals, raid the covenant, lose men to Igneous Drake's fire, and may soon lay a formal complaint before the Tribunal.

neighbours.name: The le Poer Lands
neighbours.summary: The lands north of Waterford, granted by King John in 1210 to Robert le Poer; neither he nor his son has made the grant good, and the Déise there obey only by daylight.

neighbours.name: The Lordship of Limerick
neighbours.summary: Thomond was granted to Philip de Braose in 1210 and Limerick given to him after its charter of 1197; his son holds the city but spends so much effort keeping order inside it that the countryside slips back into Irish ways.

neighbours.name: The FitzStephens
neighbours.summary: Robert FitzStephen was granted Desmond, Cork and Kerry with Milo de Cogan; his sons build castles in Desmond, encroaching slowly through the kingdom's succession wars, but hold little of what was granted.

neighbours.name: The de Cogans
neighbours.summary: Milo de Cogan shared the grants of Cork, Desmond and Kerry with Robert FitzStephen and took Cork by force with him; his sons hold the city with the Ostmen, and little beyond its walls.

neighbours.name: The Butler Lands of Tipperary
neighbours.summary: King John made Theobald Walter Chief Butler of Ireland, an office passed from father to son, and gave him lands in the north of Tipperary, including the town of Nenagh.
neighbours.ruler: the Chief Butler of Ireland, of Theobald Walter's line

neighbours.name: The de Burgh Lands of Tipperary
neighbours.summary: William de Burgh's grant of the middle of Tipperary, between Cashel and the town of Tipperary. The de Burgo family hires out its soldiers to the King of Thomond.

neighbours.name: The de Worcester Lands of Tipperary
neighbours.summary: The south of Tipperary, granted to Philip de Worcester with Cahir castle, which Conchovor Uí Briain built in 1142.

neighbours.name: Cork
neighbours.summary:
A city at the mouth of the Lee, once a little monastic community, home of Saints Finbarr and Nessan. Ostmen raiders wintered here in 1020 and, unusually, were thrown out: Uí Briain and mac Cárthaigh warriors stormed the walls while their druids broke the earthworks with lightning. Ostmen from Dublin, Limerick and Waterford took it back, though the king of Desmond was strong enough that its leaders bowed to him; meanwhile the Uí Briain carried Saint Finbarr's relics off to Killaloe.

After the invasion the king of Desmond offered Cork to Henry II as tribute, and an English governor and garrison came; mac Cárthaigh took it back two years later, and four years after that Henry granted it to Robert FitzStephen and Milo de Cogan, who stormed it. Desmond besieged it again and again and gave up only in 1199.

Chroniclers call it an evil place. English and Ostmen inside the walls can scarcely bear each other, and none dares go outside into country held firmly by Desmond and the Déise; the harbour is the only way in or out, yet Cork is second only to Dublin for trade. Shandon Castle guards it.

neighbours.name: Waterford
neighbours.summary:
A fishing place fortified by Viking raiders early in the tenth century, full of Ostmen and foreigners. Ostmen and Déisi, no friends before, joined to defend it against the English; they held off Strongbow for a day and yielded when a badly built tower was pulled down. Strongbow spared the town, killing only its two Ostman leaders, and soon married Diarmaid Mac Murchadha's daughter Aoife.

The city of wines, with wine from Bordeaux landed every day, and the usual landing place of the English king, who kept it for himself. King John spent heavily on new walls three times as long as the old, now nearly done. The Marshal, Thomas FitzAnthony, makes his home with his household in Reginald's Tower, the city's oldest stone tower and once the Ostman lords' seat; he has little say outside the walls but is a masterful sheriff within. Most people inside are Ostmen and English, with a few Déisi, and it is the quietest of the three cities.

Before the English came, a toad was found swimming in a puddle on one of its quays, though toads were unknown in Ireland; seers called it an omen of evil, and the English landed months later. Toads have grown commoner since, and a French merchant is said to have brought in a venomous snake.

neighbours.name: Limerick
neighbours.summary:
Another Ostman wintering place grown into a city. Brian Bóramha slew its last strong Viking lord and made it Thomond's capital, and it changed hands often in the Uí Briain's dynastic wars; Domnall Mór Uí Briain burned it in 1174 rather than let the English have it. The whole district was fought over until he died in 1194; then the English seized the city and most of the country round it. It was chartered in 1197 and given to Philip de Braose, and King John's Castle, paid for by the king and named for him, went up in 1200 on King's Island in the Shannon.

The city is split in all but name: English Town is the castle with its walled precinct on King's Island, and Irish Town the walled quarter on the riverbank where Ostmen and Irish live; as an old royal seat of Thomond it is one of the few cities with Irish townsfolk. Murders by night are common, and strangers vanish easily into the harbour.

neighbours.name: Killaloe
neighbours.summary: Thomond's capital and the Uí Briain's seat of power, near where Thomond, Limerick and Tipperary meet, guarding one of the few bridges over the Shannon. It began as a monastery; its value in war led an Uí Briain king to build a palace here, Kincora, where the king still lives. An Uí Conchobhair raid from Connacht burned much of it lately.

neighbours.name: Tralee
neighbours.summary: Trá Lí, the largest town of Kerry, a harbour and market town under the Uí Súilleabháin on the northern edge of Slieve Mish. An ancient trail from it climbs into the mountains past Scota's Grave.

neighbours.name: The Cathedral of Saint Flannan, Killaloe
neighbours.summary:
An Irish church. Flannan, a seventh-century abbot of Killaloe and nephew of the Uí Briain king, had a holy gift for seeing when a man would die, led his house in peace and plenty, and was soon made a saint; Thomond's people still come to his grave for guidance. The cathedral raised in his honour was begun in 1185 and is nearly finished in 1220; its foreman says the saint comes to him at night with advice. Saint Finbarr's relics, brought from Cork, lie beside Flannan's.

A few yards from its foundations stands the Ogham Stone, waist-high, carved in ogham with a blessing on Thorgrimr and signed on the back in Norse runes by Thorgrimr as the carver. It is at least two hundred years old and magical, a strange bond between the old druids, Norse wizards and the faith; being so near the cathedral, nobody has carried it off to study.

neighbours.name: Singeal
neighbours.summary: The stone church (its name means chancel) the Dál gCais built where Saint Patrick met them on his mission through Munster; the saint, their favourite, often visits them now. One of the Dál gCais's two sacred sites, it has fallen to the English and Ostmen of Limerick, so it is in Anglo-Irish hands in 1220.

neighbours.name: The Monastery of Cloyne
neighbours.summary: An Irish house. Its abbot Cian Ua Cathain led a dozen monks when the Mercer House of Leth Moga was founded beside it in 898; his wife was Imag, the House's founder. Monks and Redcaps still get on well, despite the reforms lately imposed on the Church, and the abbot and his staff know the Redcaps well. The present abbot knows some of the tunnels under the village.

neighbours.name: The Monks of Cape Clear
neighbours.summary: An Irish monastic community on the southern half of Cape Clear Island. Its monks stop lovers clasping hands through the Marriage Stones outside Cliffheart, calling it pagan and wicked, which causes the covenant small troubles.

neighbours.name: The Schools of Cashel
neighbours.summary: A renowned seat of learning on the Rock of Cashel, which teaches anyone who can pay. It makes no books but owns a good many. The Redcap Gopstan once lived a year among its monks posing as an unlettered prince's son to get at the library; at the end of it the headmaster sent his greetings to Gopstan's parens, the first hint that he had seen through the ruse. An Irish school.

neighbours.name: Leinster
neighbours.summary:
The south-eastern province of Ireland, milder and drier than the rest of the island. Its many harbours face the Irish Sea, and its trade runs to England and Wales, Bristol above all. Behind a rich coastal strip rise the Wicklow Hills, low mountains that have always kept invaders out of the plains and sheltered outlaws and the dispossessed. The old Kingdom of Leinster has grown and shrunk over the centuries and was sometimes smaller than the province. Here the English first came, at the call of Leinster's own king, and here their hold is firmest, though the Ua Broin and the Ua Túathal fight on from the hills.

Three peoples. The Laighin, who name the province, descend from Lughaidh mac Íth, uncle of Míl Espáine. Their founder Labraid Loingsech, struck dumb as a boy after he was forced to eat the hearts of his murdered father and grandfather, found his voice on the hurling field, served the King of France, and came home with an army bearing blue-tipped spears (the laighin); he burnt the usurping High-King Cobthach and thirty kings alive in an iron house at Din Rig, and his secret, the ears of an ass, was betrayed by a harp made from the willow his barber whispered it to. The Osraighe, the Deer People of Ossory in the west, are an Érainn people. The Ostmen are the Norse who founded Dublin and Wexford, Christian since the tenth century and Irish in speech, still a distinct minority in the ports.

The kingdom. Úgaine Mór founded it; for centuries the Uí Cheinnselaig of the Wexford country and the Uí Dúnlainge of Kildare split it north and south, until the Uí Cheinnselaig reunited it in the eleventh century. Their last king, Diarmait mac Murchadha, schemed for the high-kingship, was driven out by Tigernán Ua Ruairc at the High-King's bidding, and brought in the Normans to win his land back. Grieving his son Domhnall, he wed his daughter Aoife to Strongbow, so that the royal line passed to the English when he died in 1171. The English have ruled for some sixty years, but their ways are only now taking root outside the towns.

The Hermetic province. Three covenants stand here: Ashenrise, the reformers from the continent; Lámbaird, the oldest, home of the School of Raghallach; and the Paruchia of Nerius, the Hermetic Céli Dé of Little Saltee.

Vis (each in its place): the ducks of Templeshanbo (Divine Aquam, from moulted feathers); the Faerie Fire of Baltinglass (Ignem, won by contest); the tide rock off Arklow (Aquam); the Well of Wisdom at Carbury (Imaginem); the Fruit of Saint Kevin at Glendalough (Divine vis when dried); and the raw vis in Rhiannon's bones (Ashenrise's).

Story seed: The Bay of Bannow. Bannow's harbour, where the English first landed, is silting up faster than anyone remembers, and other harbours round the coast have begun to follow. Some blame a cailleach's curse for letting the invaders land, others a fisherman who killed a seal maiden. The priest has seen in a vision that air, fire and water will finish what the mud began, and seeks learned help.

Story seed: Dousing the Fire. Archbishop Henry de Londres has sworn publicly to put out Saint Brigid's perpetual fire, and is worried: a failure would hearten the Ua Broin and Ua Túathal, whose outlaws will try to stop him. He rides to Kildare with knights and mercenaries, and is pragmatic enough to want magical help against what he takes for old druid magic, perhaps a maga, since a woman might pass where a man cannot.

Story seed: Tales of Nuadha and Bóinn. Nuadha stands for the kings of Leinster: if an epic tale mended his silver arm so he could climb the dun of Naas, the kingship rites might return. Bóinn would rather her husband serve, and favours stories of power flowing into Meath, like the Boyne, the Boroimhe tribute, or the justiciarship passing from FitzHenry to de Lacy. Either may draw characters into a reenactment of an ancient tale, here or in Elysium, with dreadful results.

Story seed: The Witches of Kilkenny. Kilkenny blames a coven of dark witches for the accidents that dog its new cathedral. The witches are secretive, and resolving their quarrel will be hard.
neighbours.secrets: The accidents are only accidents: the witches belong to the Coill Trí and are busy with a long feud among themselves.

neighbours.name: The County of Wexford
neighbours.summary: The south-eastern corner of Leinster, round the port of Wexford. In the sixty years since the English came it has become almost like England or Wales, with villages, markets and a largely Anglicized people, which makes it unlike anywhere else in Hibernia. Its towns are Wexford, Bannow, Ferns, Enniscorthy and New Ross; the Saltee islands, home of the Paruchia of Nerius, lie off its coast.

neighbours.name: The Wicklow Mountains
neighbours.summary:
The country round Carlow and Dublin: a low coastal plain that climbs steeply to the Wicklow mountains, which some say Saint Brigid raised by a miracle. They bar the way from the coast to the central plains, and turned back both Norse and English. Thick woods, caves and ravines among rocky hills make the outlaws who haunt the passes almost impossible to pin down. Here the Ua Broin and Ua Túathal, the old rulers, hide and fight on against the English, who call them O'Byrne and O'Toole.

Lámbaird lies hidden in Gleann Molúra among these hills, and Glendalough at the crossing of their two great roads.

neighbours.name: The Liberty of Kildare
neighbours.summary: Low inland country in the north of Leinster, cut off from Dublin on the east by the Wicklow hills. King John made it a Liberty in 1206 to crush the Uí Dúnlainge, whose kings he had set aside, and it is still fought over: English lords hold it down with a web of castles, while the Ua Broin and Ua Túathal wage a hit-and-run war against them from the hills. Its places are Kildare, Naas, the Hill of Allen, Carbury and Calverstown.

links.note: Saint Brigid, a patron of Ireland

neighbours.name: Ossory
neighbours.summary:
The old Kingdom of Ossory in the west of Leinster, seven great plains held by the Osraighe, descendants of Oengus Osraigh. Once mighty, they fell to the Ulaidh at the Battle of Tola in 571, were worn down by wars with the Vikings and the Laighin, and split into three at the start of the twelfth century; their túatha were folded into Leinster. They rose when Diarmait mac Murchadha was driven out, were beaten by Strongbow, and William Marshal built castles to tame them. Kilkenny and Kells now hold them down, though many still hate the English despite the wealth the conquest has brought. They are especially devoted to Saint Ciarán.

Their royal house, the Mac Giolla Phádraig, has mostly accepted English rule and now goes by fitz Patrick. The Uí Riain, whose ancestral ráth held Rhiannon's grave, live here too.

neighbours.name: The Liberty of Carlow
neighbours.summary: The valley of the River Barrow, between Ossory and the Wicklow hills, north of New Ross: English castles along the river, and Irish túatha, the Uí Riain and several Déise families, who resent every English lord on its banks. Ashenrise stands here.

neighbours.name: The Duck Pool of Templeshanbo
neighbours.summary:
A pool by the church of a tiny hamlet under Mount Leinster, where Saint Colman once had a monastery (long gone; his feast is still kept on 27 October). It has a Dominion aura of 3 and thirteen wild ducks, very tame. Hunt or harass them and they fly away, and the pool goes brackish and foul until they come back; kill one and the pot it is cooked in will not boil, and unless the killer does proper penance the saint strikes him dead.

Vis: the feathers the ducks moult are Divine Aquam vis, and anyone may gather them. No covenant claims them.

neighbours.name: Ferns
neighbours.summary:
An old royal seat of Leinster, now a small town and village with a Dominion aura of 3. Diarmait mac Murchadha hid here before he called in Strongbow, with Derbforgaill, the Meath king's daughter he had stolen from her husband, Tigernán Ua Ruairc of Bréifne; she is sung of still as the Helen of Ireland, and the tale feeds a faerie, Aonghus son of Bóinn, who loves to stir up elopements and abductions that end in war.

Here stand William Marshal the Younger's new castle, the Augustinian St. Mary's Abbey and the seat of the Bishop of Ferns, a centre of the reforming party in the Irish Church.

Story seed: The Marshal's Curse. William Marshal the younger promised his father to keep his Irish lands whole and will not give back the two manors the Bishop of Ferns claims, yet he will not remarry and sire an heir until the bishop's curse on his line is lifted. Did the kiss of peace the Pope forced on them lift it? The bishop swore it would hold till the lands came back, so William may seek unusual help, even Hermetic.

Story seed: Helen of Ireland. The tale of Derbforgaill feeds the faerie Aonghus, who stirs elopements and abductions to start wars and still does so gladly. The Bishop of Ferns has warned William the younger of him, which is why William's great new castle is meant to keep his young daughter safe from abduction as she grows up.

links.note: Saint Abbán, venerated in Wexford and Ferns

neighbours.name: Baltinglass
neighbours.summary: A tiny settlement under a hill on the western edge of the Wicklow mountains, named for the hero Glas, who killed one of the six Swine of Drebrenn here: the witch Garbhdalbh's three daughters and their husbands, turned into monstrous boars that laid Ireland waste until Queen Maebh and Aillil hunted them down. A faerie swine still haunts the district, wasting the land until a hero kills it again. On the hill is the Faerie Fire; below it, the Cistercian abbey.

neighbours.name: The Faerie Fire
neighbours.summary:
A ráth on the hill above Baltinglass, holding a mound with a stone doorway; its Faerie aura is 1 for most of the year. Druids are said to have kept an undying fire here. At midsummer a bonfire appears on top of the mound and burns until the season's first rain, and while it burns the aura rises to 3.

Vis: a rich source of Ignem, but whoever would take it must beat the mound's folk at a contest of their choosing. The contest changes each year with the faerie set to guard the fire and the tale it plays out: dancing, music, storytelling, climbing and javelin throwing have all been tried, and it is never the same twice. The monks of Baltinglass mean one Christmas Day to plant a great wooden cross on the mound.

neighbours.name: Glendalough
neighbours.summary:
The valley of two lakes, where the road east and west through the Wicklow Gap crosses the road south from Dublin: Saint Kevin's hermitage, then his monastery. It headed its own diocese until 1214, when the English joined it to Dublin's. A round wall rings the whole community, which is a sanctuary; the aura is Dominion 5 in the church and churchyard and 3 elsewhere.

Sanctuary here lasts until the fugitive steps outside the walls, and the English have not yet dared to break it, so many have fled here: rebels against English rule (villains and brigands, to the English) and lesser criminals too.

At the centre are the church and a hundred-foot round tower, plain but for four little windows facing the four quarters, from which a hand bell calls the faithful to Sunday mass and warns of good news and bad. Beyond them is the graveyard, fenced with bent willows. A few hermits live in stone cells inside the inner wall, holding out against the English churchmen; most of them, the abbot sometimes among them, are manaim with ties to the world beyond. The monks and their abbot's house, guesthouse, infirmary, kitchen and rectory fill the second wall, and outside it lay folk of every rank live much as continental villagers do.

The Fruit of Saint Kevin. When a sick pupil begged for fruit and the monastery had none, Kevin prayed, and an old willow by the graveyard bore white, oblong fruit in minutes that cured the boy. The monks ringed the graveyard with its saplings, and each year, on the evening of the miracle, the willows fruit again: up to twenty-four a season, each adding +20 to recovery rolls for the season it is eaten in. The monks share them out to the sick across Ireland. Dried for a month by someone who knows Magic Theory, a fruit becomes Divine vis, Corpus if dried in a Magic aura, Creo in a Divine one.

Tradition holds that whoever is buried among the willows goes to Heaven without passing through Purgatory, and many heroes lie there; the English churchmen scoff at it.

Story seed: Divine Vis. Saint Kevin's Fruit can be dried over a month by someone versed in Magic Theory, and then yields Divine vis: Corpus if dried in a Magic aura, Creo if dried in a Divine one.

neighbours.name: The Pool of the Púca
neighbours.summary:
On the road to Glendalough a waterfall spills down a rock face into a still, black pool. A Púca, or kelpie, haunts it: a handsome black horse that seems to have strayed onto the road; whoever mounts it is carried off at a gallop into the pool and drowned, or eaten. Locals shun the road, above all by night. Nobody knows whether it is a beast of Magic, a faerie or something Infernal, so the book gives the place no aura (for kelpies, see the Bestiary). It may be cleverer than it seems.

Story seed: The Púca Speaks? The Púca may not be the mindless beast it seems. It might give up its killings for favours or conditions, and might ask to be ridden to Tribunal to speak for itself there.
neighbours.secrets: It may instead be a powerful Infernal being, whose wishes will be neither pleasant nor easily met.

neighbours.name: The Tide Rock off Arklow
neighbours.summary: A rock in the sea a few miles off Arklow where the tide falls on one side as it rises on the other: a strong magical place (Magic 4 here; the book gives no number), whose treacherous waters have drowned many sailors. Vis: Aquam, unclaimed. Not to be mistaken for Arklow Rock, a hill some miles inland.

neighbours.name: The Hill of Allen (Dún Ailinne)
neighbours.summary: A hill looking west over the Bog of Allen: once the palace of the kings of Leinster, later Finn's home. A great ráth on it still holds a Faerie aura of 4, and it is no place to walk after dark.

neighbours.name: Saint Fechin's Cross
neighbours.summary:
A stone cross in the marketplace of Naas, raised where Saint Fechin's monastery of Tulach-Fobhair stood, south of the town, in memory of the day he came to bargain for captives. A prisoner within earshot who calls the saint's name sets an old blessing working that frees every captive, as The Captive Made Free (a saint's power; see the Bestiary). The aura is the town's Dominion, taken here as 3.

The Ua Broin and Ua Túathal rebels all know it: they let themselves be caught, are held in the castle, and slip away with the saint's help as they are marched out to the gallows.

neighbours.name: Sídh Neachtain
neighbours.summary:
The faerie mound of Nuadha at Carbury, in the north of the Liberty of Kildare, beside the motte and bailey that Meiler FitzHenry built when he was Justiciar, which Hugh de Lacy seized and his son Walter de Lacy now holds. Every English lord there has been troubled by the hill's old magic. Nuadha of the silver arm still sleeps beneath it. The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 at the mound and 5 in the regio are this pack's.

Nuadha's wife is Bóinn, the river goddess, who often goes as a shining white cow (see the Bestiary). Long ago she came to the spring and it burst out in a flood that became the River Boyne. The two quarrel; she bore Aonghus to the Daghda, which explains Aonghus's taste for tragic love that ends in strife and Nuadha's open dislike of him. Nuadha stands for the kings of Leinster; Bóinn would rather see him ruled than ruling, and favours tales of power flowing into Meath, as her river does. Both like to draw mortals into acting out the old stories.

Vis: the Well of Wisdom (Imaginem), in the regio.

levels.name: The Well of Wisdom
levels.enter: Only with Nuadha as guide, or by following the Boyne upstream all the way to its source; on Trinity Sunday the regio shows itself for a while in the mundane world.
levels.notes: A faerie spring ringed by nine willows, where magical salmon who know great secrets swim. Whenever nuts drop into the well it gives a great deal of Imaginem vis.

links.note: the white cow goddess of the Boyne

neighbours.name: The Pass of Achad-ur
neighbours.summary: The pass through the hills from Ossory into Munster, where in 1169 Diarmait mac Murchadha and his English allies broke the Osraighe of Mac Giolla Phádraig with a Norman cavalry charge, took the pass and then fell back to Ferns. It is still a main road, and bandits plague it.

neighbours.name: The Rock of Dunamase
neighbours.summary: A rocky outcrop fortified since old times. Meiler FitzHenry saw its worth and built a castle; through Aoife's marriage it passed to Strongbow, who gave it to William Marshal. Marshal raised a strong castle, which his son William now holds.

neighbours.name: Kilree Tower
neighbours.summary: A woodland clearing a few miles from Kells with an old graveyard, deeply peaceful, with a Magic aura of 4 and perhaps other secrets. Its round tower stands eighty feet, roofless, with a window to each quarter; the High-King Niall mac Áeda is said to lie here. The Priory of St. Mary at Kells owns it and leaves it to sleep; a new covenant could be founded among the dead here if the prior agreed.

neighbours.name: Little Saltee
neighbours.summary:
The smaller of the two Saltee islands, five miles off the Wexford coast, empty but for the Paruchia of Nerius: the hermits' beehive cells, a small chapel, a cave system that holds their laboratories, a tall library tower, and a little graveyard of earlier hermits. It has no Magic aura; its aura is Divine 3.

The tides are dangerous and the rocky shore has no good landing. By custom no woman, maga or not, may come ashore.

neighbours.name: Great Saltee
neighbours.summary: The larger Saltee, home to twenty-eight people (two farming families and three fisher brothers, with wives and children) and the parish church of St. Mary. They serve the hermits of Little Saltee as covenfolk but never set foot there. A small clifftop shrine keeps the Paruchia's cathach, the arm of Saint Nerius, and the islanders watch over it. The book gives no aura beyond the church's.

neighbours.name: Gleann Molúra
neighbours.summary: A narrow dead-end glen in the Wicklow Mountains, seven miles long and under half a mile wide, between walls some 2000 feet high. One road runs in, and it ends at Lámbaird. The glen has a Magic aura of 2, rising to 4 where the covenant stands, and is home to what is left of the Uí Broin.

neighbours.name: Ashenrise Castle
neighbours.summary: A square English castle north of New Ross, some miles from the Barrow on its eastern side, with a square tower at each corner; its grounds hold a Magic aura of 1. Ralph fitz Stephen holds it, and the magi of Ashenrise live in three of its towers as his guests, two to a tower; the fourth is for the household. The courtyard has wooden barns, storehouses and stables. Half a mile west of it stands Rhiannon's corpse, facing Connacht and Munster.

neighbours.name: The Liberty of Leinster
neighbours.summary:
Strongbow's inheritance, the old kingdom of Leinster, held as a Liberty under the Lord of Ireland: its lord gathers the king's revenues and does justice in his name, and his wool and grain help feed the English crown. It is held by William Marshal the Younger, second Earl of Pembroke and Marshal of England like his father, the great William Marshal, the most famous knight of the age, who died last year (the same man is regent for the young king; see that record). The ports of Dublin, Wexford and Wicklow were kept back by Henry II under his own hand.

William is a widower since 1215, bringing up his six-year-old daughter quietly in Ireland; his short spell as a rebel in the barons' revolt in England has been forgiven. At Ferns he is building a square stone keep with a round tower at each corner, far ahead of any castle in England, Wales or Ireland. He also holds the Rock of Dunamase, and his father built Kilkenny and New Ross.

The curse. When he would not give back two manors his father had wrongly taken from the see, the Bishop of Ferns cursed the Marshal line to die out. The Pope has patched the quarrel up, but William keeps the manors, has no heir, and will not marry again until the curse is lifted; he swore to his father to keep the Irish lands whole.
neighbours.ruler: William Marshal the Younger, Earl of Pembroke

neighbours.name: Theobald Butler
neighbours.summary: Butler of Ireland, nineteen years old, holding Arklow, whose castle guards the harbour. His office gives him the right to hand the King of England a cup of wine at the coronation, and to take two barrels from every ship that lands wine at an Irish port, so his agents are busy in every harbour; at New Ross they enforce the right strictly.

neighbours.name: Sir Gerald de Prendergast
neighbours.summary: A young English knight of the chivalrous kind, holding the fortified manor of Enniscorthy, who dreams of raising a great castle there to match William Marshal the Younger's. Brave and romantic, he is well liked by the Irish round about as well as by the settlers.

neighbours.name: William fitz Maurice fitz Gerald
neighbours.summary: Son of Maurice fitz Gerald, Strongbow's Norman ally, who built the Black Castle on its headland over Wicklow harbour; he is married to Strongbow's daughter Aoife. Naas Castle is his seat, but he rules from the port of Wicklow, a stronghold of English power that the hill clans often attack, and leaves Robert de Birmingham as castellan of Naas.

neighbours.name: Ralph fitz Stephen
neighbours.summary: A second cousin of Raymond le Gros, given the castle now called Ashenrise for his part against the Uí Riain. He was captain of the grogs at Moles Magna in Normandy and brought its surviving magi here to his kinsmen; they live in his castle as permanent guests. He commands four knights and fifteen men-at-arms and is on good terms with the English lords nearby.

neighbours.name: Peter de Norrach, Baron Norragh
neighbours.summary: A descendant of Robert de St. Michael, a companion of Strongbow, holding Castle Norragh at Calverstown (Baile an Chalbhaigh). The Augustinian abbey of Kilrush, founded by William Marshal, is close by.

neighbours.name: William fitz Robert, Baron of Kells
neighbours.summary: Son of Geoffrey fitz Robert, whom William Marshal made seneschal at Kilkenny and who styled himself Baron of Kells; Marshal later came to distrust Geoffrey and held him hostage at Hereford, where he died in 1211. William succeeded him and holds Kilkenny's castle today.

neighbours.name: Thomas fitz Anthony
neighbours.summary: A Welsh lord who served Strongbow and founded Thomastown, half a mile north of the Irish settlement of Grianán, the sunny place. He lives there contentedly among many Welsh-speaking retainers and settlers, has walled the town against Osraighe raids, and built Grennan Castle as his home.

neighbours.name: Mac Giolla Phádraig (fitz Patrick) of Ossory
neighbours.summary: The old royal house of Ossory, the sons of Patrick, named for a great king of the Osraighe. They have largely accepted English rule and taken the name fitz Patrick, and as subjects of the English crown they keep much influence and power in the region. Many of their people remain hostile to the English. Irish.

neighbours.name: Mac Gilla Mo-Cholmóg (fitzDermot)
neighbours.summary: King of the Uí Dúnchada, one of the three families of the Uí Dúnlainge, ruling the land nearest Dublin. He came to terms with the invaders at once, allied with them and took the name fitzDermot. Irish.

neighbours.name: The Ua Túathal
neighbours.summary:
A family of the Uí Dúnlainge, the O'Tooles to the English, who lead the alliance of hill clans resisting the English from the Wicklow Mountains; they owe and pay the English no tribute. Each of the three families proclaims its own king and tries to rule the others. Saint Laurence O'Toole, archbishop and peacemaker, was of this clan.

With the Ua Broin they massacred three hundred of Dublin's newcomers on Black Monday, Easter Monday 1209. They are now hunted men and seldom come near Dublin, but they harass Naas, Wicklow and every road through the hills.
neighbours.ruler: the king of the Ua Túathal (the book does not name him)

neighbours.name: The Ua Broin
neighbours.summary:
The O'Byrnes: a branch of the Uí Faelain, a royal line of Leinster, who lost their old lands round Cilldara to the Normans. What is left of them lives in Gleann Molúra beside Lámbaird, whose covenfolk they have been since its founding, and fights the English from the hills beside the Ua Túathal. They owe no tribute. Irish.

Their chief, Cathasach Ua Broin, is young and green and leans on Dalton Ballaugh of Lámbaird; their seanchaidh Tadg Ua Broin keeps their traditions.

neighbours.name: The Uí Riain
neighbours.summary: An Irish túath of Ossory, once vassals of Raymond le Gros, whose ancestral ráth held the grave of Rhiannon, a daughter of the clan and once Prima of House Merinita. Raymond drove them from their homes after rumours of a rising, and in the fighting her body was taken. They bear a long grudge against every English lord on the Barrow.
neighbours.ruler: the chief of the Uí Riain (unnamed)

neighbours.name: Dublin
neighbours.summary:
A Viking port on the Liffey, for centuries a great slave market where English and Welsh captives were sold, a trade that has ended under English rule. The Ostmen who once ruled it have moved across the river to Ostmantown since the invasion. The English, once besieged here, have replaced the Norse stockade and ditch with a strong stone wall. Henry II kept Dublin, Wexford and Wicklow under his own hand, out of Strongbow's reach.

A great fire in 1190 burnt many houses and three churches, and many people left. A charter modelled on Bristol's brought settlers from Bristol and Wales to take their place: by 1220 a third of the citizens come of Bristol families, many of them merchants and craftsmen. Plague struck in 1208. On Easter Monday 1209 the Ua Broin and Ua Túathal fell on the newcomers at archery practice at the Hogges outside the walls, or gathering sticks in Cullen Woods, and killed three hundred; Black Monday is still kept with a militia march and the city on alert.

Royal power here lies with the viceroy, Archbishop Henry de Londres, whom his tenants and many citizens hate. Dublin Castle, begun by King John's order in 1204, is unfinished: a square curtain wall about a courtyard, with no keep but great round towers at each corner, immensely strong. The city has two cathedrals, Christchurch and St. Patrick's.
neighbours.ruler: the viceroy, Archbishop Henry de Londres

neighbours.name: Wexford
neighbours.summary:
A walled port at the mouth of the Slaney, on the south side of its harbour, busy with ships for England and the continent, still Norse in character. Long ago the youth Garman Garbh stole a queen's crown and fled across the mudflats; a witch raised river and sea together, drowning him and casting the crown ashore. The flats are still dangerous, and some think her curse lingers. Saint Yvorus, who preached here before Patrick, drove out the rats: none comes ashore from a ship, and none can breed in the town.

Diarmait mac Murchadha and Robert FitzStephen besieged it in 1169, the first blow of the conquest, until the Bishop of Ferns persuaded the town to let them in. It has taken English rule quietly since, with much intermarriage. Henry II, sailing from here for France in 1172, gave its milling rights to the Templars, who keep a small garrison.

neighbours.name: Bannow
neighbours.summary: A thriving port on a fine natural harbour where Strongbow's English first came ashore, camping in an old ráth on the headland before they marched on Wexford. Lately the bay has been silting up faster than anyone remembers, and the bigger ships must unload elsewhere.

neighbours.name: New Ross
neighbours.summary: An English town beside the old monastic ráth of Saint Abbán's monastery, in the old kingdom of Ossory. Chartered by the king in 1207, it was made a great port by William Marshal, who built a stone bridge over the river. It is as famous for pirates as for merchants, Irish raids have people talking of a town wall, and Theobald Butler's agents watch the wine ships closely. A frontier town, lawless whenever the younger Marshal's men look away.

neighbours.name: Ferns Castle and town
neighbours.summary: The small town at the heart of Ferns, with William Marshal the Younger's new castle rising in its centre, the most advanced in these islands. He lives here with his young daughter.

neighbours.name: Wicklow
neighbours.summary: Cill Mhantáin to the Irish, the church of the toothless one: a Viking port that still feels Norse, overlooked by the Black Castle on its rocky headland. A seat of English power, it is heavily garrisoned against the Ua Broin and Ua Túathal, who often strike at town and castle from the hills.

neighbours.name: Arklow
neighbours.summary: A harbour town guarded by Theobald Butler's castle; the Uí Enechglaiss, driven out of Meath in the fifth century, still live round about. The tide rock lies offshore.

neighbours.name: Kildare
neighbours.summary: Cill Dara, one of the largest ráths in the region, a flourishing market centre where Saint Brigid founded a double house of monks and nuns late in the fifth century. It was the seat of the Uí Dúnlainge, the royal line of northern Leinster; they have not reached for a crown in two centuries, but their three families, the Ua Broin, the Ua Túathal and the Uí Dúnchada, still hold the region and scheme against each other. Saint Brigid's sacred fire still burns here.

neighbours.name: Naas
neighbours.summary:
Nás na Ríogh, where kings once met: a small town growing fast as English settlers arrive. They have rededicated Saint Patrick's church to Saint David, and the Knights Hospitaller run it. The kings of Leinster were once made here in sacred rites on the great earthwork called the dún of Naas; holding Naas is thought to carry some right to rule the kingdom, but the rites may be forgotten. Saint Fechin's Cross stands in the market.

It lies on the border of the Ua Broin and Ua Túathal, who once fought each other here and now raid the town together, so King John, who called the nobles here to submit in 1206, had a strong castle built.

The Boroimhe. King Eochaid Aincheaun of Leinster married Darina, daughter of the High-King Túathal Techtmar, then craved her sister Fithir: he shut Darina up in his hall here, told her father she had died, and wed Fithir. Darina broke out during the feast, Fithir dropped dead at the sight of her, and Túathal came for vengeance, beheaded Eochaid and burnt Naas. Leinster then owed Tara a tribute every second year of 15,000 each of cows, pigs, linen cloths, silver chains, goats and copper cauldrons, a vast cauldron, and 30 red-eared white cows. Brian Bóramha revived it; a clever priest later had a King of Meath give it up for ever.
neighbours.ruler: William fitz Maurice fitz Gerald (castellan Robert de Birmingham)

neighbours.name: Kilkenny
neighbours.summary:
Cill Chainnigh, an old monastic community by a ford of the Nore with a church of Saint Canice. William Marshal built a great four-towered castle here in 1195, walled and ditched, to hold down the Osraighe, married Strongbow's daughter Isabel de Clare here, and walled the town; it was chartered in 1207 and has thrived.

It has two hearts: Irishtown about the monastery, outside the walls, and the English Hightown within them. Irishtown has the great stone cathedral of Ossory, still being built and dogged by accidents. The fitz Patricks keep much influence in the district.
neighbours.ruler: William fitz Robert, Baron of Kells

neighbours.name: Kells (Ossory)
neighbours.summary: A small walled town, not the Kells in Meath, called the city of the seven castles for the seven towers the English built to guard the Augustinian Priory of St. Mary. It has grown prosperous under English rule, but Osraighe clans still attack it. Kilree Tower is a few miles off.

neighbours.name: Thomastown (Grianán)
neighbours.summary: Thomas fitz Anthony's walled town, beside the Irish village of Grianán, full of Welsh speakers; Grennan Castle is his home. Jerpoint Abbey is near.

neighbours.name: Bishopric of Ferns
neighbours.summary: Irish. Its elderly bishop, the Cistercian Ua Maíl Mhuaidh, is Irish-born yet a favourite of the English crown and of Rome, though he once preached that Irish clergy only took to sins of the flesh after English and Welsh priests showed them how. He is famed for holiness and justice. He cursed the Marshal line to die out when William the Younger would not return two manors his father had seized; the Pope has made them reconcile, but the manors are still held. The first bishop was Saint Yvorus, who came before Patrick and drove the rats out of Ferns and Wexford.

links.note: Saint Abbán, venerated in Wexford and Ferns

neighbours.name: St. Mary's Abbey, Ferns
neighbours.summary: Irish. An Augustinian house founded by Diarmait mac Murchadha where Saint Máedóc of Ferns's monastery once stood; a centre of the reforming party.

neighbours.name: Baltinglass Abbey
neighbours.summary: Irish. The Valley of Salvation, a Cistercian house founded by Diarmait mac Murchadha in 1148 with monks from Mellifont: 38 monks and 50 lay brothers. It is caught up in the Conspiracy of Mellifont, officially backing its mother house against the Cistercian Order; the abbot is all for Mellifont's defiance, but his monks are loyal to Cîteaux. The monks are mostly keen to march up the hill one Christmas Day and set a great wooden cross on the faerie mound; so far the abbot urges caution.

neighbours.name: The Monastery of Glendalough
neighbours.summary: Irish. Saint Kevin's monastery, a sanctuary within its round wall, whose hermits resist the English churchmen. It was the seat of a diocese until 1214, when the English joined it to Dublin's. Its monks gather and share out the Fruit of Saint Kevin. Indrechtach of the Paruchia was a monk here until his Gift drove him out.

neighbours.name: Christchurch Cathedral, Dublin
neighbours.summary: Anglo-Irish. The Norse cathedral King Sitric built in the eleventh century, which looked to Canterbury, not Armagh. In 1168 the saintly archbishop Lorcán Ua Túathal (Saint Laurence O'Toole), a great peacemaker between English and Irish, made it an Augustinian priory; it holds his shrine, though he died and lies buried in Normandy, and a chapel Strongbow gave to the English Saint Edmund. The Augustinians are rebuilding it in stone.

neighbours.name: St. Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin
neighbours.summary: Anglo-Irish. Dublin's second cathedral, begun in 1198 by the English archbishop John Comyns, Lorcán's successor, and served by thirteen canons. Henry de Londres carries on the building and has let the canons elect a dean.

neighbours.name: The Sacred Fire of Saint Brigid, Kildare
neighbours.summary:
Irish. Saint Brigid's abbey at Kildare was ruled by an abbess, the comarba Naomh Bríd, head of one of the mightiest paruchiae and the only one led by a woman. Diarmait mac Murchadha threw out the abbess in 1132 for his own niece; the reformers made the abbess answer to the bishop at the Synod of Kells in 1152; and when the niece died in 1171 the English shut the abbey.

A few stayed to tend the fire Brigid lit herself, which has never gone out, even without fuel. It burns outside the church inside a hedge of sharp thorns that only the nineteen nuns of its vigil can pass unharmed; one keeps watch each night, and any man who forces his way in is said to fall under a divine curse. Archbishop Henry de Londres has sworn in 1220 to put it out, to prove it superstition, and also because Naomh Bríd is the patroness of the restless Uí Dúnlainge.

links.note: Saint Brigid, a patron of Ireland

neighbours.name: Kilrush Abbey
neighbours.summary: Anglo-Irish. An Augustinian abbey near Calverstown, founded by William Marshal.

neighbours.name: Bishopric of Ossory
neighbours.summary: Irish in its origins. In 1202 Bishop Felix O'Dulany moved the see to Kilkenny and began a great stone cathedral of Saint Canice in Irishtown; he died the same year, but the work goes on, plagued by accidents. The book does not name the bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Priory of St. Mary, Kells
neighbours.summary: Anglo-Irish. An Augustinian priory founded in 1193 by Geoffrey fitz Robert, guarded by the seven towers of Kells. It owns Kilree Tower and lets it lie undisturbed.

neighbours.name: Jerpoint Abbey
neighbours.summary:
Irish. The Cistercian abbey of St. Nicholas, which Donogh O'Donoghoe, an Osraighe king, founded in 1180; his line backed the Irish reformers. Before it stood a Benedictine house that failed, founded in 1160 by King Domnall Mac Giolla Phádraig to keep the relics of Saint Nicholas, which Nicholas de Frainet, one of seven knights home from crusade, had brought. The abbey has joined the revolt against the Cistercian Order.

The grave of Saint Nicholas lies in a ruined church inside the grounds: the ancient bishop of Asia Minor who raised three murdered children from a pickling barrel, honoured with a mass each Christmas.

neighbours.name: St. Mary's Church, Great Saltee
neighbours.summary: Irish. The parish church of Great Saltee, where the hermits of the Paruchia cross every Sunday for mass. Its priest, Father Diarmaid, is a firm friend of the covenant and guards his lonely parish; some old fault got him sent here.

neighbours.name: Meath
neighbours.summary:
Mide, 'the middle': the fifth province of Ireland and the smallest, counted a province rather than one more kingdom because of what it means. The legend says Túathal Techtmar, son of a deposed high-king, was carried in his mother's womb to Scotland when the four provincial kings rose against his father (his mother Eithne may be Bóinn under another name). Twenty years of famine followed under the usurper from Ulster until Túathal came back with an army, beat the kings of all four provinces in turn, and called them to Tara, where he gave laws and carved out a new province round the hill to be the high-kings' own land.

Late in the fifth century the Uí Enechglaiss were driven south to Arklow, where they still live, and the Uí Mael Sechlainn, the Southern Uí Néill, took Meath and gave Ireland several high-kings. They in turn fled when the English came: the last king of Meath was put down in 1172 and the kingdom given to Hugh de Lacy, who kept it until he died in 1186 though Henry II had turned against him. Tighearnán Ua Ruairc of Bréifne contested the grant and was slain at a parley on the Hill of Tlachtga, and Hugh's son Walter de Lacy holds Meath for the English today. It is the one province with no Gaelic dialect of its own.

A Liberty. Meath, Leinster and the earldom of Ulster are Liberties: the Crown governs each through a grantee, here Walter de Lacy, who gathers the king's revenue and does justice, and answers in turn to the Justiciar of Ireland. The wool and grain of the Liberties leave the Crown a surplus, but the king distrusts his great Irish lords; he takes their sons as hostages, orders them off to England or France, or hands their lands to others before any grows too strong.

Justice. Since 1217 itinerant justices have ridden circuits through the Liberties, holding assizes under English common law. An Irishman in their court needs an interpreter, has little hope in a law he does not know, and finds his word weighed below an Englishman's; among themselves the Irish keep the Brehon Laws and see the assizes as a shield for English privilege.

Places: the Hill of Tara, where the Tribunal meets; the Hill of Uisneach at the centre of Ireland; the Brú na Bóinne and New Grange on the bend of the Boyne; the Hills of Tlachtga and Tailten; Clonmacnoise on the Shannon; and the Eiscir Riada, the ridge dividing Leth Cuinn from Leth Moga. Towns: Drogheda-in-Meath, Trim and Kells. Churches: Mellifont, Bective, Kells, Trim and Clonmacnoise. No covenant stands in Meath, though Praesis looks across Lough Ree at it from the Connacht side.

Story seed: The Swords of the Fer Caille. Savage warriors put villages on the Meath bank of the Sionainne to the sword, and the Bishop of Athlone asks Leinster's magi for help. The raiders are Fer Caille, faeries seeking mortal heroes to fight, and Connachta men are following their lead against Meath's holdings. How do the magi arm their people, and what do they order done with the men of Connacht?

Story seed: The Cry of the Banshee. A banshee wails, and the youngest of the family of Congal Mac an Fhailghigh sees her by their door. The boy runs into the night to find the characters and begs them to stop her or change his family's doom. Why, on this cold dark night, are so many English clergy and knights riding into town?

neighbours.name: The Hill of Tara
neighbours.summary:
Cnoc na Teamhrach, the seat of Ireland's ancient kingship and the setting of countless Irish tales, where the Hibernian Tribunal meets every seven years. In 1220 it lies quiet, famous everywhere yet left to grass and briar. It is a broad, low mound ringed by the ditch of an old ringfort, with lesser ráths and other ancient, magical works about it, and a Magic aura of 6 over the whole site except the Mound of Hostages, which is the Tuatha Dé's (Faerie 7). The aura has a Respectful aspect (Realms of Power: Magic), giving everyone present a Respectful +2 Personality Trait, and every Samhain, when sacred fires used to burn here, the auras rise by 2.

The Uí Mael Sechlainn styled themselves Kings of Tara until de Lacy took Meath in 1172, though by then the title was only ceremonial. In the sixth century Saint Ruadán foretold that King Diarmait would die in his own hall here, for dragging men out of sanctuary in the saint's church; the hall burned and a falling beam killed him as foretold, and ever since it has been held that the saint's curse lets no hall stand on the hill. The greatest of Tara's kings was Cormac mac Airt, whom Fionn mac Cumhaill often served; his reign was a golden age, and many earthworks are the ruins of his halls. Here too King Conaire, son of a bird-man and so bound never to harm a bird, was made king after shapechangers in bird form laid geasa on him and sent him naked into Tara, fulfilling the chief druid's omen; he reigned well until he broke those geasa one by one and fell to three exiled brothers.

Faeries replay the old stories here, such as Áillen mac Midgna setting the hall alight and Fionn driving him off; Áillen, a three-headed faerie magician of northern Connacht, still burns Tara from time to time. Mortals seldom come, except that every seventh year the magi of Hibernia gather here with the Coill Trí's envoys and great beings of Magic and Faerie. Circulus Ruber raises a temporary camp by magic for each meeting, and the sessions are held in the large ráth on the hilltop around the Lia Fáil. The five High Roads of Ireland start from the royal fort at Tara.

neighbours.name: The Mound of Hostages
neighbours.summary: A mound on the Hill of Tara that belongs to the Tuatha Dé, the one part of the hill outside its Magic aura: a Faerie aura of 7, rising by 2 at Samhain like the rest of Tara.

neighbours.name: The Lia Fáil
neighbours.summary: The Stone of Fál, or Stone of Destiny, one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé brought to Ireland, which cries out under the foot of the rightful king. It stands at the top of the Hill of Tara inside the great ráth where every session of the Hibernian Tribunal is held, in the hill's Magic aura of 6.

neighbours.name: The Hill of Uisneach
neighbours.summary:
The hill (OOSH-nakh) at the mystic centre of Ireland, with a strong Magic aura of 5, where all five provinces touch at the Stone of Division. The druids kindled a great Bealtaine fire here, visible from Tara, to open the feast for the whole island. Here the Milesians met Ériu, Banba and Fódla, and Ériu gave Ireland her name; Saint Brigid made her vows here, both as a nun and as a bishop. Many of the Tuatha Dé lie asleep under the hill's numerous sídhe, and the druid Merlin carried off many of the stones of Stonehenge from this place.

The aura drew a covenant here in the Order's first years in Hibernia, but one summer evening it disappeared without trace; only scraps of record remain and even its name is lost (see the ruin of the covenant of Uisneach). Country tales tell of a great magician who wished to rule all Ireland, broke a geas, and was taken by the Good Folk for his pride. Another covenant will probably be founded here one day.

neighbours.name: The Ail na Míreann
neighbours.summary: The Stone of Division on the Hill of Uisneach, where the borders of Ulster, Meath, Leinster, Munster and Connacht meet. It is an Arcane Connection to all five provinces, for anyone bold enough to try a spell on a whole province, and gives a x3 Sympathetic Magic modifier. It is the customary place to swear oaths and seal treaties that bind the whole Tribunal.

neighbours.name: The Brú na Bóinne
neighbours.summary:
A plain of nearly two thousand acres in the bend of the Boyne, crowded with sídhe, standing stones and dolmens, the river closing it on the south, west and east. Until lately it lay wild and half forgotten; now Mellifont's monks have laid nine granges over it, fortified farms the size of manors whose barns and outbuildings ring each one and sit on high ground, often on old sídhe and ráths. With the scrub cleared the forty sídhe stand out plainly, and the faeries asleep inside may be stirring.

Many stones, and some old bones and slates, carry marks in a wholly unknown script, which, gathered and somehow read, might open the old mysteries once worked here (Ancient Magic). Magic and Faerie auras of many strengths shift and wander across the plain (the pack gives it Faerie 4), and no magus has found out why. Hibernian magi mostly keep away, fearing to wake the Tuatha Dé who sleep here. The Dagdha built it, and Bóinn (see the Bestiary) is often met here, but it is the home of their son Aonghus mac Óg, god of youth and lovers, who tricked his father out of it; he is perilous to cross. In 778 the four founders of the Order in Hibernia dug the Dagda's cauldron out of one of its mounds, then held a barrow here for a year against the high-king's men.
neighbours.secrets: The monks working among the barrows may have stumbled on some old magical secret, which could lie behind the Conspiracy of Mellifont.

neighbours.name: New Grange
neighbours.summary:
Mellifont's newest grange on the Brú na Bóinne, and beside it the greatest sídh of the plain, the home of Aonghus mac Óg, which people are starting to call Newgrange after the farm. The lay brothers here tell of frightening happenings, and trooping faeries (see the Bestiary) have trampled and spoiled the crops many times. The book gives the sídh no number; the pack gives it Faerie 5.

Story seed: The Haunting of New Grange. Mellifont's lay brothers at New Grange tell of terrors and of trooping faeries wrecking the crops; then the steward and his family vanish one summer evening, and Abbot Thomas, troubled enough by his revolt, seeks help at once. Can the characters save the monks from Aonghus's anger (see The Conspiracy of Mellifont)?

neighbours.name: The Hill of Tlachtga
neighbours.summary:
A ráth-crowned hill, one of the royal sites of Meath, where the faerie druidess Tlachtga, Mug Ruith's daughter, sleeps in her sídh. Mug Ruith still calls now and then in his marvellous flying machine, and she sometimes comes out to talk with mortals who wander onto the hill. She helped her father build that machine while he studied under Simon Magus, until Simon raped her; she fled home, her father broke with the sorcerer (whom Saint Paul later slew), and here she bore the triplets Doirb, Cumma and Muach before withdrawing into the hill. The druids lit their Samhain fires on it in her memory. The book gives no aura; the pack gives Faerie 3.

Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair called a vast assembly here in 1168, and in 1171 Tighearnán Ua Ruairc of Bréifne met Hugh de Lacy here under truce to dispute Meath; a brawl broke out, de Lacy's interpreter was killed, de Lacy ran, and his men speared Tighearnán as he mounted, perhaps by design. Tlachtga stirred for neither.

neighbours.name: Tailten
neighbours.summary:
The burial place of Tailtu, a Spanish princess wed to Eochaid mac Eirc, last Fir Bolg high-king, who built his capital here; it was razed after he fell against the Tuatha Dé, and nothing of it is left, though the Uí Néill still hold the site dear. Captured by the Tuatha Dé, Tailtu fostered Lugh, and died of clearing Ireland's plains of forest for the plough; she was buried here at Lammas amid great grief.

Tailten Fair each Lammas (1 August) remembers her and the games the Fir Bolg and Tuatha Dé held before they came to battle: a merry, bawdy gathering and one of Ireland's few great markets, with wrestling, horse races, foreign wares and luxuries. Tailten Marriages, for a year and a day, were made here until the English and the Church reformers banned them a few years ago, to the people's disgust. Strangely, the site has a Magic aura of 3 by day and a Faerie aura of 3 by night.

neighbours.name: The Eiscir Riada
neighbours.summary: The best known of the eskers, long banks of sand and gravel that rise as much as fifty feet over the flat bogs and plains of central Ireland and have served as roads since ancient times; some say the Fomórach, the Fir Bolg or the Tuatha Dé built them, others that they are serpents turned to earth when Saint Patrick banished them. The Eiscir Riada runs from Galway Bay toward Dublin and carries the Great Highway (An tSlí Mhór), one of the High Roads, along its crest from Durrow Abbey to Clonmacnoise. It is the line between Conn's Half, Leth Cuinn, to the north and Mogha's Half, Leth Moga, to the south, which gave the two Mercer Houses their names.

neighbours.name: Clonmacnoise
neighbours.summary:
One of Ireland's most renowned old monastic sites, on the east bank of the Shannon where Meath meets Connacht: a busy town grown round the monastery, yet calm and holy, with a Dominion aura of 3 over the whole town, stronger in the graveyard and by the three high crosses that stand in its streets. A high-king built the stone cathedral in 909, and Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, the last High-King of Ireland, was buried here in 1198. Pilgrims visit Saint Ciarán's tomb in the oldest church and then pray in each of the others, as custom now asks. The English have put a small stone keep on the hill above.

The Uí Mael Sechlainn, who settled here after losing Meath in 1172, built Temple Melaghlin in 1200 as their dynasty's church, and the little Romanesque church by the river with its bell tower, home of one of Ireland's ancient sacred bells, and Temple Connor; from here they plot to win back Meath. Derbforgaill, wife of Tighearnán Mór Ua Ruairc and the 'Helen of Ireland' whose abduction by Diarmait began the English war, endowed the Nun's Church in 1160.

neighbours.name: The North Cross of Clonmacnoise
neighbours.summary: One of the three great carved crosses, thirteen to fifteen feet high, in Clonmacnoise's streets; its shaft bears an old pagan carving of Cernunnos, the Celtic god of fertility. Taken away from Clonmacnoise, the stone might take back its first aura, but the whole countryside would rise against the thieves. The South Cross and the Cross of the Scriptures show ordinary Bible scenes in superb work. The book says only that the Dominion is stronger by the crosses; the pack gives Divine 4.

neighbours.name: The Faerie Stone of Clonmacnoise
neighbours.summary: One of several big yellow sandstone boulders in Clonmacnoise, also called the Horseman's Stone. It bears the same strange script as the stones of the Brú na Bóinne and the prints of two human feet, and locals hold it the door of a faerie fort: a rider in golden armour was said to come out and cross the land on Midsummer night, the Feast of John the Baptist, but none has seen him for centuries, perhaps because the priests lead a procession to the rock and bless it that day. It sits in the town's Dominion aura of 3. Twenty years ago Josiane of Merinita, of the Normandy Tribunal, shrank it with Terram magic and led it off on a mule for her laboratory, but by morning it was gone, and back in Clonmacnoise she found it where she had first seen it; she sensibly did not try again.
neighbours.secrets: Whatever makes the stone return, it is bound to this spot; the faerie fort behind it may still be inhabited.

neighbours.name: Henry III, Lord of Ireland
neighbours.summary:
Henry III, King of England and Lord of Ireland, a boy of fourteen in 1220. His lordship takes in the Liberties of Meath, Leinster and Ulster, the royal shires and cities round Dublin, Waterford and the other ports, and the tribute of the Irish kings who have submitted, Connacht's under the Treaty of Windsor among them. He rules through a regent, William Marshal the younger, and in Ireland through his viceroy, Archbishop Henry de Londres of Dublin.

Like his forebears he eyes his great Irish lords warily: he keeps their sons as hostages for their good behaviour, calls them away to serve in England or France, or gives their estates to rivals. Lords of the Liberties keep what their lands yield; the king's shires pass most of their rents to him, and a shire with a city in it can make its keeper richer than a lord of a Liberty. The Liberties' wool and grain leave the Crown a surplus.

neighbours.name: William Marshal the Younger, Regent
neighbours.summary:
The regent for the young king, as the book has it: William Marshal the younger, thirty years old, Earl of Pembroke, who took up the regency when his famous father, the greatest knight of the age, died in 1219. He lives about Kilkenny, Ferns and Trim (his lands in Leinster are that part's to tell), and is betrothed to the king's five-year-old sister, Eleanor of Leicester.

In real history the elder Marshal's regency passed to others in 1219; the book makes the son regent, and the pack follows the book.

neighbours.name: Henry de Londres, Viceroy of Ireland
neighbours.summary:
Henry de Londres, Archbishop of Dublin, holds the king's authority in Ireland as viceroy, the Justiciar to whom the lords of the Liberties answer; his see is the Church part's record. He is energetic, ambitious and personally fearless, and almost universally loathed. He once summoned his tenants to show the deeds to their lands, then tried to throw the parchments on the fire; they seized him, thrashed his men, pulled their deeds back by main force and frightened him into granting their rights, and they call him 'Henry the Scorcher'. He squeezes Dublin's tithes hard, cared little for those the fire of 1190 ruined, levied the royal tallage on the citizens in 1217, and simply takes what he fancies from merchants.

He has sworn to put out Saint Brigid's Sacred Fire at Kildare. He will appoint only English-born bishops, a policy the Pope has ruled unlawful, and claims for Dublin primacy over Armagh (and Cashel), which has turned even the Irish reform party against him and wrecked much of the trust between the reformers and the English clergy. Itinerant justices hold his assizes in the Liberties.
neighbours.secrets: The Pope's ruling against his English-only bishops has not yet reached Dublin; he does not know he has lost.

neighbours.name: Walter de Lacy, Lord of Meath
neighbours.summary:
Walter de Lacy, son of Hugh de Lacy the conqueror of Meath and brother of Hugh de Lacy, Earl of Ulster, holds the Liberty of Meath for the Crown: he gathers the king's revenues, does justice, and answers to the Justiciar of Ireland.
