He built Trim Castle, the largest stone castle in Ireland, as the seat of Meath's government, and is often there with his household; he also built Drogheda's castle, takes customs and imposts at its port, and holds Carbury castle in Leinster, which his father seized from Meiler FitzHenry. Tighearnán Ua Ruairc of Bréifne, who disputed his father's grant, is dead.

He has thrown castles westward to push into Connacht, among them the motte at Kilmore in Bréifne (1211). If your saga follows history, Cathal Uí Raghallaigh takes Kilmore in 1224 and pulls it down, and others of his castles go the same way.

neighbours.name: The Itinerant Justices
neighbours.summary: Since 1217 the king's justice in the Liberties has been done by judges who ride a circuit from county to county, sitting at assizes under English common law. An Irish party must find an interpreter, can make little of the strange procedure, and sees his testimony counted for less than an English witness's; to the Irish, who keep the Brehon Laws among themselves, the assizes are a tool of oppression that guards English privilege.

details.wants: To bring English common law and the king's peace to the Liberties
details.offers: Judgement at the assizes, for those who can use English law

neighbours.name: Richard de Capella, Baron of Delvin
neighbours.summary: Hugh de Lacy built the stone castle at Delvin and gave it to his brother-in-law Sir Gilbert Nugent, first Baron Delvin. Gilbert's son Richard, the second baron, called Richard de Capella, 'Richard of the horses', lives for horse breeding. He holds a fine horse fair at Delvin each year and races open to anyone with a good mount, with prizes of better horses still, and for a truly great rider a place at his court and maybe a knighthood. An English (Anglo-Irish) lord.

neighbours.name: The Uí Mael Sechlainn
neighbours.summary: The Southern Uí Néill, the Máel Sechnaill, one of the five bloods of Ireland: kings of Meath and of Tara from the late fifth century, who gave Ireland several high-kings until the English took their kingdom in 1172. They have settled round Clonmacnoise, where Temple Melaghlin is their royal church, and scheme to retake the throne of Meath. A Gaelic dynasty without a kingdom, they owe tribute to no one and receive none; the book names no living head.

neighbours.name: Mellifont Abbey
neighbours.summary:
The greatest Cistercian house in Ireland, near Drogheda, founded in 1140 by Saint Malachy of Armagh on land from the King of Meath; an Irish house. It is mother to Bective, Baltinglass and twenty-three more Cistercian abbeys across Ireland, and with a hundred monks and three hundred lay brothers it rules the Order in Ireland. Its first abbot, Saint Christian, reformed monastic life well beyond his Order and helped the Irish reformers bring in dioceses and weaken the paruchiae, yet Mellifont's abbots grew as mighty as any comarba: in 1154 a synod here, urged by the abbot, excommunicated and exiled Donnchadh Ua Maeleachlainn, King of Meath, and set up his brother Diarmaid instead.

The Conspiracy of Mellifont. Since the invasion Irish and English monks have drawn apart, and tales of corruption and loose living reached Cîteaux; in 1216 a visitation came to restore the Rule, and the monks barred the gates against their superiors, a thing unheard of that has shaken monks across Mythic Europe. The general chapter deposed Abbot Thomas in 1217, but he still rules, upheld by his monks and the daughter houses. Cîteaux is readying a deputation to restore discipline and remove the guilty abbots, and the Pope may step in. Its nine granges cover the Brú na Bóinne.

Irish Church. In the quarrel of the two Churches the revolt stands for more than monastic discipline: since the invasion the Irish monks and the English Cistercians have pulled apart, and the Irish daughter houses that back the abbot are also backing an Irish house against an order the English favour.

neighbours.name: Bective Abbey
neighbours.summary: A strong Cistercian abbey above the Boyne, a daughter of Mellifont, where Hugh de Lacy lies buried. Its monks welcome travellers more warmly than most Cistercians. It has joined the Conspiracy of Mellifont, standing with its mother house against the Order. An Irish house.

neighbours.name: The Monastery of Kells
neighbours.summary:
Saint Columba's monastery at Kells in Meath (not the Kells in Leinster), with a church Saint Patrick founded; the town has grown about it in the Irish way. Its abbot, comarba Columcille, heads the paruchia of Saint Columba and rules the town. Kells was briefly the seat of a short-lived diocese, and here in 1152 began the synod (soon moved to Mellifont) that broke the comarbai's power and remade the Irish Church on dioceses rather than monasteries. An Irish house.

It keeps two famous books: the Book of Kells, closely guarded since a theft in the eleventh century, and the battle psalter of the Ó Domhnaill clan, left here for safe keeping by one of that Donegal family.

neighbours.name: The Abbey of Saint Mary, Trim
neighbours.summary: An Augustinian abbey of Saint Mary that Saint Malachy founded at Trim in 1140, beside the church of Saint Lommán, which Saint Patrick founded and which was burned twice, in 1008 and 1127, by enemies of those sheltering in it, then rebuilt. An Irish house in an English castle town.

neighbours.name: The Monastery of Clonmacnoise
neighbours.summary: Saint Ciarán's great monastery on the Shannon, with its stone cathedral of 909 and a ring of lesser churches: Temple Melaghlin of the Uí Mael Sechlainn, their small church by the river with its bell tower and ancient bell, Temple Connor, Derbforgaill's Nun's Church, and the oldest, where Ciarán is buried and pilgrims begin their round. Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, the last high-king, lies here. An Irish house; the whole town is under a Dominion aura of 3.

neighbours.name: Drogheda-in-Meath
neighbours.summary: A busy port astride the Boyne, wholly English and heavily garrisoned: Hugh de Lacy built the walled new town and Walter de Lacy the stone castle on the hill to its south. Drogheda-in-Airgialla faces it across the river to the north. Ships putting in are searched for wine by Theobald Butler's agents and pay Walter de Lacy's customs and imposts, yet trade from Scandinavia, Iceland and all the British Isles never stops. Mellifont Abbey stands near by.

neighbours.name: Trim
neighbours.summary: Home of the Cenél Lóegairi túath and, above all, of Trim Castle, the largest stone castle in Ireland, which Walter de Lacy raised on a hill to govern Meath in place of the ringwork his father built and the Irish destroyed. De Lacy and his household are often here. Saint Patrick's church of Saint Lommán and Saint Malachy's Augustinian abbey of Saint Mary stand in the town. The castle was lately the scene of a strange affair, the tale of the Three Sisters of Trim.
neighbours.secrets: The book names the Three Sisters of Trim but tells nothing more of them: the storyguide decides what happened.

neighbours.name: Kells
neighbours.summary: An Irish town grown round Saint Columba's monastery and ruled by its abbot (Kells in Meath, not Kells in Leinster). It gave its name to the synod of 1152 that remade the Irish Church, and keeps the Book of Kells.
neighbours.ruler: The abbot of Kells, comarba Columcille

neighbours.name: The Ostmen
neighbours.summary:
The Norse of Ireland's port towns, 'Eastmen' from the lands they came from. Viking raiders who began wintering in Ireland in the ninth century made the island's first cities out of their winter camps, the longphorts: Dublin, Waterford, Wexford, Cork and Limerick, which are Ostman homes still. When the raiding stopped and the Irish had learned to use Norse weapons as well as the Norse, the two settled into an uneasy peace; the Ostmen became Christian and married into the Irish, ruling their towns as a warrior elite. The English invasion ended Norse rule of the ports, but the Ostmen remain a people apart.

The Finn-Gaill, 'white foreigners', of Dublin now speak Leinster Gaelic; the Dubh-Gaill, 'black foreigners', of Wexford, Limerick, Waterford and Cork still speak the Norwegian dialect of West Norse. In Dublin they have moved north across the Liffey since the English came. Their rune wizards, whom the Order called the 'Order of Odin' in 832, fought the Hibernian magi in many indecisive skirmishes but never in open war.

details.decides: Councils of the leading families in each city
details.wants: Their trade, their quarters in the ports and their standing apart
details.offers: Ships, sea trade with Scandinavia and Iceland, and knowledge of the ports

neighbours.name: Ulster
neighbours.summary:
Ulaid, the most northerly of Ireland's provinces. In the days of King Conchobhar mac Neasa, who held court at Emhain Mhacha, its people, the Ulaidh, gave Ireland many of its greatest tales of kings and heroes, the Ruadhraigheacht or Ulster Cycle: the wars of the Ulaidh with the Connachta, Conchobhar's rivalry with Fearghus mac Róich, the strife of the two great bulls, and the deeds of Cú Chulainn. No kingdom of the province has an Ulaidh king any longer, yet Ulstermen keep a fierce pride in their past and hold together remarkably well for a people so long ruled by outsiders. The druids linked the north with war and strife, and the province's story bears them out.

In 1220 it holds three Gaelic kingdoms, Tír Chonaill in the west, Tír Eóghain in the north and centre and Airgíalla in the south, with the English Earldom of Ulster in the east under Hugh de Lacy; off the north coast lie the islands of Tír Fhomóraig, the last refuge of the Fomórach. Three houses of the Order stand here: the Mercer House of Leth Cuinn on Lough Neagh, Qui Sonant Pro Quieto in the Cuailnge mountains and Vigil on Cionn Mhálanna.

The peoples. Long ago the north was Tír Fhomóraig, the Fomórach's land from coast to coast, lording it over the Nemedians and the Tuatha Dé; when that race was driven out the Érainn took the land. The Érainn, one of the four root races sprung from Míl Espáine and once a client tribe of the Connachta, survived longest here as the Ulaidh, worshipping Dáire (a northern name for the Dagda) and Macha, goddess of horses and sovereignty. Legend says Conchobhar died on the day of the Crucifixion of an old wound dealt by magic, his soul kept in his skull until Saint Patrick, hearing it cry out, wept over it and so baptised it into Heaven.

The Connachta pressed north up the Boyne valley until the Ulaidh fell back into the east; two of the four sons of Niall of the Nine Hostages carved out the west and centre, and the nine sub-kingdoms of Airgíalla each gave the high king a hostage, hence his byname. Hence the commons of the west and middle are Érainn with Connachta lords over them. The Ulaidh of pure descent are the Dál bhFiatach, lords of the east from Downpatrick until the English arrived, sometimes allied with and sometimes rivals of the Dál nAraidhe; some of their families still suffer Macha's Birth-Pangs, the curse laid on Ulstermen of the true blood.

The Cruithnigh, the Picts of Scotland, are not a root race. They came seeking wives, having no women, and Éireamhóin mac Míl gave them Mílesian widows on condition that women lead them, as they still do. Their kingdom of Dál nAraidhe once reached over the north-east, the Isle of Man and Kintyre, but it was failing when its druids were ground between Diedne, who hunted pagan priesthoods that would not join her House, and Pralix, who stood with Damhan-Allaidh. A few túatha remain in the north of the province and about Drogheda, with scattered folk elsewhere in the north and west. They run a little shorter and darker than the Gaels, love clothes of many colours and often tattoo themselves; a few pockets of their old religion survive, in Tír Fhomóraig at least, with priests just like the gruagachan.

The English. John de Courcy was granted Ulster by the English king if he could win it, and took the grant at its word: with twenty-two knights and some three hundred men he marched through Meath and Airgíalla and fell on Down on 1 February 1177. Ulster's king, Ruaidhrí mac Con Ulad Mac Duinn Sléibe, could not meet him in the field while Macha's curse lay on his men; he came back a week later with an army, but the Ulaidh broke at the sight of armoured knights on horseback, and even with the Cenél nEóghain beside them later that year they could not shift him. De Courcy, who seemed to have God's favour, soon held everything east of the Bann. In 1196 he beat the king of Tír Chonaill and made him pay tribute, and after an Irishman killed his brother at his court in 1198 he laid waste the north. When his old enemy John became king in 1201 he unwisely made common cause with Cathal Crobhdearg Ua Conchobhair of Connacht, and in 1203 Hugh de Lacy, younger son of the Lord of Meath, arrested him as a rebel; in May 1205 John made Hugh the first Earl of Ulster, with all the land de Courcy had held on the day of his defeat.

Plagues. Tír Chonaill has loosed several plagues great enough to be named in the annals: the Crom Chonaill in the sixth century, the Buidhe Chonaill in the seventh, a pestilence in 986 when demons were seen dancing among the dead, and the Rogh Rámhach of 1084, said to have killed a quarter of Ireland; the Scuab a Fánait foretold in 1096 never came. A great dragon is said to have flown overhead before each, and some note that the Fomórach once killed the Partholónians with plague, and that their last remnant lives on the islands just north of Tír Chonaill.

Vis lies at Sliabh Crúibe (stones carried to its summit), held by no one.

Story seed: Recovering the First Christian Mission. An Ulster monastery's book says Palladius, hounded by worshippers of Crom Cruach, was destroyed by the god at the church of the Kindred of Cormac. His followers buried his books, with relics of Saints Peter and Paul, under a stone church that the cult pulled down; its successor may not stand on the spot, and the cult may live on.

links.note: Saint Columba, a patron of Ireland
Saint Malachy, once Archbishop of Armagh
Saint Dympna, whose staff is kept at Tydavnet

neighbours.name: The Black Pig's Dyke
neighbours.summary:
The Gleann na muice duibhe, a ditch twelve feet deep in places between banks up to four feet high, which runs along Ulster's southern border between Donegal Bay on the west and Lough Cairlinn on the east. An enormous black faerie boar rooted it out with its snout and cleared it again every third year, until the magi of Vigil killed it and kept its tusks as their cathach; nobody has ploughed it since. It is broken now and badly neglected, but what survives is a faerie trod with a Faerie aura of 1.

Restored, it would ring the whole of Ulster in one boundary, though a Target: Boundary spell covering the entire province would need seven size modifiers.

In Connacht. Through Bréifne the dyke runs north to south across the west, then west to east, then climbs south to north through the east, passing west and south of Carrick and round Kilmore and Cavan. As a faerie trod it is worn and broken in places. The Connachta druids want it left that way: dug out again, it would ring Ulster with a boundary that bites into Connacht and opens more land to the Order's claims.

neighbours.name: Tír Chonaill
neighbours.summary:
The land of the Cenél gConaill in the west of Ulster, a branch of the Uí Néill, the dynasty that also rules Connacht. It takes its name from Conall Gulban, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages, who won his byname by running up Beann Ghulban and back within a day without collapsing; for that feat the druids accepted him as king, and the lesser kings soon bent the knee. King Domhnall Mór mac Eicnechain, of Conall's line and the second king from the Uí Domhnaill, rules it with the help of his Lucht Tighe, the household families, and keeps it free of the English by the strength of his gallóglaigh. It is close allied with Tír Eóghain.

A country of mountains: the Derryveagh range (Cnoic Dhoire Bheatha) to the north and the Blue Stacks (Cruacha Gorma) to the south, which cut the kingdom in two, with deep green sheep valleys between. The best farmland is the valley of the Finn and the Laggan round Raphoe.

The Lucht Tighe. The Uí Domhnaill hand much of the running of the kingdom to household families, and other dynasties do the same; some covenants have copied the custom among their covenfolk. The book calls them eight and lists nine: the Mac Robhartaigh keep the clan's cathach, the Mac Suibhne lead the gallóglaigh and marshal the Uí Domhnaill's hosts, the Uí Breisléin are the brehons, the Uí Cléirigh the scribes and historians, the Mac Duinnshleibhe the physicians, the Uí Firghil the keepers of the clan's rites, the Uí Gallchobhair the captains of horse, the Uí Tiománagh the herdsmen, and the Mac a'Bháird the bards.

neighbours.name: Lough Dearg
neighbours.summary: A wide, shallow lake known above all for its island of Inisphadraig, where the Purgatory of Saint Patrick draws pilgrims from across Ireland (see that church). Tales say tunnels beneath the water join some of its other islands.

neighbours.name: The Poisoned Glen
neighbours.summary: A glen on the coast across from Toraigh Island, whose black, scorched mountainsides show where Balor of the Evil Eye, the Fomóir champion, glared at Ireland from his tower on the island. A standing stone at its mouth is said to be a warrior Balor turned to stone for his cheek. Magic aura 1, perhaps higher in places. The slopes of the Seven Sisters, the tallest of them An tEaragail (Mount Errigal), fall into it.

neighbours.name: Beltany Tops
neighbours.summary: A great stone circle on a lonely hill two miles south of Raphoe: sixty broad triangular stones, most about four feet tall and leaning a little outward, some touching and some parted by low boulders, ring a space nearly fifty feet across, with pillars over nine feet high at east and west. A carved stone head among them pulls a face as if blowing or shrieking; there were once at least three more, now broken or carried off. Magic aura 2.

neighbours.name: Tír Eóghain
neighbours.summary:
The kingdom of the Cenél nEóghain, named, like the Inis Eóghain peninsula, for Eóghan, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages and brother of Conall Gulban. It is a young kingdom that broke free of its old overlords at Aileach and now dominates them; Aed Meith mac Aeda Ua Néill, who took power from Aileach in 1185, is its first Uí Néill king.

The Foyle, the Bann and the Blackwater roughly bound it, and the Sperrin Mountains (Sliabh Speirin) fill it. Between the mountains and Lough Neagh stretches a flat peat bog no crop will grow on, so most people live on the north coast or on the grain lands of the south toward Airgíalla.

neighbours.name: Inis Eóghain
neighbours.summary: The northern peninsula of Tír Eóghain, between Lough Foyle and Lough Swilly, which holds the hillfort of Aileach and, at its tip, Cionn Mhálanna, where Vigil stands.

neighbours.name: Aileach
neighbours.summary:
A hillfort on Inis Eóghain, once the capital of a kingdom that held Airgíalla and Ulster as vassals; Saint Patrick baptised Eóghain mac Neill here in 450. The King of Munster broke its power in 1101, the English wore away more of it, and the Cenél nEóghain have ruled it since 1185.

Its fortress, the Grianán Ailigh, is the Dagda's work, built to honour the sun, and was for a while the headquarters of the fight against the Fomórach. It stands empty, shattered by the Munstermen: Muirchertach Ua Briain, whose own fort the king of Aileach had razed twenty years before, had each of his soldiers carry a stone home to rebuild with, but a faerie-built fort is not so easily stolen, and every stone taken was replaced. The ring wall: 17 feet tall, 13 thick, 77 across. The book gives it no aura; Faerie 2 is assumed for a fort of faerie make.

It would make a fine covenant site, but Vigil has declared an interest in it. Vigil has no right in law to keep others from exploring it, but would likely back its claim with certamen and Wizard War.

neighbours.name: The Sperrin Mountains
neighbours.summary: Sliabh Speirin, the mountains at the heart of Tír Eóghain. In their foothills House Diedne founded the first covenant of Vigil, the Diedne Vigil, raided by Dublin's rune wizards in 830 and sacked by the Merinita after 851.

neighbours.name: Beaghmore
neighbours.summary:
An Bheitheach Mhór, 'the big place of birch trees', a peat bog in the south-eastern foothills of the Sperrins full of contradictory auras and strange happenings. Seven stone circles, a dozen cairns and ten dead-straight stone rows, all set along a line from north-east to south-west, poke through the peat. The circles stand in three pairs and one alone; the lone circle is packed with a thousand upright triangular stones the locals call the dragon's teeth.

Each pair of circles has its own Magic aura, from 1 to 3, the lone circle has 4, and every stone row has an aura of 2 tied to a different Form. Bressal of Bonisagus (Bressal Ua Boniségeas), who has studied the moor at length, thinks the clash of auras marks a shattered regio, broken by design or by chance he cannot say.

neighbours.name: Leacht Ábartaigh
neighbours.summary:
A dolmen near Slaghtaverty over the grave of Ábhartach, a dwarf and sorcerer who ruled the district by fear and evil spells. A chieftain killed him, Fionn mac Cumhaill say some, Cathán, forebear of the local Ua Catháin, say others. Buried upright, he was back in his ráth the next day as wicked as ever; killed and buried again, he came back again. The third time a druid had him buried head down with a monument on top, and his magic stayed in the grave. He is a neamh-mairbh, one of the walking dead.

The monument is long forgotten and the land is being cleared for farming.

Story seed: The Neamh-Mairbh. Ábhartach's forgotten grave is being cleared for farming. Felling a hawthorn over it, a workman cuts off his own hand, and his blood soaks into the ground; the earth rumbles, the men flee, and that night the evil dwarf magician rises again, perhaps a dark faerie, perhaps an infernal sorcerer, and begins to master the land once more.

neighbours.name: Lough Neagh
neighbours.summary: The great lake at the centre of Ulster, made when the giant hero Fionn mac Cumhail fought the Scottish giant Benandonner: he tore up a clod of earth and flung it at his rival, it fell short into the Irish Sea as the Isle of Man, and the hole it left filled with water. Rumour still speaks of a péist, a monster, in the lake, but Dáire Farranta, founder of Leth Cuinn as it now is, killed it centuries ago. The Mercer House of Leth Cuinn stands on its north-eastern shore.

neighbours.name: Inisclabhall
neighbours.summary: A thickly wooded island of about nine acres in the south-west of Lough Neagh, more than half a mile out, reached by Saint Patrick's Road, a sunken causeway less than two feet under water in summer. The saint is said to have used it as a retreat. Its great beauty is a natural tether for a Magic aura of 2, and it would be an ideal covenant site but for the English knight just granted leave to raise a motte on it.

neighbours.name: Airgíalla
neighbours.summary: Oriel to the English: a league of nine sub-kingdoms in southern and central Ulster, ruled by the heirs of the Three Collas and their followers over a people of the Érainn. The Collas, Colla Uais, Colla Meann and Colla Fochra, came home from exile in Scotland after killing the father of the high king Muireadhach Tíreach, who pardoned them and urged them to win Ulster; they won six great battles against the Ulaidh, and the seventh raged a day and a night until the fighters stood waist deep in blood. The name means 'givers of hostages', for the nine noble hostages, chained in gold, that it gave the Connachta. Its king is Donnchad Ua nAnluain, at Clogher.

neighbours.name: Emhain Mhacha
neighbours.summary:
A hillfort of eighteen acres a few miles west of Armagh, the seat of Ulster's ancient kings, of Conchobhar mac Neasa and the Red Branch. It bears the name of Macha, chief goddess of the Ulaidh, a goddess of war and horses and a face of the Mór-Rióghain, whose consort was Dáire. Several mortal women named Macha belong to the place; one, the wife of Crunnchu, was made to race the king's horses while heavily pregnant because her husband had boasted she could outrun them, and won, and collapsed, and bore twins; dying, she cursed the men of Ulster to suffer her pangs for five nights and four days in their hour of greatest need, the ces noidhen.

Conchobhar's palace, the Chraobhruadh or red-branched house, was a richly carved hall on posts of red yew, six rings of them round an oak pillar over forty feet tall that gave the Red Branch heroes their name. Long ago someone filled it with boulders at least six feet deep and burnt it, an enemy's attack or a rite after a king's death, no one knows. Treasure hunters still dig for the gold said to have clad the roof.

Nearby lie the ruins of Bron Bherg, the 'house of sorrows' to the east, which Macha Mhuingruadh built, by tradition Mythic Europe's earliest hospital, in use until it was destroyed in 22 AD; Loughnashade, the 'lake of the treasure', to the north-east, where Macha's druids threw gold, horses and enemies' heads to the gods; and the King's Stables to the north-west, where the king's sacred horses were kept. Their descendants still run about Armagh, and some are fíorláiridhe, true mares (see the Bestiary). The book gives no aura.

links.note: true mares, born now and then of the old royal horses

neighbours.name: Cuailnge
neighbours.summary:
The Cuailnge peninsula and its mountains, once the heart of Conaille Muirtheimne, a kingdom tributary to Ulster whose people are still Cruithnigh, of the Uí Echach Corbo; they held the land from the peninsula to the mouth of the Boyne, but the Earl of Ulster has given most of it to English knights hoping to make baronies of it. Qui Sonant Pro Quieto stands high on a ridge here.

The plain of Muirtheimne is said to have lain under the sea until Conchobhar mac Neasa, before he was king, caught a daughter of the god Ler on the strand; to be let go she raised the plain and taught him to make a shield that strengthened its bearer and weakened his foes. The smith Culann left his forge on the Isle of Man to make it and was given the plain, the same Culann whose hound gave Cú Chulainn of Muirtheimne his name.

Donn and Find. Two faeries, Donn the dark and Find the bright, have fought each other since memory began, changing shape between swineherds, hawks, fish, stags, warriors, phantoms and maggots; their best-known forms were the Donn Cuailnge, the dark bull of Cuailnge, and Findbheannach, the white bull of Connacht, whose rivalry began the Táin Bó Cuailgne. Find stands for light, wisdom and day; Donn for the dead, ghosts and night. Both forever try to draw mortals into their war. Donn has lately caused a number of faerie-blooded children to be born, meaning them for the heart of a new army; Find has made no answer yet.

neighbours.name: Fermanagh
neighbours.summary: Fir Managh, once among the strongest of Airgíalla's tributary kingdoms, which kept itself half free and half bound to Connacht while staying on good terms with Airgíalla. In the early thirteenth century it has lost most of its independence.

neighbours.name: Lough Erne
neighbours.summary:
The River Erne winds through Fermanagh and opens into two loughs. Lower Lough Erne has more than a hundred and fifty islands, many with Augustinian houses; the round tower on Daimhinis guides boats through them, its monks ringing the bell when visitors appear and the next tower taking up the message, so word passes bell by bell up the lough. The Uí hEódhasa bardic school stands on the shore.

Boa Island, the largest, is named for Badhbh, one of the Tuatha Dé's bloodthirsty war goddesses, and bears a two-faced idol with hunched shoulders and a jutting tongue. White Island has eight statues, all by one mason two or three centuries ago, which the monks call saints though no one agrees which: a grinning naked woman, a Sile na gCíoch, displaying herself; a king on a throne; a cowled figure holding a staff; a king gesturing at his mouth; a man with two winged beasts, dogs or lions; a warrior with sword and shield; a figure with no features at all; and a scowling head.

neighbours.name: Magh Sléacht
neighbours.summary:
The 'plain of adoration', holy to the pagan Érainn, where an idol of Crom Cruach stood with twelve lesser gods; some Merinita say he was a sun god and the twelve the months. Saint Patrick threw it down and made the idols sink into the earth, and since then the idol has been told of as Crom Dubh, 'the dark croucher', an image of the Antichrist. Faerie aura 3.

Now and then someone who has turned from God comes here for power and, instead of the Antichrist, finds himself talking to its faerie copy. Crom Dubh gladly teaches faerie wizardry dressed up as infernalism when it feeds his own story.

The Infernal chapter tells it otherwise. A huge standing stone shaped as the god Crom Cruach and plated in beaten gold once rose among the drumlins of this plain in north-east Connacht, and here alone in Ireland the old people offered human sacrifice for mild winters and good harvests. Demons have always lived here, drawing men to the plain to shed one another's blood. Patrick drove the demon Crom Cruach deep under the earth and the sacrifices ended, but not the slaughter: the Diedne destroyed the surviving druids of the Masraige here in her pogrom, the Uí Raghallaigh fought the Uí Conchobhair and the Uí Ruairc here, and magi spilled one another's blood here in the Schism War. It is still thought a key to the land; if the saga follows history, the Uí Raghallaigh and the Uí Ruairc meet here again in 1256, and Bréifne is split between them. That chapter gives it a malevolent Infernal aura of 5, as one of the battlefields whose patron demons send dreams of victory to lure armies back; the Ulster chapter gives Faerie 3. The storyguide picks one, or keeps both: the faerie Crom Dubh mimicking the demon who truly haunts the plain.

neighbours.name: The Sídh of Fionnachaidh
neighbours.summary: The sídh of Lir which opens on Tír Tairngire, his Otherworld, the Land of Promise; there fish graze like sheep and the White Fields (fionnachaidh) turn to foam-capped waves. Swans love to rest here in memory of Lir's four children, cursed by a jealous stepmother to spend nine hundred years as swans. The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is assumed.

neighbours.name: Millmount
neighbours.summary: A huge mound in Drogheda-in-Meath holding the grave of Amairgen mac Míl, chief druid of the Milesians. Hugh de Lacy has built a bailey on top of it, to the alarm of the locals, who fear it will trouble the druid's restless spirit.

neighbours.name: The Earldom of Ulster
neighbours.summary: The English earldom in the east of the province, on the old lands of the Dál bhFiatach and the Dál nAraidhe: won by John de Courcy, held since 1205 by his great rival Hugh de Lacy. To the English a castle says that what they have taken they mean to keep, and they have built them everywhere: besides Belfast, Carrickfergus and Dundrum, de Courcy and de Lacy have fortified Dunseverick, Dundalk, Dromore and Green Castle, and their knights have put up baileys and stone towers beyond counting.

neighbours.name: The Round Tower of Antrim
neighbours.summary: Antrim is a town of note that grew round Saint Aebh's monastery of the late fifth century. Its 90-foot round tower was the bell tower of that early house, burnt in 1147 and never rebuilt. The Bullaun Stone at its foot bears the print of the knee and foot of a witch who threw herself from the top when the tower was finished.

neighbours.name: Bangor
neighbours.summary: Beannchor, the 'horned curve' of its bay: a town round the abbey of Beannchor Mór (see Bangor Abbey). Within earshot of the abbey's unbroken song the Dominion aura is 6, usually with a Calm temper.

neighbours.name: The Vale of Angels
neighbours.summary: A valley near Bangor Abbey where Saint Patrick saw a vision full of angels. Divine aura 2, with the way into a Celestial regio of aura 5.

levels.name: The Celestial regio
levels.notes: Home of Victorius, the angel set over Ireland, one of the choir of principalities, and of the throng of angels under him who tend every part of Ireland and its people. A visit here gave Patrick his vision.

neighbours.name: Belfast Castle
neighbours.summary: Beal Feirste, the 'mouth of the sandbank', an old fortress site; the present castle is John de Courcy's, of 1177.

neighbours.name: The Giant's Ring
neighbours.summary:
A vast earthwork near Belfast Castle, almost 200 paces across, its bank 15 feet high with three gaps, and inside the bank, set side by side in the Irish way, standing stones twelve feet tall. A little passage tomb lies just east of the centre. Magic aura 3.

The giants of Ireland meet here, though they have held no council for centuries. A magus who wants a giant's ear cuts the giant's name in ogham on a stone and leaves it in the tomb; within forty days the giant sends a messenger.

neighbours.name: Carrickfergus Castle
neighbours.summary: Carraig Fhearghais, the 'rock of Fergus', for King Fearghus, wrecked nearby. John de Courcy built the castle on the promontory in 1177, a small bailey at its tip above Belfast Loch inside an inner ward and a great curtain wall, as the base of his wars on the Ulaidh. It is still the caput of the earldom; Hugh de Lacy has strengthened it with a new eastern tower and a wall along the seaward side.

neighbours.name: Erenagh
neighbours.summary:
The ruined monastery of Erenagh, destroyed by John de Courcy in 1177; its survivors went to his new abbey of Iniscourcy. Ghosts of its murdered monks still walk it, and survivors meet here in secret with brothers from Iniscourcy, first to plot the English out, now, at the ghosts' whispering, to take bloody revenge.

Story seed: Echoes at Erenagh. Survivors of the 1177 slaughter at Erenagh meet in its haunted ruins with monks recruited from Iniscourcy, plotting to drive out the English. An English friend of the characters is attacked without cause by an Irish monk who proves to have been possessed, and the trail leads back to the ruined monastery.
neighbours.secrets: The murdered monks' ghosts have been whispering compulsions to their living brothers, and the plot has turned to bloody revenge.

neighbours.name: Saulpatrick
neighbours.summary: Sabhall Phádraig, where Saint Patrick died. For twelve days after his death no night fell here, and on his feast day the sun still does not set, so it draws a small pilgrimage that usually ends at Downpatrick, where his body lies. A Christian who sees the unsetting sun gains a Faith Point. A spell with Duration Sun cast here on his feast day lasts until the sun sets where its target is, up to a day and a half, and Parma Magica likewise. The book gives no aura; Divine 3 is assumed.

neighbours.name: Dundrum Castle
neighbours.summary: De Courcy's castle of 1180 on an old fort's site, on a hill 200 feet above the bay. Beaten by de Lacy, de Courcy ran to King Ragnold of Man, his wife's brother, and came back with a hundred longships of Norsemen, landed at Strangford and besieged it, but he had built it too well; he was taken and lived out his days in poverty. Its stone tower is new (the book credits an Earl Henry). The town below is now an important port of the earldom.

neighbours.name: Lough Cuan
neighbours.summary:
The 'calm lake', called Strangford Lough from the Norse for a strong fjord. The Ards Peninsula shuts it off from the sea, with a round tower at Kirkistown held and enlarged by the English le Savage family and the Cistercian abbey of Mainistir Liath; the Leath Cathail Peninsula closes its southern mouth. It has many islands, the largest Machaoi Island.

Saint Machaoi, a swineherd Patrick baptised, founded Nendrum on that island and taught Saint Colmán of Drom Mór. Gathering wood one day, he met a wondrous bird that sang him three strains; each seemed a moment but took fifty years, and he came out of the wood to find his hermitage a monastery with a shrine to his memory. His feast is 23 June. Patrick gave him the eiteach, a crozier fallen from Heaven that could fly; the Bishop of Down holds it now.

neighbours.name: Machaoi Island
neighbours.summary: The largest island of Lough Cuan, where Nendrum Monastery lies in ruins, wrecked in 806 in the magical battle between Diedne and Pralix, though no one knows which of them did it. Magic aura 3. The aura seems to stir up discord and strife among women, which is why no Hermetic covenant has settled here.

neighbours.name: The Leath Cathail Peninsula
neighbours.summary: The peninsula at Lough Cuan's southern mouth, where Diedne and Pralix carried their fight on after Nendrum; it has a Magic aura of 2 throughout, with the same taint of strife between women as Machaoi Island.

neighbours.name: The Giants' Causeway
neighbours.summary:
Clochán na bhFomóraig, a mass of locked many-sided rock columns on the north coast that step down from the clifftops and on under the sea; wind and waves draw a weird whistling from it, like hundreds of pipes out of tune. Faerie aura 3.

One tale says Fionn mac Cumhaill built it to walk to Scotland and fight Benandonner. An older one says the Tuatha Dé laid their curse on the Fomórach here: each column is a year of the curse, and when sea and wind have ground all 40,000 to sand, Ireland lies open to the Tuatha Dé's old enemies again.

neighbours.name: The Mountains of Mourne
neighbours.summary:
Beanna Boirche, Boirche's Hills, heather mountains in the south of the earldom, notorious for thick mists in which travellers lose their way; the locals blame the faeries. While mist lies on them they have a Faerie aura of 2.

The highest, Sliabh Dómhanghairt, is named for Saint Dómhanghart, a follower of Patrick, who never died but keeps watch on its summit for ever over the graves on Sliabh Crúibe.

neighbours.name: Sliabh Crúibe
neighbours.summary:
The 'mountain of the hoof', across a valley north of the Mournes, said to be where twelve kings lie buried. On Cairn Sunday, the first Sunday in August, the locals climb it, each bringing a stone to help bury the kings, though the legend does not say why.

Vis: some of the stones carried up hold vis, gathered over many years and spread among many stones; magi have noticed. No one holds it.

Story seed: The Demon Kings of Sliabh Crúibe. On Cairn Sunday local people carry stones up the mountain to help bury twelve kings, and magi have found that some of the stones hold vis, gathered over many years.
neighbours.secrets:
The kings must stay buried. Eleven of the twelve graves hold a demon bound into a dead tyrant's body. The Cailleacha Phiseogach know a legend that if mortal hands uncover the kings they will rise, and that when a twelfth king joins them the world will end. They cannot dig the graves themselves, so they mean to lure vis-hungry magi into doing it.

Eleven of the graves hold a demon bound in a dead tyrant's body. The Cailleacha Phiseogach know that if mortal hands uncover them they will rise, and that the world ends when a twelfth king joins them; unable to dig themselves, they make sure greedy magi hear of the vis.

neighbours.name: Rath Chinneich
neighbours.summary:
A fortress the four sons of Madán Muinreamhair, king of the Fomórach, built for Nemed in a single day at his command; when it was done Nemed killed them so they could build no better for anyone else. Four hills nearby mark the graves of Bog, Robhog, Ruibhne and Rodan. Chapter two sets the fort, Ráth Cinn-Eich, on the slopes of Slieve Croob, with passages the brothers dug beneath it; House Diedne later built the Widow's Throat over its ruins.

Fomórach are hard to kill, and some say the Mac Madáin only lie in a sleep like death, held by the Tuatha Dé's curse; the day they wake they will hunt Nemed's descendants for revenge.

neighbours.name: Ballynoe
neighbours.summary:
A great stone circle in the Mournes, named for the nearby settlement of an Baile Núa: over fifty close-set stones six feet tall in a ring almost 30 paces across, with a portal entrance on the west and, facing it inside, a horseshoe of stones over a stone-lined chamber underground. Magic aura 3.

It is an exact twin of the circle at Swinside in Cumbria, and the two are joined by a lasting enchantment like Opening the Intangible Tunnel but of no apparent limit. Magi know of it but not where it came from or how best to use it. Original research here could yield a Major Breakthrough letting Hermetic magic join two places the same way; the flawed Hermes' Portal spell and Mercere's Portal enchantments may help.

neighbours.name: The Ring of Gullion
neighbours.summary: A strange perfect ring of hills round a central mountain, Sliabh gCuillinn, which has a Faerie aura of 2; the Cailleach Beara, a winter goddess of the faerie kind, haunts the lake on top.

neighbours.name: The Lake of Sliabh gCuillinn
neighbours.summary: The Cailleach Beara's lake, Faerie aura 5. Whoever swims in it comes out old, fifty years older with Aging Points enough to raise their Decrepitude by 2. She may be begged to undo it, but even then some mark remains; Fionn mac Cumhaill, whom the crone goddess tricked, got his white hair here.

neighbours.name: Tír Fhomóraig
neighbours.summary:
The Kingdom of the Fomórach, on the islands north of Ireland since the Tuatha Dé threw them out after the Second Battle of Magh Tuireadh. Its two chief strongholds are Rathlin and Toraigh, though Fomórach are rumoured as far off as Islay and Arran in Scotland. Pure-blooded births have all but stopped; they do not age but still die of mishap and sickness, and fewer than a hundred may be left, a number still falling.

Their king, Madán Muinreamhair ('thick-neck'), has no love for men, since Nemed killed his four sons at Rath Chinneich, but he has come to see humans as his race's only hope and has arranged marriages with the Cruithnigh of Rathlin. His people loathe these half-breeds and Pict-bloods, but may have no choice.

neighbours.name: Rathlin Island
neighbours.summary: Inis Reachlainn, Pliny's Reginia and Ptolemy's Rhicina, where the Dál nAraidhe and the Fomórach live together and have held off both the Norsemen of Man and the Normans. The humans are Christian and the Fomórach are not; between them stand human priests with Fomóir blood who worship the Fomóir gods, Domnu the primal darkness above all, and are otherwise just like the gruagachan. King Madán keeps a tower on the southernmost point, from which he stares at the land he may never set foot on.

neighbours.name: Toraigh Island
neighbours.summary: An island nine miles off the north coast, home to some two dozen Fomórach, where no human dares land. It was once the Fomóir capital: King Conand ruled from a great tower the Nemedians threw down, which Balor Bailcbhéimneach ('strong smiting'), Balor of the Evil Eye, who came after him, built again. No Fomóir king lives on Toraigh now.

neighbours.name: Túr Bhalair
neighbours.summary:
'Balor's Tower', an unclimbable peak on Toraigh. Here Balor locked away his daughter Eithne, yet Cian of the Tuatha Dé got in and fathered Lugh on her; from its top Balor glared over Ireland, and the bare slopes of the Poisoned Glen still show it. Rumour says an Aspect of Balor sometimes comes back.

Balor is among the mightiest of the primal Fomóir, a great daimon of the Magic realm who acted in the world through Aspects; since his half-blood grandson Lugh beat him at the Second Battle of Magh Tuireadh he has kept out of the mortal world, as he agreed with the Tuatha Dé. His usual Aspect was a huge monster with one venomous, fiery eye under seven covers: with one off plants withered, with three wood smoked, with five sparks flew, and with all seven gone whatever he looked on burst into flame, and living things in his gaze burned, turned to stone or fell dead as he chose. Anyone caught even by the edge of his glance was his for a year, to curse when he pleased.

neighbours.name: Earl of Ulster
neighbours.summary: Hugh de Lacy, a younger son of Meath's English lord and brother of Walter de Lacy, who arrested John de Courcy for rebellion in 1203 and in May 1205 was made the first Earl of Ulster by King John, with all the lands de Courcy had held. The earldom is a Liberty: he runs it for the English crown and owes the Lord of Ireland his service and the king's revenues. He holds it from Carrickfergus, which he has strengthened, and has fortified Dundrum, the Millmount bailey at Drogheda and more. He has given most of Cuailnge and Muirtheimne to English knights hunting for baronies, and a knight leave to put a motte on Inisclabhall. Whether Tír Chonaill still pays the tribute de Courcy forced on it in 1196 the book does not say.

neighbours.name: King of Tír Chonaill
neighbours.summary: Domhnall Mór mac Eicnechain, of Conall Gulban's line, the second king of Tír Chonaill from the Uí Domhnaill, a branch of the Uí Néill. He rose by leaning on the Lucht Tighe, his eight household families, and keeps his kingdom free of the English with his gallóglaigh rather than a levy of clansmen: better armed and trained, but fewer. He is close allied with Tír Eóghain. De Courcy made Tír Chonaill pay tribute after beating its king in 1196 and ravaged the north in 1198; Raphoe's cathedral still lies as he left it.
neighbours.ruler: Domhnall Mór mac Eicnechain Ua Domhnaill

neighbours.name: King of Tír Eóghain
neighbours.summary: Aed Meith mac Aeda Ua Néill, the first Uí Néill king of Tír Eóghain, who took power from Aileach in 1185; the Cenél nEóghain have ruled Aileach ever since, and the young kingdom now dominates its old overlords. Allied with Tír Chonaill, and one of the 'five bloods', the greatest túatha of Ireland. Doire is under the Mac Lochlainn, who were the Cenél nEóghain's kings until the Uí Néill took over.
neighbours.ruler: Aed Meith mac Aeda Ua Néill

neighbours.name: King of Airgíalla
neighbours.summary: Donnchad Ua nAnluain, king of the nine sub-kingdoms of Airgíalla, ruled from Clogher. Since the English came he has moved soldiers into his half of Drogheda and seems ready to stop them taking it, though they already hold the lands just north and west of it. Fermanagh, once among his strongest tributaries, has lost most of its freedom.

neighbours.name: Bishopric of Raphoe
neighbours.summary: An Irish see. Saint Columba settled Ráth Bhoth and founded a monastery here, which his kinsman Saint Adomnán enlarged; the bishop's cathedra is dedicated to Adomnán, but the church has not been rebuilt since John de Courcy destroyed it in 1198. Beltany Tops stands two miles south.

neighbours.name: Bishopric of Doire
neighbours.summary: An Irish see of the province of Armagh, whose cathedral, the great Tempull Mór, was finished in 1160. Saint Columba founded a monastery at Doire in the sixth century after beating the druids of its oak grove in a battle of words; they swore to return and never did.

links.note: Saint Columba, a patron of Ireland

neighbours.name: Bishopric of Clogher
neighbours.summary: An Irish see, its bishop more often called the Bishop of Airgíalla. Its cathedral keeps the golden stone that gives Cloch Oir its name, a gold-clad idol once the relic of a pagan cult: its god, Cermand Cestach, spoke through a ban fáith, a druid priestess, and saw the future uncannily well.

neighbours.name: Bishopric of Down
neighbours.summary:
The see of the earldom, Anglo-Irish since the conquest, seated at Downpatrick, where Saint Patrick is buried in the cathedral grounds. Saint Malachy gave up Armagh in 1137 to become Bishop of Down, ruled the diocese from Bangor, enlarged the cathedral and brought Augustinian canons; in 1183 John de Courcy made it a cathedral priory of Benedictines from Chester.

The bishop holds the eiteach of Saint Machaoi, the crozier from Heaven that once belonged to the abbots of Nendrum: a relic with 2 Faith Points that lets up to four people fly while they keep hold of it.

neighbours.name: Bangor Abbey
neighbours.summary:
Beannchor Mór, Saint Comgall's abbey of 555, an Irish house famed for its learning, the equal of the great theological schools abroad, and for the missionaries it sent across Mythic Europe. Viking raids in the eighth and ninth centuries hurt it badly, but a miracle saved it. Saint Malachy was abbot here until lately, and Bishop of Down too.

Its perpetual harmony is an antiphonal chant that never stops, praising God without a break; the choir holds a Holy Tradition of Cantores, who can turn the monks' endless prayer to miracles. Anywhere the song can be heard has a Dominion aura of 6, usually of Calm temper.

neighbours.name: Downpatrick Cathedral Priory
neighbours.summary: Anglo-Irish: the Benedictines from Chester whom John de Courcy set in Down's cathedral in 1183, keepers of Saint Patrick's grave. When Ulaidh and Uí Néill fought over the saint's body, it was carried off on a cart drawn by two oxen, but a miraculous vision of a second cart and team fooled the Uí Néill, and the body stayed at Dún Leathghlaise.

neighbours.name: Iniscourcy Abbey
neighbours.summary: An Anglo-Irish Cistercian abbey John de Courcy founded in 1180 to atone for destroying Erenagh nearby in 1177; its monks came from Furness in England, with Erenagh's survivors. Some of those survivors meet in secret at Erenagh's ruins.

neighbours.name: Mainistir Liath
neighbours.summary: An Anglo-Irish Cistercian abbey on the Ards Peninsula, founded by John de Courcy's Manx wife.

neighbours.name: The Abbey of Iúbhar Chinn Trábha
neighbours.summary: An Irish Cistercian house, 'the yew at the head of the strand', called Newry by the English, in the valley between the Mournes and the Ring of Gullion. The old monastery was rebuilt in 1142 and given to the Cistercians, and a small town has grown up to serve the monks.

neighbours.name: The Purgatory of Saint Patrick
neighbours.summary:
One of Ireland's greatest pilgrim shrines, on Inisphadraig in Lough Dearg, kept by an Irish chapter of Augustinian canons. To settle the doubts of some converts, Patrick asked God for a proof and a pit opened where he stood, through which the joys of Heaven and the pains of Hell can be seen.

The canons house and feed the penitents and draw lots among them for who keeps the night's vigil; those who keep it are taken through the horrors of Purgatory.

neighbours.name: Daimhinis
neighbours.summary: An Irish Augustinian house on an island of Lower Lough Erne, one of many there, whose round tower is a landmark for boats among the islands; its monks ring the bell when they see visitors, and the call passes from tower to tower up the lough.

neighbours.name: Donegal
neighbours.summary: Dun na nGaill, the 'fort of the foreigners', the largest town of Tír Chonaill and a stronghold of the Uí Domhnaill, founded by Norse settlers as a port. Most of the king's gallóglaigh live here, twenty corrughadh of about a hundred men each camped in and around the town, which is not always happy to have them.

neighbours.name: Doire
neighbours.summary:
Derry to the English, 'oak grove' in Irish, on the Foyle: a ritual site of the druids before Saint Columba founded his monastery, and now the seat of one of Armagh's bishops, with the Tempull Mór. Vikings from Man still raid it, and its sea side is strongly walled. From the market square at its heart four streets (Butcher's gate, Shipquay gate, Ferryquay gate and Bishop's gate) run out to four gates in the walls. The Mac Lochlainn protect it.

The English have just built the fort of Greencastle at the mouth of Lough Foyle; the book names its builder Hugh de Burgos.

neighbours.name: Armagh
neighbours.summary:
Ard Mhacha, seat of one of Ireland's four archbishops and, to many, the first holy place of Ireland. Saint Patrick founded it when a series of miracles persuaded a lord named Dáire to give him the hill of Droim Saileach, whose monastery grew into the city. Built into the wall of the cathedral's nave is a pagan idol of Nuada of the Silver Arm, king of the Tuatha Dé, found at Tóin re Gaoith nearby; the cathedral also keeps the skull of Conchobhar mac Neasa.

The Shrine of the Bell holds Bethechan, a little iron handbell Saint Colm Cille took from Patrick's grave, in a bell-shaped reliquary rich with gold and gems; the Ua Mellain family have kept it for four hundred years.

neighbours.name: Clogher
neighbours.summary: Cloch Oir, the 'golden stone', capital of Airgíalla and its bishop's seat, named for the gold-covered idol in the cathedral.

neighbours.name: Drogheda-in-Airgíalla
neighbours.summary: Droichead Atha, the 'bridge of the ford', is split by the Boyne. The English hold Drogheda-in-Meath on the south bank, with the Norse fortress they took and strengthened (chartered 1194); Drogheda-in-Airgíalla on the north bank grew from the trading post that served the castle. The king of Airgíalla has garrisoned it and seems ready to keep the English out.

neighbours.name: Downpatrick
neighbours.summary:
Once Dún Leathghlaise, lately renamed Dún Phádraig, 'Patrick's stronghold', for the saint buried in its cathedral grounds; it was the capital of the old Dál bhFiatach kingdom, and the pilgrims from Saulpatrick end here.

Its first fort, Rath Cealtchair, belonged to Celtchair mac Uitheachair, a huge ugly man whose bulbous nose, wing-like ears and rough grey hair betrayed Fir Bolg blood. He fought in all of Conchobhar's great battles, but for a murder done in rage he was bound by a geas to save Ulster from its three worst evils: the Fomóir Conganchneas, 'horny skin', whom no weapon could hurt until Celtchair's daughter learned that red-hot spikes through his soles would kill him; the monstrous hound Luchdhonn, whose heart he tore out through its throat; and his own dog Daolchú, one of Luchdhonn's three whelps (the others became Mac Da Thó's hound and the smith Culann's), meek with him but a terror when he was away. He speared it, its blood poisoned him, and he died.

His spear, the Lúin Cheltchair, which Celtchair picked up where the Second Battle of Magh Tuireadh was fought, is a weapon of great power and almost certainly one of the Four Treasures of the Tuatha Dé. It had to be kept in a cauldron of blood or its shaft would burst into flame and it would run its owner through, and the silver rings round its head spun and rattled when battle was near. After Celtchair it passed to the sinister Dubhthach Daol Uladh, who died by it, as did Cúscraidh Meann Macha after him. Where it is now no one knows. Celtchair very likely knew the clesrada.

neighbours.name: Dundrum
neighbours.summary: The port that has grown round Dundrum Castle, now one of the earldom's most important.

neighbours.name: The Lucht Tighe of Tír Chonaill
neighbours.summary: The household families that carry the running of Tír Chonaill for the Uí Domhnaill: Mac Robhartaigh (keepers of the cathach), Mac Suibhne (chiefs of the gallóglaigh), Uí Breisléin (brehons), Uí Cléirigh (scribes and historians), Mac Duinnshleibhe (physicians), Uí Firghil (the clan's rites), Uí Gallchobhair (cavalry), Uí Tiománagh (herdsmen) and Mac a'Bháird (bards). The book calls them eight but names nine. Some covenants keep a Lucht Tighe of their own among their covenfolk.

details.wants: Their hereditary offices under the Uí Domhnaill
details.offers: Brehons, scribes, physicians, bards, horse and the gallóglaigh

neighbours.name: The Gallóglaigh of Donegal
neighbours.summary: The 'foreign warriors' of the Uí Domhnaill, mostly of mixed Norse and Gaelic blood come over from the Isles, the Norse kingdom off Scotland's west coast: twenty corrughadh of about a hundred men, superb with battle-axe and greatsword and all in mail. Tír Chonaill relies on them and not on a levy, and owes its freedom from the English to them, but they are a sore point in Donegal.

details.wants: Pay and plunder
details.offers: Heavy infantry, the defence of Tír Chonaill

neighbours.name: The Burial Grounds of Qui Sonant
neighbours.summary:
A ridge high in the Cuailnge mountains, reached only by dangerous winding tracks and often snowbound in its hard winters, where local lore says the giant Finn MacCumhaill sleeps. Dolmens, cairns and mounds of pale grey stone are scattered over the hills and peaks round Qui Sonant, few easy to reach, most cold, bleak and lonely: the graves of Ireland's magi, hedge wizards, faeries and magical beasts.

Magic aura 7. Each time a new tomb is raised at its edge the aura stretches to take it in (under the Realms of Power: Magic rules, each spread calls for a roll on the Aura Weakening Table). Nothing that works through an Arcane Connection reaches a target inside it: spells cannot find their mark, and magi feel their talismans drift from them; so neither the bodies nor their grave goods can be used to summon the dead while the aura shields them.

neighbours.name: Cionn Mhálanna
neighbours.summary: Malin Head, Ireland's most northerly promontory, a ragged coast thrust into the Atlantic, good grazing land often battered by storms off the sea. Vigil spreads across it as halls and homesteads in ringforts, one to each magus, each in a moderate Faerie aura (3 is assumed). Faerie auras are scattered all over the headland, and there seem to be as many faerie kings along the coast as mortals; Vigil keeps the peace between them. Its warriors most often fight a Fachan king and his Fer Caille.

neighbours.name: The Old Fortress of Vigil
neighbours.summary: The fortress the first Merinita of Vigil built on the rocks over the sea, long abandoned; little is left, its stone carted off for newer buildings. Beneath it lie the vaults, flooded and mostly forgotten.
neighbours.secrets: Many magical weapons and devices brought from distant lands have outlasted centuries of rot in the drowned vaults, with a library of casting tablets and lab texts against Infernal sickness and foul weather. The old records are lost and Vigil's magi have no idea what lies under their feet, but the Vitae Magorum of Hibernia's magi mention the vaults.

neighbours.name: Banbha's Crown
neighbours.summary:
The northernmost point of mainland Ireland, where the spire the first Merinita of Vigil raised stands in a faerie regio. In the mundane world it is a fallen stone pillar, and the spire shows only to those passing through the regiones. On the first level mossy stairs wind round it, and it climbs through two more levels until mist hides the ground and cloud the top. A stone seat crowns it, and whoever sits there can watch and listen to any spot in Ireland (Penetration +35). The stairs are the only way through the levels, and climbing them costs two Long-Term Fatigue levels going up and two more coming down. The book gives the regio three levels but no auras; 4, 5 and 6 are assumed.

Some Hibernian elders know of it, but most take it for a prepared casting space and know nothing of its own power. Its secret is taught at Vigil from master to pupil.

levels.name: The first level
levels.see: Mossy stone stairs wind up round a spire some thirty feet high.
levels.enter: Only by the stairs round the spire.

levels.name: The second level
levels.enter: Only by the stairs round the spire.

levels.name: The third level
levels.see: The ground is lost in mist below and the top hidden in cloud.
levels.enter: Only by the stairs round the spire.
levels.notes: At the top a stone chair: whoever sits in it can watch and listen to anywhere in Ireland (Penetration +35).

neighbours.name: Inishtrahull
neighbours.summary: An island some six miles north-east of Cionn Mhálanna, home of the faerie princess who is Maoilfhinnéin mac Lir's wife. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Connacht
neighbours.summary:
The western province of Ireland, beyond the Sionainne (Shannon), which serves as its eastern border; Ulster lies north of it, Meath and Leinster east, Munster south. Its coasts to the north, west and south are all cliffs, inlets and islands with good harbours, where villages live off the sea and graze beasts on the slopes; inland there are plains in the middle, ridges of mountain to the north, west and south, wide peat bogs in the north and west, and lakes without number. The great rivers are the Muaidhe (Moy), the Gaillimhe and the Sionainne. The land is fertile.

Closed to covenants. By the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh the Order may found no covenant here, and no magus may stay more than three nights running under a Connacht sky or roof, even at a druid's invitation. Every hedge wizard in the province counts as one of the Coill Trí, who must hand seven Gifted Connachta children to the Order at each Tribunal; the druids resent the tithe as the Fir Bolg once resented the Fomórach's, and as the kings resent the English tribute. Whether the Treaty's Connacht ends at the Sionainne or takes in all the lands its kings rule (Bréifne reaches far east of the river) is unsettled. Younger magi with continental ideas see an untouched prize here.

Rule. The kingdom of Connacht rules the province and takes fealty from the kingdom of Bréifne in the north. Both have kept the English out so far, guarding their borders hard, but both pay tribute to the English and rule by agreement. The Connachta clans descend from Conn of the Hundred Battles and are cousins of the Uí Néill. The Uí Briúin rose five centuries ago through their friendship with the druids; their branches are the Uí Briúin Bréifne (the rival Uí Ruairc and Uí Raghallaigh) and the Uí Briúin Ai, whose Uí Conchobhair hold the crown. The older Uí Fiachrach and the fading Uí Maine sing of the days when they ruled. The last of the Fir Bolg live on the Aran Isles.

Magic. Few places in Ireland are so magical. Magic and Faerie auras are everywhere, and hedge wizards prosper even inside the Dominion. Vis is common but rarely plentiful in one place, much of it extraordinary vis, with herbs and things of virtue the druids use. The nobles keep and consult druids, and few would block one's road; druids who read omens warn that within a generation the English may cross the border.

Booleys and crannógs. Many villages move with the seasons after their herds or the harvest, leaving booleys, rough huts lived in for a season or two; between times faeries use them, and a traveller who shelters in one when they are home may never leave. Crannógs, lake dwellings raised on timber and stone, once held homes and whole villages; most now stand empty, given over to faeries and druids.

Vis (each in its place): Glencar's healing water (spell-like), the Lough Conn hills (spell-like), Omey's holy well (Divine).

Story seed: The Lair of Lentinus. Lentinus of Flambeau sold protection to hedge wizards for vis, and those who refused his terms soon suffered a magical attack. He belonged to no covenant and died in a Wizard War, and his hoard of vis and books has never been found; magi still slip into Connacht to look for it.

Story seed: An Appeal. The clergy of Mayo ask a clerical companion to carry their case against the diocese's dissolution to Rome, hoping an outsider's voice adds weight. Menacing visitors, apparently sent by the Archbishop of Tuam, show that someone will go to supernatural lengths to keep Mayo under Tuam.

Story seed: The Devils of Tuam. With no cathedral and little leadership, Tuam's merchants govern themselves and grow rich while harvests fail and sickness spreads outside the walls. Desperate men turn to robbery and raiding, and hedge wizards, perhaps magi too, feel it. Do the characters punish the strays, or face what drove them?

Story seed (The Broken Treaty): a magus named Faolán, whose parens was one of the true Ollamhain and whose grasp of the Arts is slight, fled into Connacht before Praesis fell and counts himself nearer the druids than the Order. His long stay is a plain breach of the Treaty. When the Tribunal learns where he is and that he has turned his back on the Order, the characters are sent to bring him back, with the Coill Trí's help or without it: a manhunt in hostile country.

links.note: Saint Brendan the Navigator, whose relics lie at Clonfert
Saint Grellan, guardian against the Fir Bolg

neighbours.secrets:
The archbishop may be only a pawn in a larger game.

Demons are stirring both the greed and the hardship.

neighbours.name: Bréifne
neighbours.summary:
The northern kingdom, subject to Connacht, stretching from Sligo on the western sea nearly to Kells in the east, with Ulster to its north and Meath to its east. It crosses the Sionainne, which is why the Treaty's reach here is in doubt: no covenant stands in Bréifne, and the Coill Trí claim all of it. Lough Allen splits its western half, mountains to the north and gentle plain to the south-east. Most of its people live by its brief stretch of sea, round Lough Allen, or beside the Sionainne and the Erne.

Few people and wild, unspoilt country leave Bréifne full of Magic auras rooted in the land's own beauty, with little pull from the other realms. West Bréifne, the Uí Ruairc's, is wooded and ringed by high mountains, rich in boar, deer, game birds, wolves and eagles; East Bréifne, the Uí Raghallaigh's, is hemmed in by Ulster, Meath and Leinster and feels English pressure, yet keeps many magical places and strong magic.

Story seed (Falling on Deaf Ears): in Bréifne, a farmer promises a seventh part of his harvest for seven years to whoever will free his son from a witch's enchantment; the witch is protected by an Uí Raghallaigh noble. Finding no druid, he comes east to the magi. Can they act themselves, or only through agents?

neighbours.name: The Glencar Waterfall
neighbours.summary: A fifty-foot fall in the north-west of Bréifne that runs clean all year. Its beauty anchors a strong Magic aura (4; the book gives no number), and its water is said to wash and heal wounds, the work of the spell-like vis in the fall. No one holds it.

neighbours.name: The Crannógs of Cavan
neighbours.summary: A tangle of small lakes north and north-west of Cavan, many with crannógs. Most are overgrown and look like islets near the shore; fishermen and booley folk still use a few. Some were druids' homes, and their Magic auras (2; the book gives no number) have not yet faded. With a little work they would make a covenant site, easy to defend and near markets, but they lie east of the Sionainne in lands the Coill Trí call Connacht's.

neighbours.name: Druim Leatan
neighbours.summary:
The ridge between the Uí Ruairc and the Uí Raghallaigh, with a priory on it that marks the line between the two halves of Bréifne. The priory itself is in a Dominion aura of 6, but the ridge round it has a malevolent Infernal aura that at times reaches 4, and demons there urge both clans to raid and avenge; the priory, as the border's emblem, is often sacked. Magh Slécht lies some miles west.

If history runs its course, Bréifne splits along this line in 1256, both halves still subject to Connacht.

The ridge dividing the Uí Ruairc from the Uí Raghallaigh in Bréifne, a few miles east of Magh Slécht. Its land carries a malevolent Infernal aura that now and then rises as high as 4 (the pack records the peak), and its demons egg both clans on to raid and avenge in equal measure. The priory on the ridge has a Dominion aura of 6, but as the mark of the boundary it is sacked and damaged again and again.

neighbours.name: The Stags of Broadhaven
neighbours.summary: Sheer island rocks off the far north-west coast in the diocese of Killala, thick with seabirds. A cave passes clean through one of them: it is a regio's way into the Otherworld of the Tuatha Dé who hold the Atlantic shore. The dolphins and seals of the bay are their messengers and envoys. Faerie 3 outside and 6 within (the book gives no numbers).

levels.name: The Otherworld of the western shore
levels.enter: Through the cave that runs right through one of the islands
levels.notes: The realm of the Tuatha Dé who rule the Atlantic coast.

neighbours.name: Lough Gara
neighbours.summary: A lake near Sligo that covers a drowned village. A faerie widow with a baby begged at every door one night and was turned away by all; leaving, she cursed the place, and the brook rose and drowned the sleepers in their beds. Magi after ghosts of the drowned, or spirits of regret, may still find them on the lake bed. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Cnoc na Ré
neighbours.summary: A hill at the western end of the Cúil Irra peninsula, two miles from Sligo, between Sligo Bay and Ballisodare Bay, among rolling hills covered in stone circles and tombs. On its top is an enormous cairn of loose stone, some 180 feet across and about 35 high: the grave of Queen Maedhbh, buried standing and facing north-east toward Ulster in case its men try their luck. Her body lies here, but her spirit keeps court at Cruachan. Faerie 3 (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: Drumcliffe
neighbours.summary: A village north of Sligo Bay, where the old druid Bran Bodhar spends his days in a round tower. He truly has the gift of divination, sometimes seeing as far as the next day, but he is deaf and cannot read, so anyone who comes to ask him must bring great patience and small hopes. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: Binn Ghulbain
neighbours.summary: A flat-topped mountain seen from all round Sligo: 1,700 feet of steep grass and then a sudden cliff. The Fianna, Finn mac Cumhail's young landless warriors, kept here, and some say their spirits still do, lending their deeds to whoever will make the climb. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: Loch na Súl
neighbours.summary: The Lake of the Eye. When Lugh's sling-stone burst Balor's eye at the second battle of Mag Tuired, its fire scooped a hollow in the ground and the falling giant's blood filled it. The blood is long gone, but a shard of the eye remains in the lake and is the source of its Magic aura of 2. A covenant wanting a cathach could take the shard, and the aura would die.

neighbours.name: Maol Réidh
neighbours.summary: Cnoc Maol Réidh, Connacht's highest mountain at over 2,500 feet, falling steeply into Killary Harbour, with thin woods on its flanks: the mountain that names the Treaty. Its beauty gives it a weak Magic aura (2), built up by centuries of spells cast on its top and strongest (3) where it looks over the harbour; the book gives no numbers. The view from it reaches far across the land, which some spells can use.

neighbours.name: Néifinn
neighbours.summary: Connacht's second mountain, also over 2,500 feet, named for Nemed of the ancient invasions. Its Magic aura (2) rises toward the summit (3), where druids have long stood to cast their spells; the book gives no numbers. Like Maol Réidh it commands a wide view, and Lough Conn can be seen from it.

neighbours.name: Lough Conn
neighbours.summary:
Lough Conn and Lough Cullin, joined to it, make a chain of water nearly ten miles long that empties to the Atlantic by the Muaidhe (Moy), a river lined with rich churches. They say a magic boar fleeing Fionn mac Cumhaill and his hounds Conn and Cullin poured water from its feet as it ran until the lakes formed and drowned the hounds; it was never caught, and roams the Faerie realm still, unseen in the mortal world since.

The hills above the lake are full of spell-like vis of every kind (unheld; the hedge druid Umor Ard Mac Adar of the Pact of Oireadh lives here), in a Magic aura of 2, with a hidden regio of 4 where Umor sleeps by day; the book gives no numbers.

Story seed: An Evil Wind. An Infernal wind spreads a sickness the magi cannot cure, but a Fir Domhnann healer is said to live among men in Connacht. Barred from crossing, the magi send companions to find Umor Ard Mac Adar in the hills above Lough Conn and bring him back in time.

levels.name: Umor's hiding place
levels.enter: By day, where Umor Ard sleeps; he can be found outside it only by night

neighbours.secrets: Umor's three cousins have come into Connacht to kill him, and the companions must run their gauntlet.

neighbours.name: The Stones of Dooncarton
neighbours.summary: Dooncarton is a village of shellfish farmers below the high cliffs south of Sruwaddacon Bay, with a small church, a devout flock and a strong Dominion. A short walk out, on the slopes of Caubeen Mountain above it, stands a ring of seven stones, four feet high and no more than ten across, in a strong Faerie aura (4; the book gives no number).

neighbours.name: Achill Island
neighbours.summary: A mountainous island: Croaghaun, over 2,000 feet, drops from its northern face straight into the Atlantic, Slievemore stands to its east, and more mountains fill the south. The wild land gives the whole island a Magic aura (2; the book gives no number), broken only by the Dominion round its church bells. Farmland is scarce, so most of the inland people move with the seasons between booleys. Its harbours, sheltered by cliffs, are Keel and Keem in the west and Cashel in the east.

neighbours.name: Clew Bay
neighbours.summary: A great bay guarded at its mouth by mountainous Clare Island and inside by drumlins, small drowned hills whose tops just break the water. Some call them faerie whales that swim free at high tide and turn to stone as it ebbs; certainly no one who counts them twice on different days gets the same number. Faerie 1 (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: Croagh Patrick
neighbours.summary:
A mountain of more than 2,000 feet looking over Clew Bay, above Murrisk and Lucanvey, some four miles out of Westport. Saint Patrick fasted forty days and nights on its top while the she-demon Caoranach plagued him with a cloud of crows and every snake in Ireland; at the end he flung a silver bell into the air, and its noise scattered the crows and drove the serpents out of the island for good.

A great pilgrimage site in a strong Divine aura (5; the book gives no number), ringed by shrines to Patrick, with a small church on the summit. Its roads are dangerous: robbers, faeries and demons all test pilgrims bound for Lough Nacorra, trials that serve as opposition for a pilgrimage (The Church's pilgrimage rules).

neighbours.name: Lough Nacorra
neighbours.summary: The lake below Croagh Patrick where Caoranach fell when the bell struck her from the sky. Its Divine waters held her for a time; when she broke free, Patrick tracked her to Lough Derg near Donegal and destroyed her there. Divine 3 (the book gives no number).

neighbours.name: The Field of the First Battle of Mag Tuired
neighbours.summary: Near Cong, where the Tuatha Dé beat the Fomórach in the first battle. Woods have grown over most of it, and magical and faerie relics of the fight may still lie under the trees. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: Lough Mask and Lough Gaillimhe
neighbours.summary: Lough Mask, the lesser lake, drains into the great Lough Gaillimhe (Corrib), and that into the sea; streams under Cong join the two. Manannán mac Lir of the Tuatha Dé claims Lough Gaillimhe as his own, so when the Friar's Cut, a canal from the lake through the settlement round the Dún to the Atlantic, was dug, the druids of Tuam had to agree its course with him. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Dún Bhun na Gaillimhe
neighbours.summary:
A fort at the mouth of the Gaillimhe (Corrib), facing south over Loch Lurgain, built by Tairrdelbach Uí Conchobhair in 1124 as a naval base, guarded by bog to the north and wide tidal mud to the south and east. It never was strong: hard to supply and easy to batter, it was razed by Munster raiders after the cattle of the Maigh Seola in 1132 and again in 1149, and it keeps the same flaws today. Something Infernal hangs over it (Infernal 2; the book gives no number).

If history runs its course, the Normans attack the fort and its settlement again and again once they enter Connacht, about 1230.

The Infernal has its hand in the fort's failings: a naval base big ships cannot use, a stronghold that cannot be resupplied under siege, a garrison too far from the people to shield them from Munster raiders. Rebuilt and wrecked over and over, it gives its defenders false hope and its attackers easy prey, and its assailants are helped by demons whether they want it or not: bowstrings snap, walls weaken, and a safe way through the marsh shows itself, so that defence is futile and cruelty and despair grow. If the saga follows history, it is besieged again and again in the 1230s as the Normans push into Connacht; unless the Infernal is fought alongside them, it will go on falling.

neighbours.name: Connemara
neighbours.summary: The country west of Lough Gaillimhe, split north from south by the short range of the Twelve Bens; the feuding families of each half think the line matters greatly. The Ó Cadhla rule it, but families from Leinster and Munster pushed out by the English are coming west looking for land. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: Clifden
neighbours.summary: A village where the Owenglen River meets Clifden Bay, its hills scattered with barrows and stone tombs. Unlike most Irish folk, its people no longer fear or honour the Tuatha Dé, and have carried stones from the cairns and graves to build houses and churches. The Tuatha Dé are furious, and both worlds need a go-between. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: Omey Island
neighbours.summary: A tidal island reached on foot across the sands at low water, where the villagers race ponies all August, a time for trading, friendship and courting. Saint Feichin's monastery here is failing and may be abandoned unless new patrons come, but its stone church is sound, and its holy well has a Divine aura of its own (3; the book gives no number) and yields Divine vis. Vis: the holy well, Divine (no one holds it).

neighbours.name: Inishbofin and Inishark
neighbours.summary: Twin islands some five miles off Connemara under a strange magical curse: for all their mild weather and good food, those who live there age faster than mainlanders (a -1 Living Conditions penalty). Ruins of monks who died out with no one to follow them litter the islands, the latest Saint Colman's monastery on Inishbofin, gone since the tenth century. Whether something like the Aegis of the Hearth could shield settlers from the curse would take research. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: Cruachan
neighbours.summary:
Rathcroghan, the Ráth of Cruachan, near Tulsk, from which Queen Meadhbh ruled ancient Connacht. Only ruins and worn banks are left of her fortress, but a way still leads into the Faerie regio that holds her court. Mounds and barrows surround it, and from them monsters, beasts and faerie folk break into the mortal world, most of all at Samhain; druids, nightwalkers among them, guard the villages round about. Faerie 3 outside and 6 in the court (the book gives no numbers).

Queen Maedhbh: the scheming, lustful queen of legend knew every magic for ruling a man's mind and heart, and death has not taken her power. She offers it to kings, princes and druids who give themselves to her, and loves Connacht jealously: if the men of Ulster attack, she may bring an army out of the Otherworld against them.

levels.name: Queen Maedhbh's court
levels.enter: By a way into the regio among the ruins of the ráth
levels.notes: Her spirit still holds court here, and kings, princes and druids seek her out.

neighbours.name: Rathbeg
neighbours.summary: A small group of barrows nine miles north of Roscommon, where Fir Bolg warriors slain in battle were laid long before Saint Patrick made their people Christian. Their spirits sleep on below, waiting for someone to call them. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: The Castlestrange Stone
neighbours.summary: A lone egg-shaped stone a yard long near Athleague, on a gentle slope, carved all over with a single winding line.
