There is no aura, but those who have touched it call it unnatural, so few would move it. A larger, more upright stone at the Rath of Fir Mhor near Bullaun bears almost the same design; studied together, the two might give up the carvings' meaning.

neighbours.name: Lough Ree
neighbours.summary:
A long lake on the Sionainne between Connacht and Meath. Its western shore is a faerie trod: the shoreline has a Faerie aura of 5 and can carry a traveller to several other trods across Connacht. Annaghmore lies on the western side, Agharanagh on the eastern. The covenant of Praesis stands on a wooded island out in the water, and the villages of both shores now fear its magi and their men.

During the siege of Praesis, Ballack's forces camped on the eastern shore.

neighbours.name: The Island of Praesis
neighbours.summary: A wooded island in Lough Ree, far enough from either shore that a spell at Voice range cannot reach it, chosen because it lies between the Coill Trí's land and the Order's. The rubble of the first tower and its outbuildings is strewn about, and the trees, burnt and broken in the siege, are greening again. Magic 2 (the book gives no number). The island lies in the lake, not on the Connacht shore, so the covenant stands outside the Treaty's Connacht.

levels.name: The tower's regio
levels.see: The mortal world sees only the island and its rubble
levels.notes: The new tower and the Gáe Bulg on its platform stand here, warded.

neighbours.name: The Rath of Fir Mhor
neighbours.summary: A great ring fort close to Bullaun village and the bigger town of Loughrea. Local nightwalkers use it to guard the harvest from storm spirits, faeries after their cattle and plagues the Infernal sends on the wind: at such times the true Rath, palisade, buildings and all, comes down out of the Magic regio that usually hides it, and from it they shield the land for about twenty miles round. A yard-high rounded stone covered in a swirling line stands here, kin to the Castlestrange Stone, perhaps with the same enchantments. Magic 1 outside, 3 in the regio (the book gives no numbers).

levels.name: The true Rath
levels.enter: It comes down into the mortal world when the nightwalkers gather
levels.notes: Palisade and buildings entire.

neighbours.name: The Aran Isles
neighbours.summary:
Three islands off Gaillimhe Bay, in the small diocese of Annaghdown, home to the last Fir Bolg of Ireland, one tribe to each island. Driven west into Connacht by the Tuatha Dé and then out to the islands by the Milesians, they now serve the kings of Connacht as counsellors of long memory. All but the Fir Domhnann are Christian, converted by Saint Patrick. No aura is given for the isles as a whole.

Story seed: The Missing Mercere Envoy. When the Fomóir and the Tuatha Dé sided with Diedne, the Redcap Blakehalloc sailed to Aran to learn whether the Fir Bolg would join them, and never came back. Counted among the Schism War's dead, he was never sought, and his mission remains a mystery.

neighbours.name: Árainn Mhór
neighbours.summary:
The largest and westernmost island, seat of the Fir Bolg royal line. King Rudraige Ua Sláine lives in Dún Aonghasa, a huge old ring-fort of four dry-stone walls on a clifftop, built by Aonghus mac Úmhór when the Fir Bolg came into exile in Connacht; three lesser forts built the same way (Dún Eoghanachta, Dún Dubhchathair and Dún Eochaill) house other royal kin, and the rest live in clóchan, beehive huts of dry stone. A dozen monasteries hold human and Fir Bolg monks together. Ruaidhri Uí Conchobhair came here for counsel before he made his peace with the English.

The Brannock Islands, two islets to the west: one is the island Gerald of Wales wrote of, where the dead are left in the open and never rot, so a man may go there and look on any number of his forefathers; no mouse can live there either, and any brought over drown themselves or drop dead. The magi of Qui Sonant long to learn more of it, but the Treaty keeps them out of Connacht.

neighbours.name: Árainn Meáin
neighbours.summary: The middle island, home of the Fir Domhnann, smallest of the three tribes, who all live inside the Dun Chonchuir ring-fort. They feel their Fomóir blood and worship the Fomóir goddess Domnu, whose power their druids channel; they have never forgiven the rule of men, since their ancestor Gannan was the one given Connacht to rule when the Fir Bolg first came. There is no church here and no Divine aura; the book gives no other aura.

neighbours.name: Árainn Thiar
neighbours.summary: The smallest island, home of the Fir Gaileoin, Christian in name but hardly practising; the island has a single church. No aura is given.

neighbours.name: Tempull Bheanáin
neighbours.summary: A tiny oratory on a high ridge in the south-east of Árainn Thiar that looks like a deserted ruin. Step through into the terrestrial regio over it and the church is large and overwhelmingly lovely, and nothing can harm those inside. Divine 2 outside and 5 within (the book gives no numbers).

levels.name: The great church
levels.enter: By stepping through the oratory's door
levels.notes: A terrestrial regio: the church inside is vast and wondrous, and no harm can come to anyone within.

neighbours.name: Kingdom of Connacht
neighbours.summary:
King Cathal Uí Conchobhair, of the Uí Briúin Ai, who rules Connacht and takes Bréifne's fealty as a tributary of the English: under the Treaty of Windsor, signed on 6 October 1175, the kings of Connacht hold their crown in return for a yearly tribute to the Lord of Ireland, still paid. His half-brother Ruaidhri, the last free king and the last High-King of Ireland, rose by hard politics, arms and the druids' help; his exile of Mac Murrough brought the English in and lost the other four provinces. Taking the counsel of Fionntan from the Fir Bolg kings of Árainn Mhór (that a tribute can be borne or escaped), he made terms, gave up the high-kingship and died a monk at Cong in 1198. The see of Tuam matches the kingdom's bounds and so props up its authority.

The kings guard the Sionainne fiercely and crush any raid across it. The Templars were given land at Ballymote to shield the kingdom, and the king may think of giving the Order land for the same reason, to steer who settles in Connacht; his druids advise strongly against it.

Tribute owed: a yearly tribute to the Lord of Ireland (Treaty of Windsor).

If history runs its course, Cathal reigns until 1224, when his son Aedh follows him, and the high-kingship is never restored, though two attempts are made.

neighbours.name: Kingdom of Bréifne
neighbours.summary:
King Ualgarg Uí Ruairc, sworn to Connacht. The crown of Bréifne passes by choice, not birth: the men of the Uí Briúin Bréifne pick a king from the male line, and claimants have often blinded or gelded rivals to bar them; its politics are still savage. The Uí Ruairc in the west and the Uí Raghallaigh in the east, rich, strong and fiercely served, have fought over it time and again, each with friends inside Connacht and beyond; the Uí Conchobhair back the Uí Ruairc. The English meddle from outside the province.

Tribute owed: fealty to the king of Connacht.

If history runs its course, Ualgarg loses the throne for a year in 1228 to his cousin Niall, wins it back when Niall dies, and keeps it until his own death in 1231; in 1256 the clans' feud splits Bréifne in two along Druim Leatan, both halves still under Connacht.

neighbours.name: The Uí Raghallaigh
neighbours.summary:
The clan of East Bréifne, the Uí Ruairc's great rivals for its crown, pressed by the English and their Irish vassals on three sides. One of their nobles shelters a witch who has bewitched a farmer's son.

If history runs its course, Cathal Uí Raghallaigh takes Walter de Lacy's castle at Kilmore in 1224 and pulls it down.

neighbours.name: The Ó Cadhla
neighbours.summary: The clan that rules Connemara, facing families driven out of Leinster and Munster by the English who now seek new land in the west.

neighbours.name: The Mac Diarmaid
neighbours.summary: A rich family near Boyle, patrons of its Cistercian abbey. Unlike the other nobles of the region they have often spurned druids' advice, and since 1161 no druid has been allowed at their court.

neighbours.name: The Ó Sheachnasaigh
neighbours.summary: A family of the Uí Fiachrach whose busy stronghold is Gort, beside Cill Mhic Dhuach Monastery, in a diocese grown rich but too weak in arms to stop raiders crossing from Munster.

neighbours.name: The Uí Fiachrach
neighbours.summary: The clan that ruled Connacht for generations before the Uí Briúin overtook them, and whose songs still tell of it; they hold the middle and west of the province, and Cill Mhic Dhuach is their ancestral country. Among their families are the Ó Cléirigh and the Ó Sheachnasaigh.

details.wants: The rule of Connacht they once held
details.offers: Old songs, long memories and a rich southern diocese

neighbours.name: The Uí Maine
neighbours.summary: The clan that drove the Fir Bolg west when it took their lands by the Sionainne; its strength has faded of late, and the Fir Bolg still bear it a grudge. The Ó Fallamháin, the Ó Ceallaigh and the Ó Domhnalláin are among its families.

details.wants: To hold their Sionainne lands as their power wanes
details.offers: Fighting men on the eastern border

neighbours.name: Diocese of Triburnia
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. The see of Bréifne, also called Kilmore, whose bounds are the kingdom's and whose bishop sits at Kilmore. It answers to Armagh, not Tuam, which ignores Bréifne's subjection to Connacht and has been quarrelled over ever since. Bishop Tuathal Ua Connachtaig caused an uproar in 1172 when, as Bishop of Kells, he swore fealty to Henry II, and the Church seems a party to opening Bréifne to the English, something newcomer magi might exploit. The present bishop, Flann Ó Connachtaig, is a scholar with no wish to stand against English influence.

neighbours.name: Druim Leatan Priory
neighbours.summary:
Of the Irish church. The priory on the ridge between the Uí Ruairc and the Uí Raghallaigh, a holy island in an evil land and often sacked as the emblem of the border.

Its Dominion aura is 6, higher than a priory's usual 5, but the ridge around it is malevolently Infernal (up to 4), and the demons there make the priory, as the boundary's mark, the first thing each side burns.

neighbours.name: Diocese of Killala
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. The north-western tip of Connacht, mostly mountain with few people, wide inland marshes and peat bog; the Stags of Broadhaven lie off its coast. The book does not name its bishop.

neighbours.name: Diocese of Achonry
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. The see round Sligo, cut off from Killala by a mountain ridge and from Bréifne by nothing but goodwill, so its people must keep both the Uí Ruairc and the Uí Conchobhair kings content. The book does not name its bishop.

neighbours.name: Diocese of Mayo
neighbours.summary:
Of the Irish church. A see that is no more: a papal legate dissolved it in 1202 and gave its lands and monasteries straight to Tuam, and Pope Innocent III confirmed it in 1216, but its clergy still resist and would take their case to Rome. Croagh Patrick, Aughagower and Achill lie in its old lands.

If history runs its course, another legate confirms the dissolution in 1221 and Pope Gregory IX does so finally in 1240.

neighbours.name: The Church on Croagh Patrick
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. A small church on the summit where Patrick fasted, the goal of pilgrims, amid shrines to the saint.

neighbours.name: Aughagower
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. A village church on the pilgrims' road in Patrick's steps. In a slim tower in its grounds lives a druid whose power is Divine, a lone cantor who blesses travellers whose faith is wavering and who need a sign they are on the right road (the Cantores of Realms of Power: The Divine).

neighbours.name: Cong Abbey
neighbours.summary:
Of the Irish church. Founded by Saint Deichin early in the seventh century; its monks lately took the Augustinian rule and left the old Celtic ways. Burnt early in the twelfth century, rebuilt about 1135, sacked by the English knight William de Burgh in 1203 though it lies deep in Connacht, and rebuilt again. Ruaidhri Uí Conchobhair retired here after giving up the high-kingship.

The Cross of Cong, a golden processional cross that Tairrdelbach Uí Conchobhair had made nearly seventy years ago, is a reliquary of a fragment of the True Cross (3 Faith Points). It was meant for Tuam's cathedral and came here when the abbey was last rebuilt.

neighbours.name: Diocese of Elphin
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. The eastern edge of Connacht, along the Sionainne, whose people watch the far bank for the English. Saint Patrick made Elphin a see when the druid Ono, lord of these lands, was converted and gave him his castle for a monastery. Many of its men have died fighting for the druids against those of Leinster, and they fear an English attack will follow. Bishop Dionysius Ó Mórda has little patience or sympathy for druids.

neighbours.name: Boyle Abbey
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. A Cistercian house not sixty years old, built with the wealth of the Mac Diarmaid and still being built; its church was consecrated only in 1218. It is the Cistercians' third try at a site in Connacht, where they have struggled to take root.

neighbours.name: Diocese of Annaghdown
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. A small see with few people, which matters because Ireland's Fir Bolg on the Aran Isles fall within it. The book does not name its bishop.

neighbours.name: The Monasteries of Árainn Mhór
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. A dozen monasteries on the largest Aran island, where human and Fir Bolg monks live side by side.

neighbours.name: Diocese of Cill Mhic Dhuach
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. The old home of the Uí Fiachrach in the south, rich now but too weak in arms to keep out raiders from Munster. The book does not name its bishop.

neighbours.name: Cill Mhic Dhuach Monastery
neighbours.summary:
Of the Irish church. A monastery beside Gort that has grown in standing over the past century: a fine stone church and other buildings, and a tall round tower with a marked lean to the east. They say no one in this diocese can be killed by lightning.

If history runs its course, its wealth sees it plundered many times in the thirteenth century.

neighbours.name: Diocese of Clonfert
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. The south-eastern see, whose cathedral grew from the older monastery, its church begun about 1180. A magical stonemason carved the great arch round its doors so beautifully that supernatural beasts of every realm came to watch him, and the stone still bears the faces of those who came. The book does not name its bishop.

links.note: Saint Brendan the Navigator, whose relics lie at Clonfert

neighbours.name: Saint Feichin's Monastery, Omey
neighbours.summary: Of the Irish church. Saint Feichin's foundation on Omey Island, hard pressed in recent years and likely to be abandoned without new patrons; its stone church is sturdy and its holy well gives Divine vis.

neighbours.name: The Temple House at Ballymote
neighbours.summary: Of neither Irish church: a house of the Knights Templar, Connacht's only one, under their own order. A plain square castle with no keep, built in 1181 on the edge of Ballymote, ten miles south of Sligo and five west of Lough Arrow, close enough to Bréifne to provoke. A few foreign Templars and many Connachta lay brothers live in it. The kings granted the land about forty years ago for politics' sake, as a shield against anyone with designs on Bréifne.

neighbours.name: Sligo
neighbours.summary: A town on the Sligeach estuary, home to fishermen who gather the shellfish along its shore; the river comes down from Lough Gill, a lake some six miles long. It has no walls, castle, abbey or cathedral, only many small religious houses scattered round about. Lough Gara, Cnoc na Ré, Drumcliffe and Binn Ghulbain are near.

neighbours.name: Carrick
neighbours.summary: A small Bréifne town at a natural ford of the Sionainne, with a soldierly air: if the English ever invaded Connacht, both sides would race to hold it, for it commands the supply road. The Black Pig's Dyke passes west and south of it.

neighbours.name: Kilmore
neighbours.summary:
The seat of the bishop of Triburnia, twenty miles east of the Sionainne and a couple of miles from Cavan, guarded by a motte-and-bailey castle Walter de Lacy raised in 1211, one of many he has built to push into Connacht. The Black Pig's Dyke encloses Kilmore and Cavan on the west, north and east, about five miles out on each side.

If history runs its course, Cathal Uí Raghallaigh seizes the castle in 1224 and razes it, the fate of many of de Lacy's castles.

neighbours.name: Cavan
neighbours.summary: A town of East Bréifne just south-east of a cluster of small lakes full of crannógs, a couple of miles from Kilmore.

neighbours.name: Ballymote
neighbours.summary: A town that has done better since the Templars built their castle beside it: it keeps off the bandits that used to trouble it, and supplying the knights keeps its merchants busy.

neighbours.name: Tuam
neighbours.summary: A city whose political weight is fading. The Uí Conchobhair built a castle here in 1164 to tighten their hold on Connacht, but it has gone downhill since: it has five monasteries and several high crosses, yet its cathedral burnt down in 1184 and, with the king's abdication in 1185 and the strain on the borders, nobody has rebuilt it. Its markets and fairs thrive and its merchants grow rich, but the great men have left, and an archbishop without a cathedral presides over ground some would call ripe for the Infernal.

neighbours.name: Cong
neighbours.summary: A town on an island made by the streams that flow round it, above underground channels that link Lough Mask to Lough Gaillimhe, near the field of the first battle of Mag Tuired and home to its abbey. A rich nobleman of Cong keeps the druid Ádhamh Brathair, who works his magic for the noble and his family.

neighbours.name: Elphin
neighbours.summary: A pious town south of Carrick and north of Boyle. When Patrick came through, the druid Ono ruled here; converted, he gave the saint his land and castle for a monastery, and a spring of pure water that broke out at Patrick's miracle still runs through the town.

neighbours.name: Boyle
neighbours.summary: The Mac Diarmaid's town, with its new Cistercian abbey.

neighbours.name: Roscommon
neighbours.summary: A market town with charters aplenty and many roads through it, yet strangely listless. Every three years ill luck comes back: three years ago an Ollamh singer was driven out, three before that the church bell cracked, three before that a magical swan was killed. Whatever the cause, something like a fog is settling over its people.

neighbours.name: Athlone
neighbours.summary:
The English foothold in Connacht, ten miles south-east of Roscommon below Lough Ree, at an old ford: south of here the Sionainne cannot be crossed until Clonmacnoise, so the place has always mattered. Tairrdelbach Uí Conchobhair built a bridge and ring fort a century ago; John de Gray, Bishop of Norwich, justiciar from 1209 to 1212, put a stone castle in the fort's place ten years ago. Walter de Lacy now holds it with a small garrison, and the English keep the great stone bridge that links Meath and Leinster with Connacht. The town thrives under English rule, its market selling goods hard to find in the west, and the trade of the Sionainne and the Great Highway passes through. The castle keeps Connachta armies out of Meath but not the small bands that slip across the river to try themselves against the English.

At night the banshee's dreadful cry is often heard here, for many local families carry the death omen; those who hear it weep and mourn, but a quick-witted listener who learns which kinsman is doomed can sometimes turn the death aside.

neighbours.name: Gort
neighbours.summary: The bustling stronghold of the Ó Sheachnasaigh in the south, beside Cill Mhic Dhuach Monastery.

neighbours.name: Oireadh
neighbours.summary: A village where the druids of the Pact of Oireadh meet every season, no more than two days' journey for any of them. Its villagers are well paid for their hospitality and loyal; they know where to reach each druid, eye strangers asking after them (-1 to social rolls with them), and quietly send word to Mór Greannach at nearby Carrowmore. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Carrowmore
neighbours.summary: The village near Oireadh where Mór Greannach lives, gathering herbs and things of virtue from the hills and woods round it.

neighbours.name: Rosbeg
neighbours.summary:
A coastal village west of Oireadh, where Tuathal an Iarrainn keeps a well-equipped smithy and workshop with two mundane apprentices.

Story seed: The Diabolist's Dying Wish. Tuathal an Iarrainn's goetic master has died in Dublin, leaving money and a large book in Latin and cipher to be sent to Tuathal at Rosbeg. Someone saw what the book was, and it has reached the player covenant through a companion. It is a book of Infernal Lore about particular demons. Keep it, deliver it, or look across the border for diabolism?

neighbours.name: The Pact of Oireadh
neighbours.summary:
Eight druids of mixed traditions, sworn to work together toward a single theory of their magic. Unlike the Order they make no distinction of tradition: witch, learned magician, goetic sorcerer and Fir Bolg all sit together as equals. They do not live together but meet each season at Oireadh, each keeping an aura that suits his own magic; living apart blunts the Gift's ill will, which bites only face to face, and their helpers and messengers, often met on the roads of the region, carry word between them. They help one another in magic and in worldly affairs, live mostly in Connacht, and have no love for the English. Hedge traditions are not modelled: the druids are told here.

History. Praesis was once where Connacht's hedge wizards met the Ordo Hiberniae, and long talk there made some of them wonder what the magi kept from them. These druids were Praesis's allies until Meadhbh asked too much of them; they left her, and began asking what gave the Order its strength and what shielded it while lesser wizards fell.

Ádhamh Brathair (55, looks 55; Charismatic +3, Determined +2, Cautious +1), a Gifted learned magician whose lineage goes back to Bologna, master of experimental philosophy, in minor orders, kept by a rich nobleman of Cong. He thought of the Pact and leads its research, which he knows will outlast him; he would like the glory but works for the greater good. Wary of how close the Coill Trí stand to the Ordo Hiberniae, he tells them little, the more so since they took a Gifted child from him for the Order's tithe.

Umor Ard Mac Adar (Autumn, looks 50; Magic Might 25; Gentle +3, Independent +2, Idealistic +1), a transformed Fir Domhnann, one of the few to leave Árainn Meáin, still faithful to Domnu: bigger than any man, with a second pair of arms from his sides for his Fomóir blood, otherwise nearly handsome; his blood gives him Might and the power to heal. Bitter at his people's exile, he helps Ádhamh to win the favour of men so the Fir Domhnann may one day return to the mainland; some of his kind call him a traitor. He fears humans but trusts Ádhamh, and often calms quarrels between the Gifted members. He lives in the hills above Lough Conn and can be found only at night.

Mór Greannach, 'grey-beard' (75, looks 75; Mischievous +3, Meddling +2, Trustworthy -1), a folk witch named for the thin beard on her chin, who has spent her long life serving her community and is as feared and mistrusted as she is honoured and asked for help. She knows the magical world deeply and enriches the herbs and objects of virtue she gathers. She has the widest acquaintance of the Pact: her coven, scores of nightwalkers, faerie-touched craftsmen, Ollamhain and the Kilkenny coven in Leinster. She lives closest to Oireadh, at Carrowmore.

Tuathal an Iarrainn (40, looks 40; Honest +3, Disciplined +2), a goetic sorcerer, master of the Ars Goetica that summon, bind and command spirits; some mistrust his magic and its source, but he never hides what he is. A master smith of Rosbeg, he binds spirits into what he forges, and lately commands them at Ádhamh's asking to hunt for things the research needs.

The other four members are not named. The Coill Trí and the Ordo Hiberniae both know the Pact as a fellowship of druids; its research is kept from both.

details.rules: Druids of every tradition sit as equals; members keep apart but for the seasonal meeting; the research stays secret
details.wants: A single theory of the magics of Ireland, and the protection it would bring
details.offers: Healing, divination, bound spirits and forged wonders, herbs of virtue, and wide contacts among the hedge folk

neighbours.secrets:
The Pact's true aim is a Parma Magica of its own; the Order knows nothing of it.
Ádhamh's vision is a theory of magic that takes in every Irish tradition and gives every practitioner each tradition's defences: a breakthrough of at least 120 points (the Original Research rules of Houses of Hermes: True Lineages). He has 15. So far he has made amulets, after the Folk Witch tradition, that give their wearer Second Sight, Dowsing or Cursing at a score of 4 for a season; they have shown him how his own magic differs from the witches', and by learning those Abilities he hopes to gain their small magical defences. His notes are hidden for those who come after him.
The Gifted child the Coill Trí took from Ádhamh is now an apprentice in a Hermetic covenant, and he may yet ask her to report on summoners she meets.
Tuathal's goetic arts are Infernal at root, though he does not hide them and Ádhamh has not yet seen it. His Goetic master has just died in Dublin, leaving him a book of Infernal Lore on particular demons.
Umor's three cousins have sworn to kill him for leaving Árainn Meáin.

neighbours.name: The Druids (draoithe)
neighbours.summary:
The learned class of pagan Ireland is gone. Its druids kept the lore in memory, judged, advised kings, served the old gods, foretold and worked magic, and would not set their secrets down in writing, so what is known of them now is rumour and story. They were already failing under Saint Patrick's missions and vanished from society in the ninth century. Irish druidry was never House Diedne's, and both are now thought extinct.

The word covered three callings. Every druid began with four years as a bard, the keeper of tales and maker of poems, who trained his memory in place of writing. Some went on to four years as a fáith (plural fáithi), the priest who tended a clan's gods and read their will by divination, and some of those to the draoi (plural draoithe), counsellor, lawgiver and chief magician of a clan: twenty years in all.

Their magic, as the tales tell it: memory so trained it seemed uncanny, divination above all, the laying of prohibitions and curses that marked out kings and champions, changing their own shape or another's (often as a curse), illusion, and for a few, weather, which in war meant mist and storm sent against the foe. The Pictish gruagachan of Hedge Magic Revised Edition have every one of these powers but weather, and may be the other branch of the same tradition; the druids had no tattoo magic, no tie to giants and no external soul. Whether Diedne's Breton and Gaulish line was kin to them is left to each saga.

Their gods were whatever was supernatural: one of the Tuatha Dé, an ancestor, a hero, a beast, a rock or an old tree, and none was god of anything in particular. Each clan had its own, placated by its fáith; the draoi dealt with every other power that the clan did not worship.

Diedne first came in 793 and offered the chief druid Sechnassach a place in her House or death; he laughed her off. She came back in 797 with twenty-seven of her House, landing near Wexford, and three bands of nine hunted the druids across Ireland. Most chose death. By 816 she told the Tribunal that none were left, an overstatement, but the tradition was broken. In 806 she met Pralix on the shore of Lough Cuan, each sure the other had come to help her; the quarrel became an unlawful Wizard War, and neither ever charged the other or said who struck first.

Today most Irish hedge wizards claim druid blood, mostly without cause. Connacht's wizards call themselves druids as members of the Coill Trí (see that faction); the Pact of Oireadh is Connacht's other druid circle (see Connacht).

Geasa. A geas (or geis) is an enchantment that punishes a forbidden act. Druids laid them on kings and champions to set them apart and on enemies as curses; some hedge wizards can still make one, and old-fashioned faeries love them. A fortifying geas is a Minor Virtue, often with a small uncanny sign, joined to the Prohibition Flaw: break the condition and both are lost, perhaps to be won back by making amends to whoever laid it. Death Prophecy is a mighty fortifying geas that holds death off while its condition stands. A prohibition geas is the Prohibition Flaw alone; breaking it swaps it for another Minor Flaw, or for a while a Major one that heals like a Heavy Wound or with amends, after which the prohibition returns. A blight geas is set off by outside circumstance, as Baneful Circumstances and Macha's Birth-Pangs (the ces noidhen) are. A geas names a kind of person, beast, thing or place, a circumstance, and an injunction: 'never' for a prohibition, 'always' for most fortifying geasa, 'while' or 'if' for a blight. Baneful Circumstances and Lesser Malediction: Macha's Birth-Pangs are in the catalog; geasa as a system are not modelled.

Sketched as a faction until the app models hedge magic: its powers are summarised here, and a member who needs them is played from The Contested Isle and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.

details.rules: Now only a title: any Gifted wizard, or any member of a hedge tradition, is called a draoi; a hedge wizard without either is an asarlaí. Many of the Code's oaths bind only druids and magi, not the asarlaithe.
details.wants: Their old lore recovered; to be let alone by the Order
details.offers: Divination, geasa, shape-changing and weather-working

neighbours.name: The Coill Trí
neighbours.summary:
The federation of Connacht's non-Hermetic wizards, of many traditions, all claiming to be the heirs of the scattered druid lore and all taking the druid's title. In 844 Cormacan the Learned, Chief Bard of Ireland, came to the Order on behalf of High-King Congalach Cnogba, whose hedge-wizard subjects complained of harassment; Fedelmid Ua Heirméais of House Mercere spoke for the Order. Diedne's pogrom had shown that Join or Die fails in Ireland, so the two sides made the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh (see the Tribunal), binding from the Tribunal's first meeting in 898. The wizards it bound were first called the Comman Cosán Chían (roughly, a league of the old way); from its three Cs (in ogham, C is coll, the hazel) the name soon wore down to the Coill Trí, the three hazels.

The Order urged, and sometimes forced, hedge wizards who fought magi over resources to move to Connacht, leaving the rest of the island to the Hermetic magi. The Coill Trí now number at least as many as the Hibernian Order and perhaps far more. It is a legal person, not a rival: it has no centre, no rules, no common aims and takes no joint action, and attempts to raise it into a native host fail on the suspicion The Gift breeds, which suits the Order. Membership is rarely a choice for a draoi.

What it gives its members is the Treaty's protection. A wronged draoi may complain at Tribunal and is owed an investigation and justice, but few do, preferring a little abuse to the Order's scrutiny; more often members bring quarrels with one another or with supernatural beings to the Sacred Council, where Hermetic judges see that the weaker side is treated fairly. Its own ambassador, chosen from its ranks, speaks for every wizard in Ireland, must see the children delivered and the parties to a case brought, and is trusted by neither side; a hedge wizard can bring a case or make a treaty only with its sponsorship.

The tithe of seven Gifted children chafes most. Not every draoi can see The Gift, so offered children are sometimes refused; when the tithe is late, Redcaps go into Connacht to demand it of known druids, and the red-capped stranger hunting children has become a Connacht bogey, more than once chased off by a mob. Some magi use their power to extort services from the Coill Trí, who dare not complain. The Treaty has never been tested at Tribunal, and the day is near: English magi call it a mockery of a Code made for Hermetic magi, and some Irish magi covet Connacht. Most members are Christian, if not orthodox, and some Connacht clergy notice that the bishop's court keeps finding deviants tied to an organization they know almost nothing of, and wonder if it is a nest of heretics or worse.

The seven túatha. Each túath is a region, takes its name from its current ceannaire, and sends the ceannaire to Tribunal; some ceannairí carry their members' complaints, others make members speak for themselves. Most túatha exist only in name, a few are run like a chief's clan with rules and courts, and ceannairí are elected, born to it or chosen by lot. Unless said, the troupe places them; the book describes four and leaves three for the troupe.

Túath Buidhe: mostly unGifted visionaries rebuilding the druid lore from its fragments into a cult on the old legends, with scores of Initiation Scripts gathered from other members and dozens more of their own making, which they will gladly use to Initiate anyone in the Coill Trí; the storyguide decides whether they like the Order or still hate it for Diedne. Their ceannaire always comes from one line of Cruithnigh wizards. Buidhe himself, a mystagogue thought mad, lives on an island off Connacht's west coast, where visitors find him naked in the rain talking to a rowan or entranced under a bull's hide; his memory holds scripts for many Supernatural Virtues, most of which he lacks, and if he can be kept attentive he usually agrees to Initiate.

Túath hEilionora: every member who lives outside Connacht, so that hedge wizards elsewhere share the Treaty's protection and magi near a tradition can treat with it at law; twice the size of any other. Its ceannaire is whoever settles in a certain Magic aura (the saga chooses it) on her predecessor's appointment. Eilionora inghean Ua Shuibne, an elemental physician who learned her craft in France, is devoted to the restoration of the old lore, reads the old tales eagerly and half believes she is Macha Mhuinge Ruadh reborn, the queen who founded Ireland's first hospital at Bron Bherg (see Eamhain Mhacha, Ulster). The native traditions think her an upstart and shun her; she bears it and stays active.

Túath Saidhbh: unusually many Gifted members, always, who avoid one another and share no culture; they draw lots for the hated post of ceannaire. Magi long to know why the region breeds The Gift, but the Treaty keeps them out, even those born there. Sadhbh Amhreaidh, a cold, bitter folk witch who sneers at the likes of Eilionora, claims endless generations of witches behind her; she and her grandmother alone survived a mundane attack on their coven, and no other coven will take in witches who teach Embitterment (Tales of Mythic Europe). She has no daughter yet to teach.

Túath Rónáin: lately shamed when a magus, not its own people, uncovered a diabolic coven among its members. Its ceannaire now keeps three inquisitors watching the rest, and suspicion weighs hardest on its Gifted. Rónán Brathair, a Cistercian monk and a draoi who helped root the coven out, uses the Holy Powers of Intervention and Understanding by Meditation and would turn the Coill Trí toward God, knowing how large a task that is.

Three further túatha: not described in the book; the troupe names them and their ceannairí as needed.

Faolán of the Younger House lives among the Coill Trí in breach of the Treaty (see Connacht).

Sketched as a faction until the app models hedge magic: its powers are summarised here, and a member who needs them is played from The Contested Isle and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.
neighbours.ruler: Seven ceannairí, one for each túath

details.rules: Every hedge wizard in Connacht is taken to be a member; those outside it wear an amulet of three hazel leaves. Each of the seven túatha must find one Gifted child every seven years for the Order. A new clause of the Treaty needs a Tribunal's vote and every ceannaire's consent, and a magus must propose it.
details.wants: Freedom from the Order's bullying; relief from the tithe of children; justice at the Sacred Council
details.offers: Seven Gifted children at every Tribunal; a single party for the Order to treat with in place of hundreds of hedge wizards

links.note: Lives among the Coill Trí in breach of the Treaty
May enter Connacht on three errands
A haven for all under the Treaty

neighbours.name: The Bards (filídh)
neighbours.summary:
Of the three druid callings only the bards lived through Christianity and Diedne, dismissed as mere poets by the one and as petty conjurers by the other, and they are little changed in 1220. They keep the old tales and Christian homilies in verse and prose and make new works for the kings who keep them, and they call themselves filídh (singular filí) rather than bards, to put their druid past further behind them.

Their schools double as Ireland's grammar schools for aristocrats' sons: four years of grammar, composition, history, genealogy, geography and custom, then the examination. Those who stay grow their memories further; a senior bard knows more than two hundred stories and builds poems with many layers of meaning. The Chief Bard is the high-king's own poet and king of the bards, who settles their quarrels with outsiders and sets the fashions of verse. The last, Giolla Ernain Ua Martain, died in 1218, and no successor has been chosen.

Bards inherit the old reverence for druids. Their immunity, once the high-king's guarantee, has lapsed, but their name still protects them: Irish households owe a known bard hospitality, feuding with one was long forbidden, and even robbers fear to touch one, so a bard walks the roads in safety.

Bard characters: the Social Status Virtues Bard (free; a filí of the rank of Dos, Local Reputation 1, aged 20 or more), Senior Bard (Minor; a Cano or Cli after five or six years, Reputation 2, 90 extra experience points) and Master Bard (Major; an Anruth after nine years, Reputation 3, 240 extra points, two seasons a year teaching or composing for a lord), with Bardic Education (the catalog's Educated (Bardic), 50 points) for the years of study; the Protection Virtue for the respect they are owed, worth more where the English are weak; Profession: Storyteller or Poet, the lores, and the Art of Memory (or Concentration). Enchanting Storytelling is Enchanting Music told as a tale. All are in the catalog.

Bards of power. A few senior bards keep the druids' magic in the making of their works rather than the telling: Máistirs whose verse is uncannily beautiful, and many of them wordsmiths, with Touched by (Realm), usually Faerie, who make wondrous tales and poems as others make wondrous items, using Communication + Profession: Storyteller or Poet, limited to Personal Range, Performance Duration and Sound Target, and usable only by the one they were made for; reciting one makes an Arcane Connection to the reciter that a magus can catch. The Uí hUiginn school has most of them, some able to work craft magic like the Rusticani. The book gives five such tales: The Youthful Exploits of Cú Chulainn (ReCo 30, listeners ignore fatigue and wounds), Fear Diadh's Last Stand (CrMe 20, +3 against fear), The Daghdha's Escape from Indech's Ráth (ReMe 20, an unbreakable sleep), Manannán Mac Lir's Chariot (MuAq(Te) 30, walking on water) and Blrrmm, Blrrmm (Mu(Re)Im 10, listeners can only babble).

The new Duration Performance (as Concentration: it lasts while the caster performs, after a Communication + Ability roll against 3) and Target Sound (as Structure: everyone who hears the sound within a Voice range of it) need Performance Magic or Sensory Magic for Hermetic use; the app does not model either.

The four great schools are Dromnea of the Uí Dálaigh, Baile Uí Eódhasa, Ceall Cluaine of the Uí hUiginn and Cahir of the Mac Craith (each its own record). The Ollamhain, faerie musicians who steal the ollamh's title, are their rivals (see that faction).

Sketched as a faction until the app models hedge magic: its powers are summarised here, and a member who needs them is played from The Contested Isle and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.

Story seed: The Ollamhain Heresy. The Ollamhain, faerie wizards who use music to conjure glamour and borrow the title of ollamh without its burdens, are scorned by the bardic schools, and wordsmiths have tried to prosecute them at the Sacred Council. A rival covenant's bard may prove to be one; the schools' enmity could be turned against him, in a war of satire and rhymed slander.
neighbours.ruler: The ard-ollamh Érenn, the Chief Bard of Ireland (vacant since 1218)

details.rules: Nine grades of learning; four years and a hard examination make a filí, twelve an ollamh, who may found a school. Only the Chief Bard may strip a bard of rank, and only a bard's son and grandson may become Chief Bard. Mixing music with bardic tales is a grave sin to the schools.
details.wants: Patrons, the old tales kept, a new Chief Bard
details.offers: Lore, genealogy, praise or satire, and schooling for nobles' sons

neighbours.secrets: Some senior bards still hold their druid forebears' magic, though not every bard of high grade can, and no bard will own that such magic exists.

neighbours.name: The Ollamhain
neighbours.summary:
A small band of faerie magicians (Realms of Power: Faerie) who call themselves the masters, taking the learned grade of ollamh for a tradition that conjures glamour with music. They are stronger in magic than the Irish bards but lack their good name. The schools teach none of it: music is a lesser art to them, using it for glamour betrays the tradition, and the Ollamhain carry the title with none of its lore or duty, so they are forbidden to call themselves filídh. Some do anyway, and wordsmiths have tried to prosecute rivals before the Sacred Council. Between single bards and Ollamhain things may be respectful, each keeping to its own sphere, or a bitter feud.

Story seed: the bardic schools' enmity could be turned against a covenant's rival, sparking a war of satire and rhymed slander.

Faolán of the Younger House is the son in magic of a true Ollamh, and an Ollamhain singer was driven out of Roscommon (see Connacht).

Sketched as a faction until the app models hedge magic: its powers are summarised here, and a member who needs them is played from The Contested Isle and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.

details.rules: Faerie wizardry worked through music, outside the bardic schools
details.wants: The bardic title, and audiences to enchant
details.offers: Glamour and music stronger than any filí's

neighbours.secrets: A 'bard' who takes the part of the covenant's rival or enemy is in truth one of the Ollamhain.

neighbours.name: Dromnea, the Uí Dálaigh school
neighbours.summary:
The school of the Uí Dálaigh, perhaps Ireland's most famous bardic family, which has given most of the Chief Bards of the last six hundred years. Its founder, Cearbhall Fionn mac Aonghus Ua Dálaigh, won the gift of poetry by drinking a faerie cow's milk; the great Cú Chonnacht Ua Dálaigh, held the best of Ireland's bards living or dead, was great-grandfather to the present head, Donnchadh Mór Ua Dálaigh. The family rule the Mhuintir Bháire peninsula, which the book puts in Connacht, as its chiefs. As political as the Mac Craith, but far quieter about it.

A bardic school, entered as a cathedral school for its teaching limits.

neighbours.name: Baile Uí Eódhasa, the Uí hEódhasa school
neighbours.summary:
The Uí hEódhasa school on the shore of lower Lough Erne in Ulster, known for epic verse of glorious battles and heroic slaughter. The taste for such poems has passed, and the school is out of fashion and short of patrons.

A bardic school, entered as a cathedral school for its teaching limits.

neighbours.name: Ceall Cluaine, the Uí hUiginn school
neighbours.summary:
The Uí hUiginn school at Ceall Cluaine (Kilcloney) in Leinster, the smallest of the four great schools. It is famed for finely built tales that stack meaning on meaning, makes more magical tales than any other school (most of the wordsmiths are its filídh), and teaches music too, though not to its bardic standard in verse and prose. Tadg Ua Broin, seanachaidh of Lámbaird's clan, studied here.

A bardic school, entered as a cathedral school for its teaching limits.

neighbours.name: Cahir, the Mac Craith school
neighbours.summary:
The school of the Mac Craith, hereditary poets and chroniclers to their Uí Briain kin, who followed them into Munster. It sits inside Cahir Castle, near Waterford as the book has it, and is the most openly political of the bardic schools.

A bardic school, entered as a cathedral school for its teaching limits.

neighbours.name: The Tuatha Dé Danann
neighbours.summary:
Ireland's pagan gods, the children of Danu: faeries first bound to the great elemental spirit of the Danube, who took up a band of Nemed's grandson's people fleeing Ireland, dwelt with them in four mysterious cities, then led them back to conquer the Fir Bolg and later the Fomórach. For two hundred years they lived among their followers, marrying them and teaching their arts, until the Mílesians defeated them and they withdrew into cairns, tumuli and buried ráths. Many remain, kings, warriors and leaders, handsome and dressed like nobles, but they are seldom met. The Irish still honour them and remember their tales.

Some of them: Aonghus mac Óg of youth, love and passion; Badhbh the war goddess, who bathes in her enemies' blood and whose sight is an evil omen; Brigid of fertility, healing and poetry, whose holy places a saint of the same name took over; Dian Céacht the physician; Donn the death god, gathering an army of spirits at Teach Duínn (see the Bestiary); Goibhniu the smith, maker of magic spears and of an ale that grants immortality, who hates Donn; Lugh of many crafts, the Tuatha Dé's saviour at the Second Battle of Moytirra; Manannán mac Lir of the sea, who drives his chariot round Ireland herding fish and whales; Oghma, who made the ogham letters; the Dagda, father of the gods as Danu is their mother, though not their leader; and Nuadha of the Silver Arm, their leader in the wars with the Fir Bolg and the Fomóir. The four treasures of the Tuatha Dé still exist.

Their ambassador is Mug Ruith, a faerie in the role of a famous Munster druid who learned his craft from Simon Magus in Jerusalem, served many Munster kings as court wizard and, some say, beheaded John the Baptist, cursing the Irish with violence. He sits on the Sacred Council every seven years for Bobd, king of the Munster Tuatha Dé, flying in on the roth rámach, his oared wheel, in a bull's hide and a bird mask. He lives on Dairbhre off Desmond's west coast (see Munster) with his faerie daughter Tlachtga, a strong druid herself, who also keeps a sídhe on the Hill of Tlachtga (see Meath). His treasures, a shining chariot, a magic shield and a stone that once became a venomous eel, draw treasure seekers to the island.

Their stories: comical tales they repeat for spectators who get caught in them (the Dagda once ate his way out of a pit of porridge, and may make a village dig and fill another); tales of craft and wonder (Manannán's cloaks of invisibility, Goibhniu's ale, Dian Céacht's healing pools); feuds, in which locals suffer; and tales of bloodshed that stir men to violence or warn them off it.

Story seeds: an Irish rebel steals one of Manannán's cloaks to raid the English along the Leinster-Ulster border, and its faerie owner torments the next village until it is returned; thieves brew Goibhniu's ale and sell it to princes and knights, not knowing it turns to poison within the month unless he brews it, and a hedge wizard asks the magi to find the barrels; a covenfolk's contagious old Irish sickness defies Hermetic healing, and only one of Dian Céacht's pools will cure it; Donn steals Goibhniu's magic cow and hides it in a local king's ráth, and Goibhniu arms trooping faeries with enchanted spears to raid it; Lugh gathers young men, some of the macgnímartha among them, to raid the Fomóir islands again, and the magi fear the raid will bring a Fomóir invasion; a physician on his way to cure his king sees Badhbh and begs the magi to drive her off (poets say Strongbow saw her washing severed heads before his last battle).

Faerie story seeds. The Tuatha Dé repeat their tales and pull onlookers in. The Dagda makes villagers hollow out the ground and heap porridge into it, or bursts into a coast village with a Fomóir's wife, her husband's ship just offshore. A rebel steals one of Manannán's cloaks of invisibility to raid the English, and the faerie harries the village until it is returned. Thieves brew Goibhniu's ale of immortality and sell it, not knowing it turns to poison within a month. A covenfolk's old Irish sickness defies Hermetic healing and needs one of Dian Céacht's pools. Donn steals Goibhniu's cow and hides it in a king's ráth, and Goibhniu arms trooping faeries to raid it. Lugh raids the Fomóir isles again with young men, among them some in their macgnímartha. A physician sees Badhbh on his way to his king. Fionn and his fian burst into a wedding to take back an eloping Leinster bride. Faeries play saints and devils too: a false Saint Patrick, a devil cat who feeds on a priest's fears, a dicing devil who leaves a grog drained and sure he met Satan.
neighbours.ruler: No one leader; Bobd is king of the Munster Tuatha Dé

details.rules: Each is an individual with his own interests, not a god of anything; they were lived with and learned from, never truly worshipped. They can handle iron freely. Their ambassador is confirmed at the Sacred Council.
details.wants: Their stories retold and lived again, and the vitality that brings
details.offers: Craft, enchanted treasures, healing, and a vote at Tribunal

neighbours.secrets: Why the Tuatha Dé sided with House Diedne in the Schism War is still unknown, after two centuries of Cliffheart's questions (see Munster).

neighbours.name: The Fir Bolg
neighbours.summary:
The people who came after the flood that ended the Nemedians, in three tribes: the Fir Bolg proper, the most numerous, who named the whole race, the Fir Domhnann and the Gaileoin. Landing in the south, they spread over the island and first cut it into the four provinces still used, all but Meath. In the north they met the Fomórach, bought peace with tribute and became their serfs, farming for idle Fomóir lords. Beaten by the Tuatha Dé at the First Battle of Magh Tuireadh, they were offered one province and chose Connacht; when the Fomórach came for tribute and found the Tuatha Dé there instead, those two went to war. Few remain in Connacht; most now live on the Aran Isles (see Connacht).

They were once like humans but greater, taller, stronger, fairer and more skilled, peaceful farmers who could make the poorest ground bear; but Fomóir lords bred with them, and now few escape deformity but the royal line of each tribe, and the monstrous blood makes them wrathful and prone to the Ríastradh. Royalty is the Gentleman or Gentlewoman Virtue, about as much as humans grant their titles; the royal caste often has a power of healing or fertility, such as Purifying Touch or Control Fertility, and one with a Dark Secret or Black Sheep may hide or show a malformation.

The Fir Bolg tribe is still the largest and leads: King Rudraige Ua Sláine, who rules the whole race, lives on Árainn Mhór with them. They are Christian, converted by Saint Grellan as this chapter has it (Connacht's chapter says Saint Patrick). The Fir Domhnann, the smallest and always closest to the Fomórach, took the Fomóir goddess Domnu as their own and keep the night as their Lady of Darkness wants; their druids have strange powers of darkness and healing that light undoes. The Gaileoin look Christian, and are a lazier, more casually sinful people than their neighbours.

Their ambassador is Fothaid, one of the king's younger sons: seven feet tall, broad and brawny, graceful, a trained speaker as handsome in manner as in looks, and fiercely vain of his pure blood, raging at any hint of a flaw. He cares little for his people and uses the Tribunal to win admirers.

Fir Bolg characters and battle transformations are as the Fomórach's (see that faction); Sláine, their leader, was the first high-king of Mythic Ireland.

Sketched as a faction until the app models hedge magic: its powers are summarised here, and a member who needs them is played from The Contested Isle and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.
neighbours.ruler: King Rudraige Ua Sláine, on Árainn Mhór

details.rules: Three tribes, each with a royal line free of deformity; their ambassador comes from the royal blood. A Fir Bolg has Magical Blood (Human), often Great (Characteristic) and Large, and unless royal the deformities of Fomóir blood.
details.wants: Respect for their titles; their old pride restored
details.offers: Counsel to Connacht's rulers, healing and fertility, a vote at Tribunal

neighbours.secrets:
A secret circle of Gaileoin infernalists rules the tribe's king; the other tribes do not know. The meddling has left the Gaileoin royal line feeble-minded, puppets in all but name, though the tribe as a whole has been slow to fall.

The Gaileoin's infernalists work as the demons of Hibernia like best: not on the king himself but through those around him, by obsession and quiet counsel, so the feeble royal line seems to rule while others steer it. Their people's idleness and casual sins are the slow corruption the Infernal chapter describes, not open devil-worship. A Chailleach Phiseogach might make them allies; the walk of Inis Doney's Dark Path would free a Gaileoin king from any demon riding him.

neighbours.name: The Fomórach
neighbours.summary:
The Fomórach (one is a Fomóir) say they were Ireland's first people, before Cessair's folk, whom they never met. Kin to the sea, the dark and the winter, they rode out the Flood that drowned Cessair, fought every people who came after until the Second Battle of Magh Tuireadh broke them, and withdrew to the northern islands, where they still are.

Their elders were children of Domnu, goddess of the abyss. The Túatha Dé Domnu's ancient kings, Balor of the Evil Eye, Cichol the Footless and Indech, are kosmokrators (Realms of Power: Magic), spirits able to take vast elemental shapes; since the faerie gods beat them they have drawn their Aspects out of the world and take no part in it. Today's Fomórach are much diminished, trapped in huge, hideously misshapen bodies; most have given up preying on others, though a few still pirate quiet sea lanes. Their kingdom is Tír Fhomóraig, Tory and Rathlin (see Ulster).

King Madán Muinreamhair, Madán Thick-neck, has no love for humans, since Nemed slew his four sons, but has come to see them as his race's hope and arranges marriages with the Cruithnigh of Rathlin, to his people's disgust. His ambassador is Ainid, chosen as the ugliest of his kin: her face all pustules, her arms badly mismatched, her bare feet clawed with horn. She flaunts her deformities, natural to her race, and enjoys the horror they cause; few know her well, but she bargains shrewdly and plays politics well, and four Fir Bolg slaves carry her on a bier so she never touches Irish soil.

Fomóir characters are Magic Humans (Realms of Power: Magic) with Giant Blood, obvious deformities no two alike (Cichol had a great serpent's hindquarters; Lot had four eyes on her back and a mouth on her chest; her husband Goll had no eyes at all), often a bent for Aquam, and Baneful Circumstances on Irish soil. Their inherited Quality is the Blessing of Domnu (MuCo 15, constant): at home under water, with no penalties there, speaking and hearing normally, and recovering Might, Fatigue and wounds as on land. Common Qualities are Gigantic, Limited Gestures and Limited Movement; common Virtues Ways of the Sea, Voice of the Sea and Warped Senses.

Fomóir blood runs in many humans, often hundreds of generations back: a mild monstrosity (Aquam Monstrosity, Disfigured, Hunchback, Obese) or a Monstrous Appearance, Giant Blood or Reserves of Strength, a wrathful temper, and the old heroes' battle transformations. The Ríastradh (Major Supernatural; Cú Chulainn's, from his half-Fomóir father Lugh) needs Fury or Wrathful and Fomóir descent: anger twists the hero into a Fomóir form built from three Qualities (Huge, Large, Improved Soak, Initiative or Attack), more for each Inferiority taken (a monstrous appearance, bloodlust, reduced Defense), resisted each round by Stamina + Concentration against 6 + the Angry trait, rising by one a round; it ignores Fatigue penalties and lasts until he falls unconscious. The Lúan Láith (Minor), the hero's light blazing from the brow, or the sian caurad, the hero's war cry, gives allied groups +3 and enemy groups -3 to Brave and Morale checks while he fights alone. Berserk counts as a battle transformation too. Ríastradh and Lúan Láith are in the catalog.

Sketched as a faction until the app models hedge magic: its powers are summarised here, and a member who needs them is played from The Contested Isle and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.
neighbours.ruler: King Madán Muinreamhair of Tír Fhomóraig

details.rules: Fewer than a hundred left, in a loose kingdom on the islands north of Ulster. A geas of the Tuatha Dé's druids weakens every Fomóir who stands on Irish soil; their ambassador comes from the royal blood.
details.wants: To keep their race alive; old vengeance on the sons of Nemed
details.offers: Sea lore and sea power, a vote at Tribunal

neighbours.name: The beasts of magic
neighbours.summary:
Ireland's magical beasts are represented at Tribunal like any people. Until two meetings ago a fíorláir, a true mare, held the post; then an English magus clumsily asked her to be his familiar, which she took for a kind of magical bondage, and she gave it up. The King of the Eagles, who claims lordship over all Ireland's birds, now sits instead; Cliodna of Lámbaird brokered his coming.

Among them: the fíorláir, sometimes born as a mare's seventh filly with no colt between, whom no ill power can touch, who keeps her rider from harm and outruns every horse. Lámbaird has tried and failed to breed one; a magus who enslaves one by magic will face the Eagle King's complaint, so she must be befriended. Where she first touched the ground grows Mary's Clover, a shamrock with four leaves, which may be enriched into a talisman: plated in silver, blessed by a priest and sung over to the Virgin daily for a season, it gives its wearer Luck. And the dobhar-chú, the king otter, white with black ears and a black cross on its back, hurt only by silver, often hunting in pairs; its killer dies of its curse within a day, but the skin with the cross, enriched by the one who killed it and survived, keeps a boat from drowning, a house from fire or a man from accident. Both are in the Bestiary.

details.rules: Beasts of the Magic realm that speak and understand men's ways choose a representative among themselves, or a magus speaks for them; they make treaties only through him.
details.wants: Not to be bound or enslaved by magi
details.offers: A vote at Tribunal; the favour of Ireland's magical beasts

links.note: Brought the Eagle King to the Tribunal

neighbours.secrets: Whether the Eagle King's claim to rule all Ireland's birds is true is unknown.

neighbours.name: The faeries of Ireland (the daoine sídhe)
neighbours.summary:
Everyone in Ireland has met the Faerie realm somehow, from the peasant who glimpses a procession far off to the king who weds a faerie woman before his clan. Assemblies meet on sacred hills, mostly in Faerie auras, and faerie homes, cairns, tumuli and mounds, stud the land. Irish faeries are either merry and helpful or cruel and deadly; some steal, kill or eat people, and the kindly ones are fickle. Folk avoid the word: they say the good neighbours (daoine maithe), the people of the mound (daoine sídhe), the host of the hills (croc na gcnoc), or just Them (iad). Most are easy to recognise: some look like better-dressed, handsomer people, some like beasts (the Salmon of Wisdom, Fionn mac Cumhaill's two hounds), many like evil hybrids of man and animal.

There are four kinds. The pagan gods, the Tuatha Dé, are the mightiest and rarest (their own faction). Social faeries, the hero-faeries, replay the deeds of heroes from the Ulster and Fenian cycles and every other tale, saints, devils and talking beasts included, and are the most peaceable; some magi hold that several faeries share one hero's saga, each living one episode ('Cú Chulainn Slaying Connla', 'Cú Chulainn Stealing Emer', 'Cú Chulainn Killing Cú Roí'), others that the Cú Chulainn of Ulster is one faerie, perhaps the Tribunal's strongest. Trooping faeries, the slua sí, are night gangs of destruction that copy fianna, Ostmen raiders or English knights, or look like the restless dead though they belong to neither the Infernal nor the Divine; they will not parley, and other faeries use them as the threat a protector guards against. Solitary faeries keep to one hill, river bend or bog: the three crones of Slievanamon, the old woman of the wood, the sea monster of Lough Derg, the crone of the River Barrow who drags swimmers down to keep her house, the old woman of the mountain who kills a girl who fails to finish her sewing, the banshee (bean sí) who wails before a death in her family, and Áillen mac Midgna, a three-headed magician of northern Connacht who keeps setting Tara alight by vomiting burning stones (see Meath).

Famous heroes the faeries play: Cú Chulainn, who held off Connacht's army alone in the Táin Bó Cuailnge; Fionn mac Cumhaill of Leinster and the Fenian Cycle; Medb, Connacht's fierce, wise, merciless and boldly amorous queen; Sláine, first high-king, of the Fir Bolg; Saint Patrick; and the Devil, gambler, drinker and good company, so famous in Irish tales that faeries copy him. Since faeries mimic saints and demons too, a creature of another realm may be a faerie in disguise.

Common powers: most have Faerie Speech and Faerie Sight and are Humanoid Faeries; Invisibility is the commonest power and Flight next. Others: Elf Shot (4 points, Init -4, Animal; darts seen by moonlight, each a Light Wound to a beast, often a cow), Faerie Stroke (5 points, Init -5, Corpus; a touch that strikes the victim dumb, like Twist of the Tongue), Thrust of the Wind (3 points, Init -3, Auram; as Charge of the Angry Winds) and Retreat to the Sídh (Corpus, 7 points, Init -7; the faerie alone goes at once to its home or anywhere it has an Arcane Connection to).

Wards: holy symbols, herbs and iron stop many (but not the Tuatha Dé); a horse skull under the house or a hearth kept lit all year stops trooping faeries; fresh milk on the threshold keeps a solitary one out; a red ribbon on a cow's tail guards her from social faeries; birds' eggs and sheep bones in the walls, holy things on the west wall and hearth soot on sleeping children guard a home. A ward against one kind seldom works on another.

Donn, the trooping faeries, Caílte mac Rónáin and his band of outlaws, and the Head of Arastotail are in the Bestiary.

Story seeds: Fionn and his fian burst into a hillside wedding the magi attend, to take back a Leinster bride for her clan's honour; a hedge wizard swears his lord is guided by a false Saint Patrick (or a false devil); a faerie cat courts a lonely widow so as to feed on her priest's alarm; a faerie devil dices on the night roads for travellers' souls, and a covenfolk who met him wakes drained, saying Satan is abroad; a local king hears the banshee call his name, and the magi go into the Otherworld to plead with her.

details.rules: Each kind keeps its own traditions and its own wards. Any faeries besides the Tuatha Dé may name an ambassador to the Sacred Council; if they do not, House Merinita puts one forward.
details.wants: Roles to play and people to play them on: vitality
details.offers: Entertainment, help, and danger, often all at once

neighbours.name: Slíghe Assail
neighbours.summary:
Runs due west from Tara toward Lough Owel over the central plain and on to Rathcrogan (Rath Cruachain) in Connacht. Its Guardian is a middle-aged woman with a crooked staff, who some magi think looks like the descriptions of Pralix. She challenges the traveller to debate some arcane question, won by the cleverer answer rather than the deeper learning.

One of the five High Roads (slíghe) found leading out of the royal fort at Tara the night Conn of the Hundred Battles came into the world; they reach every part of Ireland and are wide enough for two wagons abreast, unlike the rest of Ireland's roads, many of them mere rights of way. Each is a Faerie trod (Realms of Power: Faerie), a liminal space neither here nor there, with a Faerie aura of 2. At either end, at Tara or at the road's far terminus, its Guardian can be called: it seems to come, but in truth spirits the caller away into Faerie, where it may be won over, by beating it in its own challenge or by paying it vitality some other way, to let him travel. On the road time seems to pass as usual, but the traveller arrives having gone twenty-four times as fast, a day's journey in under half an hour, and may stop anywhere along it. One who can cross a Faerie threshold elsewhere meets the Guardian there without the Threshold's Guardian's help. Without Realms of Power: Faerie, treat each terminus as a Faerie regio boundary of 2 and the middle of the road as one of 4.

Redcaps: Hibernia has no Mercere Portals, and its Redcaps use the High Roads in their place. In his Gauntlet an apprentice Redcap must beat one Guardian in its own way, then makes a pact with it, taking a geas that feeds it vitality; from then on a token victory is enough each time he takes that road. Over a career a Redcap may make such pacts with every Guardian and use the whole network.

neighbours.name: Slíghe Chualann
neighbours.summary:
The road of Cuala: through Dublin, along the foot of the Wicklow Mountains, then down the River Barrow to Waterford. Its Guardian is Oisín son of Fionn mac Cumhaill on his faerie horse Embarr. The traveller must somehow bring him down from the saddle, and the moment he dismounts his faerie youth leaves him and he is old and shrivelled.

One of the five High Roads (slíghe) found leading out of the royal fort at Tara the night Conn of the Hundred Battles came into the world; they reach every part of Ireland and are wide enough for two wagons abreast, unlike the rest of Ireland's roads, many of them mere rights of way. Each is a Faerie trod (Realms of Power: Faerie), a liminal space neither here nor there, with a Faerie aura of 2. At either end, at Tara or at the road's far terminus, its Guardian can be called: it seems to come, but in truth spirits the caller away into Faerie, where it may be won over, by beating it in its own challenge or by paying it vitality some other way, to let him travel. On the road time seems to pass as usual, but the traveller arrives having gone twenty-four times as fast, a day's journey in under half an hour, and may stop anywhere along it. One who can cross a Faerie threshold elsewhere meets the Guardian there without the Threshold's Guardian's help. Without Realms of Power: Faerie, treat each terminus as a Faerie regio boundary of 2 and the middle of the road as one of 4.

Redcaps: Hibernia has no Mercere Portals, and its Redcaps use the High Roads in their place. Over a career a Redcap may make such pacts with every Guardian and use the whole network.

neighbours.summary:
Dála's road: south-east from Tara to the Liffey, then south-west over the Bog of Allen to Limerick and the mouth of the Shannon. Its Guardian is a Black Dog, fear made flesh; the traveller must master it and his own terror.

The Great Road: south from Tara, then along the Eisgir Riadha, the line of mounds over the central plain from Dublin Bay to Galway Bay, by Durrow and Clonmacnoise. Its Guardian is Gamal mac Figal, a doorkeeper of the Tuatha Dé, who makes the traveller prove that he is unique in an Ability of his choosing.

neighbours.summary:
North from Tara through the foothills of the Mournes to Eamhain Mhacha, round the east and north shores of Lough Neagh, ending at Derry. Its owner is a faerie lord who plays the traveller at fidhceall; a loser may not arrive quite where he meant to. A Redcap who has beaten him finds a single piece left on his board.
