neighbours.name: Tír na nÓg, the Otherworld
neighbours.summary:
The Irish faeries' Otherworld: a lovely, uncanny mirror of the land around it, close by and yet apart. It is called Tír na nÓg (Land of the Young), Tír na mBeo (Land of the Living) or Mag Mell (Delightful Plain), and Hermetic scholars cannot tell whether they name one place or many. They do know the names point to the three faerie worlds of Realms of Power: Faerie: half of Ireland's faeries live in Elysium, the land of myth that keeps a people's history; a third in Eudokia, among the turning points of single lives, where babies are taken, wives stolen and drunkards led astray; and the fewest, though more each year, in Arcadia.

It is reached from faerie homes: most often a mound (sídhe, which also names the faeries), inside either a rough dwelling of stone pillars and earth roof or a sunlit, summery mansion; also cairns, tumuli, mountaintops, lake beds, the hearts of forests and bogs. Some are only Faerie auras, but many are regiones. It is the Faerie realm itself, not a site, so it has no aura of its own here.

Story seed: faeries often move house. A child makes an abandoned faerie ráth his secret den, and after a month of play vanishes; its owner, a brutish swamp-ogre, has come home. Was the boy eaten, flayed or sold to another faerie? The magi must learn which and bring him back.

neighbours.name: Tír Tairngire, the Land of Promise
neighbours.summary: A vast Faerie regio lying over the sea all round Mythic Ireland. By the stories its one way in is on the Isle of Man, where a magical tree joins the island to it: the tree stands on four legs of white silver set on the ocean bed, and golden apples of power grow on its boughs. Whether it touches Tír na nÓg is unknown. Ulster's tale of the Sídh of Lir names it Lir's Otherworld, where fish graze like sheep.

levels.name: Tír Tairngire
levels.enter: By the tree on the Isle of Man, the only entrance the stories know; the Sídh of Lir in Ulster is said to be another (see Ulster).
levels.notes: The aura is the pack's choice; the book gives none.

neighbours.name: Teach Duínn, the House of Donn
neighbours.summary:
A rocky island off the Munster coast, the palace of Donn, the Dark One, death god of the Tuatha Dé (see the Bestiary), where the dead gather. Like any king he has sons and cattle and raids his neighbours. In wartime his three red-haired sons ride the land spreading terror, and the slain are said to rise here and join his host; in peace he roams adding to it one man at a time, killing a sleeper so that the spirit flies here, or leaving a false corpse in a living man's place and carrying the man off. His hall holds things that command the dead, walking corpse and haunting ghost alike. He fought the Order in the Schism War beside Salmon's Eye, and helped destroy Warbler's Way; Cliffheart, close by, still watches the Tuatha Dé.

Why he takes living captives no one knows: as servants, husbands for his daughters, or subjects for his druids' experiments. No one knows why he builds an army either, beyond that kings do.

levels.name: Donn's hall
levels.notes: A large, guarded regio; its aura is the pack's choice, the book gives none.

links.note: the death god, whose isle gathers the dead

neighbours.secrets: His great regio may hide a whole army, and magi wonder if he means to invade again. Munster's endless wars may set him off, and anyone starting a war with the Order would find him a ready ally.

neighbours.name: Slievanamon
neighbours.summary: A mountain of Munster, home of three crones, a small band of solitary faeries tied to no larger company. What they want of those who climb it is the storyguide's to decide. The book gives no aura; the pack sets Faerie 3.

neighbours.name: Goibhniu's ale-house
neighbours.summary: The smith god Goibhniu's secret ale-house, somewhere on an isle off the Munster coast, where he brews the magic ale that grants immortality. Many treasure hunters have searched for it. Ale brewed to his recipe by anyone else turns to deadly poison within a month. The book gives no aura; the pack sets Faerie 4.

neighbours.name: Dian Céacht's pools
neighbours.summary: Pools of magic water made by Dian Céacht, physician of the Tuatha Dé, that cure any sickness at all, even the old Irish diseases Hermetic healing cannot touch. Where they lie is left to the storyguide. The book gives no aura; the pack sets Faerie 3.

neighbours.name: Archdiocese of Armagh
neighbours.summary:
Irish Church. The see Saint Patrick founded, which many count the first church of Ireland; by old right its archbishop is primate of all the island, a claim the Archbishop of Dublin now openly disputes (Cashel's claim is the lesser one). Its province takes in the northern sees, and Triburnia (Kilmore) in Bréifne too, though Bréifne is subject to Connacht, a sore point with Tuam ever since. The archbishop keeps a fine library, where Oswald of Elk's Run copied many texts and learned the Ars Notoria. The book does not name the archbishop of 1220.

Saint Malachy (Máel Máedóc) was archbishop from 1132 and drove the twelfth century's reform of the Irish Church; chapter twelve has him hold the see until his death in 1148, but chapter nine and the record agree he resigned it in 1137 for the see of Down, and the pack follows them. Long before, an abbot of Armagh, Dub-dá-Lethe, went into Connacht to end twenty years of war within the Uí Briúin by casting out the demons that drove both sides.

The two Churches. By 1220 nearly everyone in Ireland accepts that the island has two Churches, both obedient to Rome and both parts of the one Western Church: the Irish Church of the native tradition, and the Anglo-Irish Church that looks to the English king and the English bishops. They fight over discipline and organisation, never doctrine, and each tries to put its own men into every vacant see; the papacy even files their letters as if they came from two nations, and now and then sends a legate to one and not the other. The Irish Church is itself split between a reform party, strongest among the bishops, which has pulled it toward the customs of the rest of Christendom, and traditionalists, mostly abbots of the old houses, who hold to the rule of monasteries founded by the apostolic saints. It runs on charters, bargains and particular arrangements rather than a grand structure: if a saint of old granted devils their due or faeries a place to dance, that grant can still stand. What little unity it has grows from its anger at the English churchmen taking over its hierarchy.

Paruchia and comarba. A paruchia is not a parish but a family of monasteries, often far apart, owing allegiance to their founder's house, much as Normandy's vassal covenants owe their liege. Its head is the comarba, the abbot who succeeds the founding saint (the abbot of Columba's chief house is styled comarba Colum Cille). Reformers of the eleventh and twelfth centuries replaced this with dioceses of joined-up territory; bishops now hold the upper hand, though most traditionalists still follow the comarba, and in the last half century nearly the whole island has fallen to the diocesan party. Bishops grab at neighbouring sees as lords grab land: once for clan politics or the quarrel of reformers and traditionalists, now mostly as the Anglo-Irish Church reaches for the whole island.

Confession and the sins beyond penance. Irish writers have produced so many penitentials that the whole Church respects their skill. The Irish hold confession strictly private between priest and sinner, and to betray it is held by many to be past forgiving. Saint Maelrúain of Tallaght's Rule names four sins no penance can answer in Ireland: lying with the dead, lying with one's sister or daughter, a priest or bishop falling into sin, and revealing a confession. The guilty can be excommunicated, refused the sacrament and driven into exile, and to traditionalists any sin repeated after penance is just as final. Reformers allow steep penances to the truly contrite and forgive a cleric's venial sins; the English allow penance broadly, think the Irish view dubious, and try and defrock any priest caught in these sins. A monk who sheds blood is usually sent into exile as his penance, as Columba was.

Monks, manaim and schools. Most Irish priests are monks, and secular clergy are few, though the dioceses and the English (training priests at Dublin) are making more. The monasteries teach the eldest children of their neighbours, the poorest and even daughters, so Ireland has a broad literate class and many Irish characters take the Educated Virtue. Round many houses lives a village of manaim, lay brothers of the local sept who keep the devotions but marry, raise families and fight for the house; some become priests or bishops. Some priests marry or keep concubines and pass on their office, so a few sees are all but hereditary. Reformers and English alike call this abuse; even Laurence O'Toole, the reforming archbishop of Dublin who sought peace with the English, put up with it, and to shore up the Irish Church against the English he consecrated several Uí Conchobhair bishops late in the last century. Reformers want monks freed of sept loyalties; the Anglo-Irish want the monasteries remade in the continental orders' pattern.

links.note: Saint Malachy, once Archbishop of Armagh

neighbours.name: Archdiocese of Cashel
neighbours.summary:
Irish Church. The archbishop of Munster, on the Rock of Cashel, given to the Church by the Uí Briain so the Eoghanachta kings could never win back their old seat. Its claim to primacy is weaker than Armagh's or Dublin's. Henry II's synod of 1171 met here. In 1219 the archbishop went to Rome to plead for the Irish clergy against the bar on Irish bishops, and in August 1220 he came back with the Pope's answer: the policy is against Rome's will and must end at once. Word has not yet reached Dublin. The book does not name him.

The Waterford–Lismore quarrel, the pattern of the age. The Anglo-Irish Bishop of Waterford set out to swallow Lismore: his knights took its cathedral and drove out Bishop Felix, who came back when that bishop died in 1199. King John's next man at Waterford, Robert, won the papal legate's union of the two sees and Felix retired, but Lismore's chapter defied the legate and chose Malachy, whom Robert's men seized and jailed. Malachy escaped to Rome; Innocent III restored the see, and in 1204 Malachy came home to find Robert dead. John's Welsh appointee David drove him out again; a second journey to Rome won him confirmation and men to see it done, and he returned in 1207 to find David murdered. Robert II, consecrated to Waterford only in 1210, again took Malachy by force; the Archbishop of Cashel had him restored, but armed men dragged him from the altar during Mass, with Robert present, and he was cruelly tortured. Robert was tried, yet nobody dared convict a favourite of the king. Malachy, freed, barely escaped killers at his own church door. Both sides petitioned the Pope, who put Malachy back in Lismore; with John dead, Waterford lost its backing, and both bishops still hold their sees in 1220 in an uneasy quiet.

neighbours.name: Archdiocese of Dublin
neighbours.summary:
Anglo-Irish Church. The see of the English, held since the conquest by Englishmen (John Comyns after Laurence O'Toole, now Henry de Londres, who is also the king's viceroy). Its two cathedrals are Christchurch, the Norse foundation that once looked to Canterbury rather than Armagh, and the new Saint Patrick's. The archbishop leads the Anglo-Irish Church, trains secular priests for it, and claims for Dublin the primacy of Ireland over Armagh's ancient right and Cashel's lesser one, a claim that has at last turned even the Irish reformers against him. His rule against Irish-born bishops has been condemned by the Pope, though the news has not yet reached him. He has also vowed to put out Saint Brigid's undying fire at Kildare to prove it a superstition.

The Anglo-Irish Church. English churchmen condemn Irish reformers and traditionalists alike and want the Church in Ireland run as England's is. Under Prince John it became policy, later confirmed by a decree of Henry II, that no Irish-born man should be a bishop and that cathedral chapters must take the king's nominee instead of electing their own; even loyal Giraldus Cambrensis found the same wall in Wales. This is the reform party's deepest grievance. Henry II had a synod held at Cashel soon after he landed in 1171, which mostly served the reformers; the provincial council at Dublin that John called in 1186 showed how far the English meant to go: stone altars for wooden ones, new church furnishings, every cemetery blessed by a bishop before use, no Mass in private chapels without the priest's and bishop's leave, strict celibacy, only aged women or kin as a priest's servants, marriage reformed and concubinage frowned on (no concubine's son to be a priest), tithes enforced, laymen barred from taking dues or hospitality from churches by custom, and no Christian burial for hired archers. These bound only Leinster, Meath and later English Ulster, but were felt everywhere.

Behind it lies politics: Pope Adrian's letter Laudabiliter licensed the English conquest so that the Irish Church's faults could be put right, so to admit the Irish Church is in good order is to undercut the Crown's title to Ireland. The Anglo-Irish follow the Archbishop of Dublin, and call Irish resistance to reform rebellion against Henry III in disguise. Now the Pope has upheld the right of Irishmen to be bishops at home and rebuked the English, and the quarrelling Irish Church has begun to close ranks against them.

Petitioning the Pope. Both Churches have a long habit of taking disputes to Rome, whose word is final until the next appeal overturns it; a journey to Rome on such an errand makes a good story, and The Church (page 46) has rules for petitions.

links.note: Its archbishop is the king's viceroy

neighbours.secrets: When the Pope's ruling arrives from Cashel, the archbishop must either yield or find another road; a man who dared to burn his own tenants' deeds is unlikely to bow quietly.

neighbours.name: Archdiocese of Tuam
neighbours.summary: Irish Church. The archbishop of Connacht, whose province matches the kingdom and props up its crown: eight sees, Killala and Achonry in the north, Mayo, Tuam and Elphin across the middle, Annaghdown, Cill Mhic Dhuach and Clonfert in the south. Bréifne's see of Triburnia was put under Armagh instead, which Tuam has resented ever since. Tuam itself is a fading town: its cathedral burned in 1184 and has not been rebuilt, so the archbishop has no cathedral, though markets and fairs keep the town rich. The book does not name him. A town left rich but without its rulers, it suggests, is the kind the Infernal tempts.

neighbours.name: The Céli Dé
neighbours.summary:
The Culdees to the English: ascetic Irish monks and devout laymen who split the year between their monastery and a hermit's cell, coming back to the community for saints' days and shared rites, and walking weekly to Mass at their abbey or a nearby church. Many work miracles; many are scribes and scholars. The last century's reforms have folded many into the regular orders, and others now live as manaim or married laymen, still keeping the old devotions. Reform has left few in Leinster and Munster; they hold on in the north and on the islands, a small tradition now. The Irish Church looks on them kindly, though reformers would turn their houses into ordinary ones of another order, which traditionalists resist; the English distrust their irregular ways and want them absorbed, though they leave devout lay members alone. Their practice of confessing to one another is dying out.

They are loosely tied to the Coill Trí, which accepts some as members: they sit in the Túath Rónáin, though they mistrust its Cistercian ceannaire. Each judges a wizard by whether he uses his power for God or himself, and few Coill Trí care to quarrel with them. Three Gifted Céli Dé are magi of Ex Miscellanea at the Paruchia of Nerius.

In play: a Céli Dé is a Companion or Mythic Companion with the Vows Flaw (even manaim vow to keep the hours), Purity and Transcendence unless he has True Faith, and the free Minor Virtue Educated; Ceremony does not suit them. Their Favoured Abilities are Invocation, Intervention, Purity and Transcendence, and one with True Faith learns them without the Virtues from the day of his vows (Realms of Power: The Divine).

details.rules: Not an order but a way of life under the Rule of Saint Maelrúain of Tallaght: two seasons a year of study, two of devotion and work; a strict diet and fasts; prayer standing with arms spread as on the cross; no self-scourging; confession to a fellow Céli Dé, the soul brother. Lay members may marry but keep the hours. A Céli Dé may be Poor but never Wealthy.
details.wants: To keep their houses and customs out of the regular orders
details.offers: Miracles, learning and fine scribes; a soul brother's counsel

links.note: Some sit in the Túath Rónáin

neighbours.name: The Cailleacha Phiseogach
neighbours.summary:
Infernal witches dressed as wise women, who counsel the sons of the Irish clans; barely a dozen in all Ireland. Their maleficia bargain with and command supernatural beings, curse foes, watch from afar and look into past and future; they often call up spirits and creatures of the Magic and Faerie realms and bind them to a task, for their power is Infernal but their knowledge spans every realm. A Chailleach's place in her lord's household is respected but fragile, resting on what she can learn and give. They feed their magic with sacrifice and with profaning holy things.

The Coill Trí know of them but rarely meet them and count them no great danger; some druids even seek one out for a service or a secret beyond their own powers.

In play: a Chailleach is a Diabolist made as a Mythic Companion (Realms of Power: The Infernal, chapter ten): the Diabolist Special Virtue and the Wise One status free, then 10 points of Flaws for 20 of Virtues, half of them Infernal Supernatural Virtues, including Diablerie and Incantation. Often taken: Premonitions, Protection, Phantasm, Malediction, Infernal Heirloom and Mentored by Demons, with the Flaws Witch Marks, Tainted with Evil, Demonic Familiar and Social Handicap. The app has no record for the tradition, so it is sketched here.

details.rules: Always women; each works alone, taking one apprentice, a girl stolen from her family and broken, who stays until her mistress dies. Each serves a lord in return for shelter and riches, and names her price for every service.
details.wants: Sanctuary and wealth from the lords they serve
details.offers: Secrets of a patron's enemies, curses, spying, prophecy

neighbours.secrets: Their lords rarely know what they harbour, and a Chailleach's counsel is the kind of quiet goad the demons of Hibernia prefer to open war.

neighbours.name: Inis Doney
neighbours.summary: A small island on Lough Erne whose finely built church carries a strong Divine aura (the book gives no number; 5 is the pack's): angels are said to come to it for their own Mass, and many local saints favour it. Most of the island is peaceful. But past the church a stony track runs down to a barren, hushed and cold place that no angel or saint can be made to look upon: the Dark Path, a road the Dominion never touches.

neighbours.name: The Dark Path of Inis Doney
neighbours.summary: The barren ground beyond Inis Doney's church, an Infernal aura of 1 that is the mundane level of nine Tartaran regiones (see page 16 of Realms of Power: The Infernal), each a point stronger than the one above it as the track goes down. Whoever walks it to the edge of Hell and comes back to the church is free of demons for life: none may tempt him, possess him or stay beneath his roof.

neighbours.name: Inis Saimera
neighbours.summary: An island where, somewhere underground, lies the Cup of Partholon: a horn of red gold worked with the tale of Partholon's voyage to Ireland. Partholon's wife Delgnat betrayed him with the servant Topa, and a demon let him taste their guilt on a cup they had shared; he had Topa killed, and so adultery and jealousy came to Ireland. A magus hunting a cathach may well go looking for so old a symbol of the island. The book gives no aura and does not say where the island is; the pack puts it in Ulster, at the mouth of the Erne.
neighbours.secrets: The cup is an Infernal relic of betrayal. Anyone who sees it gains Envious +3 (Penetration 15) and the urge to betray whoever owns it and take it for himself.

neighbours.name: Guillaume and Connacht
neighbours.summary:
Praesis fell to Ballack's siege, and its new masters now look west. For two seasons Guillaume Flambeau of Normandy has been telling the covenant's guests what his spies have found across the border: sites, auras and vis that the Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh keeps from the Order. Praesis plays host to a shifting company of foreign magi fresh to Hibernia, and their eyes are turning to Connacht.

Guillaume has not yet crossed the Sionainne himself. He sends his turb of Bréifne mercenaries, who serve him for pay, food, wine and plunder, to find vis sources and strip them. The villages round Lough Ree have learned to fear Praesis and its men, the Coill Trí warns hedge wizards of the new danger, and Cacht of Criamon, who fought for Ballack only for the joy of overturning things, listens closely, sensing a fresh war.

The Treaty forbids any covenant in Connacht and any magus more than three nights under its sky or roof, and no one person, druid or magus, can set a clause aside. One old clause gives the members of Praesis leave to enter Connacht in pursuit of Hermetic justice, at Manannán mac Lir's express request, or to seek bees for their hives, and its new masters may try to stretch it.

details.antagonist: Guillaume Flambeau of Praesis and his Bréifne mercenaries

stages.title: Raids by hired men
stages.clues: Bréifne mercenaries cross the Sionainne by night, guided by the spies' reports, and come back with vis. Druids find their sources stripped; Connachta nobles, who shelter their druids, blame the English; the Coill Trí's ambassador starts gathering complaints for the Sacred Council.
stages.ignored: Connacht's sources are plundered one by one, and the Coill Trí brings its anger to Tara in 1221.
stages.stopped: The raiders are caught, and their paymaster named before the Sacred Council.
stages.turned: The troupe wins the trust of the druids who were robbed, or quietly takes over the spies' knowledge.

stages.title: A magus crosses the border
stages.clues: Guillaume, or one of the newcomers he has fired with his reports, goes into Connacht in person, counting the nights, or claiming Praesis's old leave to seek bees or justice there.
stages.ignored: Others follow, and a magus in Connacht becomes ordinary.
stages.stopped: The magus is brought back within three nights and warned off by the Presiding Quaesitor.
stages.turned: The troupe tests the Praesis clause in a way that settles what it allows before the Tribunal.

stages.title: The Treaty broken
stages.clues: A magus outstays his three nights, marks a Connacht site as his own, or slays a hedge wizard without the warning of Wizard War owed to the Order's allies. The Coill Trí demands the justice the Treaty promises.
stages.ignored: The Tribunal hesitates, and the druids conclude that the Order will not keep its word.
stages.stopped: The offender is tried, and Connacht is given redress under the Treaty's terms.
stages.turned: The breach forces the Tribunal to restate the Treaty, perhaps with a new clause every ceannaire accepts.

stages.title: War with the Coill Trí
stages.clues: The druids withhold the seven children and strike back, the Connachta kings who guard their borders hard ride with them, and Fir Bolg counsellors urge old grudges. The Order must decide whether to march on its own or let the war spread.
stages.ignored: Connacht falls open to the English magi, and the Ordo Hiberniae's fear of being driven back like the peoples before it begins to come true.
stages.stopped: A peace is made at Qui Sonant, the neutral ground.
stages.turned: The troupe brokers the peace and becomes the go-between the Treaty has always lacked.

links.note: Shares a tower with his friends' killer

neighbours.secrets:
Báetáin, who handed the Gáe Bulg to Ballack, now shares his tower with Guillaume, whose fire killed the people he knew; his regret is a lever for anyone who would turn Praesis from within.

Maoilfhinnéin of Vigil is quietly steering the shards of Gráinne's broken first talisman into Guillaume's hands (see Maoilfhinnéin's Plot), which may draw Guillaume's attention east to Vigil before he finishes with Connacht.

neighbours.name: The Test of the Treaty
neighbours.summary:
The Treaty of Cnoc Maol Réidh has bound every Hibernian Tribunal since 898, and every meeting speaks of it as binding, yet it has never been formally put to the vote: any attempt to question it is shouted down before debate can begin. That day is near. The English magi say no hedge wizard elsewhere in Mythic Europe has such rights, and that the Treaty mocks a Code written for Hermetic magi; some Irish magi have long coveted Connacht too; and younger magi in their macgnímartha, who are outside the Code and venture into Connacht for sport, have heard the English message.

The Coill Trí is no happier. Its members resent the tithe of seven Gifted children at every meeting, a tithe that is sometimes rejected because a draoi misjudged the Gift, and some magi bully druids into service, knowing the druids dare not complain. Some churchmen in Connacht suspect the federation of heresy, even of worse.

Open questions sharpen the debate. Bréifne lies on both sides of the Sionainne, and the Treaty does not say whether Connacht ends at the river or wherever the Connachta kings rule; the Coill Trí claims all of it. The Black Pig's Dyke, if restored, would ring Ulster and cut into Connacht, which is why the druids keep it broken. A magical marker along the Slieve Aughty, where magi seeking familiars stray across the border, would earn the thanks of both sides. A clause can be added only when the Tribunal wants it and every ceannaire agrees.

details.antagonist: The Treaty's enemies, English and Irish alike

stages.title: Voices against the Treaty
stages.clues: The English Council and a few covetous Irish magi count votes; Guillaume's reports on Connacht pass from hand to hand; the Coill Trí's ambassador, distrusted by both sides, collects witnesses and grievances.
stages.ignored: The Treaty's enemies come to Tara with their case prepared and its friends with none.
stages.stopped: The would-be challengers are persuaded that the moment is wrong.
stages.turned: The troupe becomes the one both sides consult before the meeting.

stages.title: The Sacred Council
stages.clues: Before the meeting proper, the Praeco and the Presiding Quaesitor meet the embassies and confirm the ambassadors. The Coill Trí hands over its seven children, and brings its complaints: raids from Praesis, magi who extort services, Faolán living in Connacht.
stages.ignored: Grievances go unanswered, and the druids come to the vote angry.
stages.stopped: The disputes are judged fairly and the tithe accepted.
stages.turned: A just settlement wins the Coill Trí's ambassador, and perhaps a child of the tithe, for the troupe's side.

stages.title: The challenge
stages.clues: Someone at last asks the Tribunal to rule whether the Treaty still binds. The ambassadors vote as equals, which the English contest, and the Presiding Quaesitor may veto only what plainly breaks the Oath or Code.
stages.ignored: Whichever side loses takes matters into its own hands: magi cross into Connacht, or the druids stop paying the tithe.
stages.stopped: The Treaty is affirmed, and the question is closed for a generation.
stages.turned: The Treaty is amended with a clause every ceannaire accepts, settling Bréifne's border or marking the Slieve Aughty.

neighbours.name: The English Reform Motions
neighbours.summary:
Since England invaded Ireland, magi from across the Order, called the English after the first visitors from Stonehenge, have come to claim land and to bring the Tribunal into line with continental practice. House Tremere backed the first of them. They harvest vis when it is ready, ignore or intimidate the lesser traditions as suits them, and see Connacht as land waiting to be taken.

At every meeting they press the same motions: that law made case by case in treaties, where a ruling in Munster in 1134 says nothing about the same dispute in 1220, is unworkable; that the ambassadors' votes are illegal and demeaning; and that the Peripheral Code should be rewritten on Stonehenge's model. Helles of Ashenrise leads the debate, a Tytalus trained in both academic and Tytalus disputation, and answers charges of high crimes against himself and his sodales at every meeting. The English Council meets at the start of each Tribunal to agree its line, but its members disagree, and it needs a leader who can see past the legacy of Praesis and the menace of Lámbaird.

Against them stand Circulus Ruber, which will not change its time-honoured ways, and Cliffheart, which fights every English foundation by law; Milvia, the Praeco, keeps out of the quarrel. The Grand Tribunal of 1195 debated Hibernia's reform at length and left its Code alone, outraging Stonehenge when the parens of the apprentices who attacked Damisona were found guilty only of a Low Crime.

details.antagonist: The English Council and the reformers of Ashenrise

stages.title: The English Council
stages.clues: Before each meeting the foreign magi gather to agree a common line, and quarrel. Elk's Run's beleaguered magi lean on English nobles; Igneous Drake's killings and Lámbaird's suspected raids give each side its grievance.
stages.ignored: The council speaks with many voices, and its motions fail as before.
stages.stopped: The council breaks apart over Praesis.
stages.turned: A player magus takes the council's lead and decides what it asks for.

stages.title: Charges against Helles
stages.clues: The Ordo Hiberniae charges Helles and his sodales with high crimes again; he defends himself with a summer's worth of glosses on Hermetic law.
stages.ignored: Helles is acquitted once more, and every acquittal wins him sympathy among the newcomers.
stages.stopped: A charge sticks, and Ashenrise is silenced for a meeting.
stages.turned: The troupe wins a bargain: the charges dropped for a motion withdrawn.

stages.title: Against the ambassadors
stages.clues: The English move to strip the ambassadors of their votes, and to make law by general rulings rather than by treaty. Each new arrival from the continent adds a vote.
stages.ignored: The ambassadors keep their votes for now, but the majority against them grows with every meeting.
stages.stopped: The ambassadors' votes are affirmed by a clear vote.
stages.turned: A compromise binds the ambassadors to the Code's rulings in return for their seats.

stages.title: A Code on Stonehenge's model
stages.clues: The reformers carry their case beyond Hibernia, to Magvillus, to Durenmar, and to the next Grand Tribunal, due in 1228 if it keeps its usual thirty-three years.
stages.ignored: Hibernia's Code is rewritten from outside, and the Ordo Hiberniae fears it will be pushed back to Connacht like the druids before it.
stages.stopped: The Order upholds Hibernia's right to its own Code.
stages.turned: The troupe shapes a reformed Code both Irish and English magi can live with.

neighbours.secrets:
Lugardis of Elk's Run, sent by Durenmar to judge the Order in Hibernia, has concluded that the Tribunal keeps the Code, if with an odd Peripheral Code, and has written home in its praise; an appeal abroad may find less sympathy than the reformers expect.

Dorján and Konstanczia of Ashenrise are directed by the Transylvanian magi who hold their sigils to help Ashenrise bring the Tribunal up to date.

neighbours.name: Maoilfhinnéin's Plot
neighbours.summary:
Vigil, the Merinita covenant on Cionn Mhálanna, once stood watch over Ireland and now lives fat on its old glories. Gráinne inghean Uaitéar, its boisterous quartermaster, wastes vis without noticing, holds authority over vaults whose worth she does not guess, and has a long rivalry with Guillaume of Praesis, who would love to see her humbled. As a young maga she tired of her first talisman, a sword, broke it in a rite and threw the pieces from the cliffs.

Maoilfhinnéin mac Lir, Vigil's Ambassador to the Sea, spends his days in faerie and magical courts and is married to a faerie princess of Inishtrahull, an island six miles out from the head.

details.antagonist: Maoilfhinnéin mac Lir, Ambassador to the Sea

stages.title: Old friends and sea-worn shards
stages.clues: Vigil's ambassador is unusually warm to Lámbaird; Gráinne is goaded into ever bolder boasts; a sea-worn blade fragment changes hands among fishermen, then traders, heading south.
stages.ignored: The shards reach Praesis.
stages.stopped: The shards are found and returned to Gráinne.
stages.turned: The troupe learns who fixed the connection, and why.

stages.title: Guillaume's weapon
stages.clues: Guillaume learns what the shards are. He declares Wizard War on Gráinne in public, a month ahead as the Code requires, or simply strikes from afar.
stages.ignored: His spells find her wherever she is.
stages.stopped: Gráinne is warned and warded in time, and the connection destroyed.
stages.turned: Guillaume is persuaded the shards are a trap.

stages.title: The sacrifice
stages.clues: Gráinne is humbled or slain. The Two Dozen Men of Mhálanna, loyal to her above all, cry for revenge, and Vigil's halls fill with talk of war with Praesis.
stages.ignored: Vigil and Praesis go to war.
stages.stopped: Gráinne survives, wiser and angry.
stages.turned: Gráinne learns who betrayed her, and Vigil turns on its ambassador.

stages.title: Retreat to Inishtrahull
stages.clues: Declaring the covenant in danger, Maoilfhinnéin carries the black pig's tusks out to sea and refounds Vigil among his wife's people.
stages.ignored: Vigil abandons the mainland, leaving Banbha's Crown and the drowned vaults to whoever finds them.
stages.stopped: The tusks stay above the gate on Cionn Mhálanna.
stages.turned: The troupe claims the abandoned vaults, or Vigil's thanks for keeping it whole.

neighbours.secrets:
Maoilfhinnéin believes Ireland's old stories are bound to repeat, and that the Ordo Hiberniae will be driven back as the native wizards were; he sees the first signs already. Should Vigil be threatened, he has prepared to carry the tusks to Inishtrahull and found the covenant anew there.

He has three schemes in hand. He supports Lámbaird's positions at Tribunal, to mend the harm Éinri's feud has done. He feeds Gráinne's overconfidence, seeing that a sacrifice may soon be needed. And his allies in the sea brought him the shards of her broken sword: he has fixed them as an Arcane Connection to her and is working them into the hands of Guillaume.

neighbours.name: Ballack's Debts
neighbours.summary:
Ballack of Tytalus came from the Rhine to avenge his filius Holzner, whom Praesis executed for stealing its cathach, and after a year's Wizard War he rules the covenant. He relishes turning Hibernia's traditions on the Irish, scorns their magi and courts the English covenants and new adventurers, and Holzner's head still hangs from the palisade where Meadhbh put it.

The war cost him dearly. He owes vis and favours to many magi, and with his own resources spent he has borrowed more vis and casting tablets from distant benefactors. Until he pays them, he knows his prize is only on loan, yet he cannot be seen to give it up. Praesis must start paying for itself, and soon.

stages.title: A prize on loan
stages.clues: Ballack hunts for income: the vis Guillaume's men bring out of Connacht, services sold to English covenants, the sources around Lough Ree his siege stripped bare.
stages.ignored: Praesis's greed falls on its neighbours.
stages.stopped: Praesis finds an honest income.
stages.turned: The troupe becomes Ballack's partner, on its own terms.

stages.title: Remember who you work for
stages.clues: A player magus who has joined a cult or society is sent to remind Ballack of his debt. He is no member, and he is older and more dangerous than the messenger.
stages.ignored: The creditors lose patience.
stages.stopped: Ballack pays what he can, and the reminder is heeded.
stages.turned: The messenger gains a hold over the Lord of Praesis.

stages.title: The debt called in
stages.clues: The benefactors collect in their own coin: service in a quarrel that is not his, a share of Praesis's sources, or his votes at Tara.
stages.ignored: Praesis becomes the creditors' tool.
stages.stopped: Ballack breaks free of them, at a price.
stages.turned: The troupe learns who the creditors are, and what they want in Hibernia.

stages.title: The covenant changes hands
stages.clues: Weakened, Ballack's hold slips. Meadhbh's supporters, whom Praesis watches for every week, see their chance; so do his creditors.
stages.ignored: Praesis falls again, to Meadhbh or to the creditors.
stages.stopped: Ballack holds Praesis.
stages.turned: The troupe decides who keeps the Gáe Bulg.

neighbours.secrets: His benefactors are a powerful, secretive cult or society to which Ballack does not belong, though he took its aid; lately he has been forgetting what he owes it.

neighbours.name: Donn's Army
neighbours.summary:
Donn, the Dark One, the death god of the Tuatha Dé (see the Bestiary), holds court where the dead gather, on Teach Duínn, a bare rock in the sea beyond Munster. He behaves like any king: he has sons, keeps cattle and raids his neighbours, and he is gathering a host, a warrior here and a warrior there. His favoured way is to slay a sleeper and let the spirit fly to his island, or to leave a perfect false corpse behind and carry the living man away. In war his three red-haired sons ride through the land, crying that the slain will rise at Teach Duínn to join him.

In the Schism War Donn fought beside the Diedne of Salmon's Eye, and their forces destroyed Warbler's Way before the magi razed Salmon's Eye and drove him home. Cliffheart, founded by Warbler's Way's survivors, never learned why the Tuatha Dé sided with Diedne, and keeps watch. His great warded regio may hide a host, and magi wonder whether he means to invade again; Munster's endless wars may give him his chance, and anyone who makes war on the Order will find him a willing ally. The smith god Goibhniu hates him.

In Ulster a faerie called Donn, the dark one of the endless war with bright Find, has caused children of faerie blood to be born, meant as the core of a new army. Find has not yet answered.

stages.title: Taken in sleep
stages.clues: Men die in their beds without a mark, or are buried whole while their kin swear they saw them alive; a grog's corpse is found that is not his.
stages.ignored: Donn's ranks swell quietly.
stages.stopped: The thefts are traced to Teach Duínn and warded against.
stages.turned: A captive is brought back alive, with news of the island.

stages.title: The children of Donn
stages.clues: Children of faerie blood are born in Cuailnge and beyond, and Find stirs against his old enemy.
stages.ignored: The children grow toward their father's war.
stages.stopped: The children are fostered beyond Donn's reach.
stages.turned: The troupe claims a Gifted child, or Find's alliance.

stages.title: Three red riders
stages.clues: Donn's sons ride through Munster in the wake of Desmond's and Thomond's wars, spreading terror and promising that the fallen will rise.
stages.ignored: The dead of every battle go to Donn.
stages.stopped: The sons are driven back to the sea.
stages.turned: Goibhniu's feud with Donn is turned against him.

stages.title: The host of Teach Duínn
stages.clues: Donn's army marches out of its regio, perhaps beside some enemy of the Order, as it once marched with Diedne.
stages.ignored: Munster's covenants face a second Schism War, Cliffheart and Circulus Ruber first.
stages.stopped: The Tribunal unites and throws Donn back again.
stages.turned: The troupe treats with Donn, and learns at last why the Tuatha Dé fought for Diedne.

neighbours.secrets: Whether Ulster's Donn and the lord of Teach Duínn are one being is left to the storyguide; if they are, the faerie-blooded children are the first sign of the host.

neighbours.name: The Gaileoin Infernalists
neighbours.summary: The Gaileoin, the third tribe of the Fir Bolg, live on Árainn Thiar, smallest of the Aran Isles. They are Christian in name and hardly observant, their island has a single church, and they are lazier and quicker to small sins than their neighbours. The Fir Bolg are allies of the Order, with an ambassador who votes at Tara, and the isles lie in Connacht, where no magus may stay beyond three nights.

details.antagonist: The infernalists behind the Gaileoin king

stages.title: Idle islanders
stages.clues: Visitors to Árainn Thiar find the church empty, the fields neglected and the people cheerfully sinful; Fir Bolg monks of Árainn Mhór worry for their cousins.
stages.ignored: The rot deepens.
stages.stopped: A preacher or saint stirs the Gaileoin to repent.
stages.turned: The troupe finds a Gaileoin who will talk.

stages.title: The puppet king
stages.clues: An envoy to the Gaileoin court finds the king vacant and his councillors answering for him.
stages.ignored: The cadre's hold is never questioned.
stages.stopped: The councillors are exposed before King Rudraige.
stages.turned: The troupe learns the cadre's names and masters.

stages.title: Beyond the island
stages.clues: The cadre's reach grows: into the Fir Bolg's counsel to the kings of Connacht, toward the ambassador's vote, or across the water to the mainland.
stages.ignored: The Order's ally becomes Hell's instrument.
stages.stopped: The cadre is kept to Árainn Thiar.
stages.turned: The Fir Bolg purge the cadre themselves, with help.

stages.title: A March in Connacht
stages.clues: The truth comes out. The Code demands a March, the Treaty limits magi to three nights in Connacht, and the Fir Bolg are allies who must be warned like magi.
stages.ignored: The Order quarrels over the law while the infernalists escape or dig in.
stages.stopped: The cadre is destroyed, and the Treaty survives.
stages.turned: The troupe finds a way through the law that keeps both the alliance and the Treaty.

neighbours.secrets:
Unknown to the other tribes, a cadre of infernalists rules the Gaileoin through their king. Their meddling has left the royal line feeble-minded, puppets who speak as they are told. The tribe as a whole has been slow to corrupt.

Dealing with demons is the one crime for which the Code calls a Wizard's March without debate, which sets the Order's law against the Treaty's limits and the Fir Bolg alliance the moment the truth comes out.

neighbours.name: The Giant under Qui Sonant
neighbours.summary:
Legend says a giant sleeps beneath the Cuailnge ridge where Qui Sonant Pro Quieto stands, held asleep for as long as song is heard above him, and that if the songs end or he is disturbed he will rise and quit the island, and its magic will go with him. Day and night a choir of a dozen, magi and covenfolk, chants in the candlelit chantry where no magic is used, and every apprentice learns the songs by heart. The theory in fashion makes the giant a Fomóir, or Finn MacCumhaill himself.

Cantarus, Master of the Songs for fifty years and now 130, knows he has little time and no heir. Finn, his only filius still at the covenant, takes the office for granted and trades promises on it, but lacks the gift for leading; Cantarus would gladly name any magus willing to commit to Qui Sonant instead. Máel-ruanaid of Vigil, a master of Merinita story magic, believes the giant is held by the symbolic act of singing rather than by the songs, and wants to learn how.

stages.title: No heir for the songs
stages.clues: Cantarus looks among visitors for a successor; Finn boasts of his coming office; Máel-ruanaid asks too many questions about the chant.
stages.ignored: Finn inherits, and the covenant drifts.
stages.stopped: A worthy Master of the Songs is found.
stages.turned: A player magus is offered the office.

stages.title: Silence falls
stages.clues: A sudden power silences Qui Sonant: no sound, natural or magical, can be made or heard there. The songs stop, and the ground begins to shake.
stages.ignored: The tremors grow with every silent day.
stages.stopped: Sound is restored before the giant stirs.
stages.turned: The troupe learns where the silence came from.

stages.title: The bound daimon
stages.clues: The trail leads into the Magic realm, where a great daimon has been trapped and stripped of its power over sound on Earth. Its captor must be defeated and the power returned.
stages.ignored: The daimon stays captive and the world stays silent.
stages.stopped: The captor is beaten and the daimon freed.
stages.turned: The freed daimon owes the troupe a favour.

stages.title: The giant wakes
stages.clues: The hillside heaves, the tombs of the Order's dead crack open, and something vast begins to rise.
stages.ignored: The giant leaves Ireland and takes its magic, and the Order's cemetery is broken.
stages.stopped: Song returns and the giant settles back to sleep.
stages.turned: The troupe learns what the giant is, and what would keep it asleep without the songs.

neighbours.secrets: No one knows what the giant truly is. If Máel-ruanaid is right, some other symbolic act could take the songs' place.

neighbours.name: Áillen Burns Tara
neighbours.summary:
The Hill of Tara lies neglected in 1220. Since Saint Ruadán's curse brought a burning beam down on King Diarmait in his own hall, no hall can be raised there, and faeries replay the old tales on the hill, among them Áillen mac Midgna setting the hall alight and Fionn mac Cumhaill driving him away.

Áillen is a three-headed magician who lives in the north of Connacht. He has set Tara on fire again and again by spewing up burning rocks, and his attacks keep a regular pattern. Every seven years the hill holds the Tribunal, when Circulus Ruber raises a temporary settlement by magic and every covenant puts its cathach on show.

stages.title: Scorch marks on the hill
stages.clues: Burnt earth and blackened stones on Tara; a herder's tale of a three-headed shape in the sky; old records that, read together, show when Áillen comes.
stages.ignored: No one works out the pattern in time.
stages.stopped: The Tribunal is warned and wards are raised.
stages.turned: The troupe can tell the Praeco when he will strike.

stages.title: Fire on Tara
stages.clues: Áillen comes while the Tribunal's camp stands, raining burning stones on tents, hearths and the cathaigh on display.
stages.ignored: The camp burns, and a covenant that loses its cathach loses its votes.
stages.stopped: The fire is beaten back before it spreads.
stages.turned: The troupe saves the cathaigh, and wins great credit.

stages.title: A Fionn for Tara
stages.clues: The story needs its hero: a faerie playing Fionn, or a character willing to take the part. Áillen flees to Connacht, where magi may not stay three nights.
stages.ignored: Áillen returns on his next turn of the pattern.
stages.stopped: Áillen is driven off, as in the tale.
stages.turned: A player character becomes Tara's Fionn, with the reputation that goes with it.

links.note: The Tuatha Dé's mound on the hill

neighbours.name: The Conspiracy of Mellifont
neighbours.summary:
Mellifont, near Drogheda, founded by Saint Malachy in 1140, is the greatest Cistercian house in Ireland: a hundred monks and three hundred lay brothers, mother of Bective, Baltinglass and twenty-three more. Since the invasion its Irish and English monks have been at odds, and tales of corruption and debauchery reached Cîteaux. When a visitation came in 1216 to restore the Rule, the monks shut the gates against it. The general chapter deposed Abbot Thomas in 1217, but he still rules, backed by his monks and the daughter houses, and the Order means to send visitors who will put the house in order and remove the abbots at fault; the Pope may step in.

Mellifont's nine granges now cover the Brú na Bóinne, built on high ground among the ancient sídhe and ráths, and the forty mounds stand clear of the undergrowth for the first time in ages. The newest grange, New Grange, lies beside the mound of Aonghus. Bective backs its mother house. At Baltinglass the abbot is for Mellifont while his monks stay loyal to Cîteaux, and they long to plant a great cross on the faerie mound above their valley. Jerpoint has joined the revolt.

details.antagonist: Abbot Thomas and the rebel houses

stages.title: The shut gates
stages.clues: Rumours of Mellifont's revolt pass from house to house; Irish and English monks quarrel; the granges' lay brothers see strange lights among the mounds.
stages.ignored: The revolt hardens.
stages.stopped: Abbot Thomas quietly submits.
stages.turned: The troupe learns the revolt's true cause.

stages.title: The haunting of New Grange
stages.clues: Trooping faeries ruin the crops at New Grange and the lay brothers tell of terrors; then the steward and his family vanish one summer evening, and Abbot Thomas begs for help.
stages.ignored: Aonghus wakes, and the granges suffer his wrath.
stages.stopped: The steward's family is brought back from the mound.
stages.turned: The troupe wins the abbot's gratitude, and a say in where the granges may stand.

stages.title: The deputation
stages.clues: Cîteaux's deputation arrives to expel the guilty abbots. The daughter houses split, Baltinglass's monks against their abbot.
stages.ignored: Gates are shut again, and the quarrel turns violent.
stages.stopped: Discipline is restored, and the rebels give way.
stages.turned: The troupe shapes which abbots stay and which go.

stages.title: Rome
stages.clues: The Pope takes up the case, and a long, dark struggle begins across the Irish Church.
stages.ignored: The split between the Irish and Anglo-Irish churches deepens into open enmity.
stages.stopped: Rome settles the matter.
stages.turned: A legate in the troupe's debt decides it.

neighbours.secrets: Why the monks rebelled is the storyguide's choice: the quarrel of Irish and English, a lax life they will not give up, an Infernal corruption of the Cistercians, or some ancient magical secret the lay brothers turned up among the barrows of the Brú na Bóinne.

neighbours.name: The Pact of Oireadh's Parma
neighbours.summary:
Eight druids of mixed traditions, sworn to the Pact of Oireadh, meet every season in the village of Oireadh, no more than two days from any of them; living apart softens the strife their Gifts bring. They were once allies of Praesis, which was founded as a meeting place of magi and druids, but left Meadhbh when her demands grew too great, and began to ask what gave the Order its power and what kept it safe while lesser wizards fell. They have no love for the English.

Ádhamh Brathair, a Gifted learned magician whose magic goes back to Bologna, conceived the Pact and leads its research: a theory of magic that embraces every Irish tradition and gives each the defences of all. He has made amulets that lend the folk witches' Second Sight, Dowsing and Cursing for a season, to learn how their magic differs from his. He is in minor orders, serves a wealthy noble of Cong, and lately lost a Gifted child of his to the Coill Trí's tithe. Among the others are Umor Ard Mac Adar, a four-armed Fir Domhnann healer in the hills above Lough Conn; Mór Greannach, a folk witch of Carrowmore with the widest acquaintance among hedge wizards; and Tuathal an Iarrainn, a goetic smith of Rosbeg.

details.antagonist: Ádhamh Brathair and the Pact of Oireadh

stages.title: Strange amulets
stages.clues: Druids appear with powers not of their tradition; the Pact's messengers are busy on the roads; the villagers of Oireadh grow wary of strangers and send word ahead.
stages.ignored: The research goes on unseen.
stages.stopped: The Coill Trí learns of the work and forbids it.
stages.turned: The troupe befriends the Pact before anyone else knows.

stages.title: The words of wisdom
stages.clues: A spirit born of Ádhamh's experiments flees on the wind for fear of slavery and settles near the player covenant. The villagers start speaking of strange matters in a Latin none of them know. The spirit is a store of magical knowledge with no sense of how to use it, and it is fading.
stages.ignored: The spirit dies, and its knowledge with it.
stages.stopped: The spirit is guided back to its maker.
stages.turned: The troupe keeps what the spirit knows.

stages.title: A true summoner
stages.clues: Learning that Tuathal's arts are Infernal, Ádhamh looks beyond Connacht for a true magical summoner. He writes to the apprentice the Coill Trí took from him, asking her to tell him of any summoner her covenant meets, and she is caught sending word.
stages.ignored: The girl keeps spying, and the Pact learns more.
stages.stopped: Her covenant cuts the link and questions her loyalty.
stages.turned: Her covenant uncovers Ádhamh's research through her, and chooses what to do with it.

stages.title: A druid's Parma
stages.clues: Generations on, or sooner with help, the Pact's breakthrough nears: Ireland's druids would gain a defence like the Order's own.
stages.ignored: The hedge wizards stand as the Order's equals, and the balance the Treaty keeps is gone.
stages.stopped: The notes are destroyed or seized.
stages.turned: The theory is brought into the Order, as the Treaty's makers once hoped the old traditions might be.

neighbours.secrets:
The Pact's true aim, hidden from the Order and the Coill Trí alike, is a Parma Magica of its own. Ádhamh needs 120 breakthrough points and has 15, and doubts he will live to finish; he keeps his notes for those who come after.

Tuathal's arts are Infernal in origin, which Ádhamh has yet to discover.

characters.summary:
Praeco of Hibernia, looking sixty-eight. She is not the eldest magus of the Tribunal, but Conán Derg gave up the office. Her passion is political unity, and she has steered a turbulent Tribunal skilfully through most of its storms; she has been Praeco at the last four meetings and led Hibernia's delegation to the Grand Tribunal of 1195.

As a Bonisagus she respects Cliffheart's original research, though she fears its success would harm Hibernia's unity. She takes no side between the Irish and English magi.

characters.summary:
Hibernia's oldest Quaesitor and its presiding Quaesitor, looking fifty-six: ugly, bent and irritable, his long face scarred down both sides and his greasy hair hanging in strands. His name joins the Latin for face and ugly.

Painful Magic makes him slow to cast, so he prefers one mighty spell to several small ones, though such spells flood him with more than he can sort and details get lost. He has reversed his rulings when what he first learned proved false; he is no fool to cling to a bad judgement, but he remembers long and hates to be shown wrong.

characters.name: Conán Derg

characters.summary:
The oldest magus in Hibernia, who looks a hale twenty-nine and says his strong faerie blood keeps him young. He was Praeco when the trouble between Irish and English magi began and stood by the Peripheral Code, insisting that all the newcomers wanted could be had under it; in 1186 he accepted Ashenrise's cathach.

Two months after the meeting of 1186, wandering alone on the Connacht border, he was ambushed and his right arm was taken off at the shoulder. He would not let magic regrow it: by the old Irish belief that a leader must be whole, he gave up the office of Praeco and withdrew from Hermetic politics, and he has seemed happier ever since. Some suspect Faisgia of Cliffheart; Conán Derg neither denies nor confirms it.

Cliffheart's leader, filius of one of its founders, looking ninety-eight. He spends most of his time roaming Munster for faeries who fought in the Schism War. He keeps the cathach: each year he casts the spell that holds the Diedne magus in stone, and he works the Rego Terram magic that carries it to every Tribunal.

Since Conán Derg was maimed on ground Faisgia often travels, some magi suspect him of the ambush; he scoffs at the idea.

characters.summary:
A German magus trained in the Rhine, looking forty-three, and a born linguist, researching how to cast spells in Irish. He has made a spell that compels a faerie to talk in its old, truer tongue instead of its Faerie Speech Pretense, records what it says and builds his research on it; each interview serves only once.

He longs to meet and talk with every new faerie, but is ill at ease away from a laboratory and his sodales want no faerie visitors, so he often asks other Hibernian magi to lend him their laboratories for his interviews.

characters.summary: A Scandinavian born in Dublin and trained at Verdi, looking fifty-five. He came home to guard his family when he heard of the English invasion, found they were in no real danger, and discovered he loved his homeland; Cliffheart took him in. He lives at the back of the ráth making magic items for his sodales, and gladly takes commissions from other Irish magi.

characters.summary:
Founder and leader of Elk's Run, looking seventy: a tiny man, scarcely a boy's size, under a shock of untidy white hair. Born in Leinster to an Irish mother, he was carried off to Stonehenge in childhood and brought up there, and after his Gauntlet planned his return, befriending Lugardis.

His adventures are long behind him. He is wholly given to a rebirth of learning in Hibernia and to saving the island's texts for posterity: collecting, copying and trading books. Gentle Gifted, he has many friends among Irish and English nobles and clerics. He trusts to cunning and trickery against his enemies, whom he takes to be jealous of his standing in House Bonisagus and the Order abroad, and means one day to give his rarest texts to Durenmar.

He is teaching two apprentices at once, which takes half his time; once they pass their Gauntlets he may leave Ireland with the library if the politics turn bad.

characters.summary:
An Italian Quaesitor with raven hair, sharp features and a piercing stare, looking sixty-four, who has served in four Tribunals; she came from the Rhine, sent by Durenmar to look into the state of the Order in Hibernia after English magi wrote to Magvillus and Durenmar of hostility and barbarous customs and demanded reform. Her Blatant Gift frightens covenfolk and Irish folk, who cross themselves as she goes by, and sours milk almost at once, so she keeps away from the cattle and the dairy.

She has come to see that Hibernia keeps the Code, if with an odd Peripheral Code, and having read Oswald's books she is amused by the Stonehenge magi's fear that Connacht shelters the last of the Diedne. Her letters home and to Durenmar explain the local customs and praise the Irish Order, who still suspect her deeply. She wants a diplomatic answer to the covenant's troubles, is appalled by Igneous and worried by Oswald.

characters.name: Igneous Drake

characters.summary:
A Stonehenge magus, looking seventy-two, in Hibernia only ten years: he came because he heard English magi were persecuted here, and because the macgnímartha raiders let him test his magic on the Hermetically trained, a better fight than hedge wizards. Violent, scornful of the natives and their ways, he delights in conflict and in burning the covenant's enemies.

He has made a spell that raises a wall of fire on a Boundary, ringing the covenant during a raid; he burns those trapped inside and then hunts the survivors down. Bored of waiting for attacks, he has begun Wizard Wars against Irish magi. He backed the Siege of Praesis eagerly, spending seasons there teaching the attackers Ignem spells and doing much to bring the island covenant down, and he is a firm friend of Ballack and the new Praesis.

characters.name: Diarmait mac Fergaile

characters.summary:
Leader of Leth Moga, an un-Gifted Redcap who looks seventy-five, and Fergal's son-in-law, who took over when his parens Fergal died; the Red Book came to him from Fergal as his own property. Unlike Fergal he thinks opening the Red Book to readers would add to its worth: it must not be copied, but it should be seen.

The other Redcaps care more about whom he will name to follow him, Gopstan or Luathan. Dáire Cú of Leth Cuinn thinks him too doddering and bookish to lead the Tribunal's Redcaps.

characters.summary:
Diarmait's filius and son-in-law, looking thirty-seven, who has never left Ireland; his name comes from Irish slang for 'Poor John'. Born rich, he gave away his goods with a show when he passed his Gauntlet. He was apprenticed late and knows House Mercere's ways less well than Redcaps of his age, which weighs on Diarmait when he thinks of handing over the House.

He loves the Red Book dearly and has spent hours writing recent events into it. He once spent a year at Cashel posing as an unlettered prince's son to read its library, and was found out.

characters.summary:
Ercc Cam's filius and nephew, dashing and handsome and the best-loved Redcap of the south. He has the temper for the Cult of Heroes, but when he took his uncle's offer to train him his angry mother laid a geas on him, 'forever mundane or forever lame', so he may learn no Virtue that would give him quasi-magical powers; barred from the initiations of Leth Cuinn, he stayed south of the Eiscir Riada.

He makes good use of magic items instead: a cloak that turns him into an eagle and a harpoon that lets him breathe under water.

characters.summary:
Founder and leader of Ashenrise, looking thirty-seven. Born in Champagne and trained in the Normandy Tribunal, he joined Moles Magna because a covenant inside a dam seemed a good place to hide from the world; when the dam burst and swept it away, he chose to hide in plain sight instead, and his grog captain Ralph fitz Stephen brought him to his kin in Ireland.

A master of disputation in both the schoolmen's manner and his House's, he sees rewriting Hibernia's Peripheral Code as the greatest challenge there is. He studies and glosses Hermetic law daily to answer the high crimes charged against him and his sodales at every meeting.

links.note: Fellow founder; fled Moles Magna with him

characters.summary:
'Thumbs', a founder of Ashenrise, looking forty-two: tall, hawk-like and dressed in black, a Sicilian with four thumbs, two where his little fingers should be, from an accident in his apprenticeship. No lover of beauty, he studies deformity and deadly plague, and has visited every place in Ireland where plague killed a crowd, gathering samples of something few can name. Irish magi find him grim and frightening.

Among mundanes he is another man: his Gentle Gift lets him pass as a gloved scholar and physician of many languages, charming and pleasant, a welcome guest at the neighbouring lords' courts and much loved by the English settlers.

characters.summary: Once Decamentus, a faithful follower of his House's ways, he met Saint Patrick in a long Temporary Twilight, and the saint blessed the coarse blanket he had wrapped himself in against the cold. He chose a new life at once, came to Hibernia and renamed himself Tug, which is a shawl in Irish slang. No covenant but Ashenrise would take him. Looks thirty-eight.

characters.summary: Born and trained in the Transylvanian Tribunal and sent on to Stonehenge, he and Konstanczia asked leave to join the new Hibernian covenant and came too late to help defend its cathach. Handsome and charming, he would be Leinster's most eligible bachelor but for his Gift. Always the defender, he has fought half a dozen Wizard Wars in Hibernia and killed four magi. Looks forty-three.

characters.name: Dalton Ballaugh

characters.summary:
Dalton Ballaugh an Flámbó (DOLL-ton BOLL-odge), leader of Lámbaird, looking forty-three. His father was an Uí Broin, and the covenfolk still call him Mac ind Óc, the Young Son, though few of them are his elders. He and Brian were apprentices together and passed their Gauntlets together, and are close friends.

A great hunter, which shows in his Intellego: he reads a site as well as any Quaesitor. His mastery of fire matches it, and he is a dangerous enemy, as Éinri mac Cillíni of Vigil has learnt; the two have feuded for years, short of Wizard War. His familiar is Lóegaire Liath, Grey Lóegaire, a grizzled hunting dog, sire of the covenant's line of magical hounds.

links.note: Close friend; apprenticed and gauntleted together

characters.summary:
Brian of Cilldara an Flámbó, looking fifty-seven: small, thin and entirely hairless, a skinchanger who becomes a salmon and spends long spells in Wicklow's lakes and streams, studying the moods of the water he loves.

His familiar, a salmon like his other shape, was caught and eaten by Norman soldiers. He has not got over it and may never bind another; until then he means to destroy every Norman on Irish soil.

characters.summary: Cliodna an Flámbó (CLEE-na), the youngest at Lámbaird, looking thirty-five, who has made herself in the image of a warrior-queen of legend: as good with a sword as with a spell, a superb rider and athlete. She is called daughter of the Eagle since a clan of magical birds of prey in the mountains adopted her, and her familiar is Artt, a son of the Eagle King.

characters.summary:
Fedelmid an t-Éigse Measceal (FEDGE-el-midge on TCHAY-shuh MYES-kul), comarba Nerius, leader of the Paruchia, looking ninety-five. A young Céli Dé, he joined House Ex Miscellanea believing the Order the very spirit of learning and discipline a Gifted holy man should seek. Many of its members disappointed him; he stays loyal to his sodales but never puts them before the Church. His is not a loyalty to sees, bishops and institutions but a personal, heroic asceticism, a saint's life of his own.

His pilgrimage changed him twice over: the Alpine visions sent him in search of the few who knew Nerius's secret, and Rome taught him that the Pope has spiritual authority but that spiritual troubles are best mended locally by those they touch. He trained Indrechtach, and grieved when Glendalough cast him out.

Now very old, worn by decrepitude and long bouts of Twilight, he is preparing to leave Little Saltee to die and be buried at Qui Sonant Pro Quieto, and hopes the covenant's next visitors will escort him there.

links.note: His apprentice, trained in Holy Magic

description.biography:
Stat block printed in The Contested Isle, chapter six. Age 50, looking 47. Soak 1; Encumbrance 0 (0). Fatigue: two OK levels, then -1, -3, -5 and Unconscious. Wounds: Light at 1-5 (-1), Medium at 6-10 (-3), Heavy at 11-15 (-5; the book prints 1-15), Incapacitated at 16-20, Dead at 21 or more. Combat: dodge, Init 0, Atk 0, Dfn 0, Dam n/a; punch, Init 0, Atk 0, Dfn 0, Dam 0.

Devotions: Saint Nerius 3 (5), a bonus of 3 to invoke him. Purity is printed as 5 (9) and Transcendence as 2 (4); the numbers in brackets are not entered. The book's 'Educated Quiet Magic (2)' is read as Educated and Quiet Magic taken twice; Pious is listed among his Major Flaws. The Restriction is that his magic cannot affect women; the Vow is the Céli Dé's. He has no Magic Theory score in the book.

Casting totals as printed: Ward Against the Faeries of the Sea +16, Comfort of the Drenched Traveler +13, Bind Wounds, Cheating the Reaper and the Ritual 'For they are life' +21, Revealed Flaws of the Mortal Flesh, 'Put on the whole armor of God' and The Severed Limb Made Whole +16, the four Rego Corpus spells +22, 'Then I was the craftsman' +16, Moonbeam +16, Demon's Eternal Oblivion +19. The Severed Limb Made Whole is printed as MuCo 20 but the catalog's spell of that name is CrCo 25; Demon's Eternal Oblivion is printed at level 10.

Holy Magic. All his magic is Holy Magic, which he was taught in place of the Hermetic kind; most of his spells match common Hermetic ones, and five are the book's own (in the catalog). He may not use magic for anything sinful and refuses Hermetic spells, and only someone with Holy Magic can learn his spells from him. Aligned to both Divine and Magic, he may use either column of the aura interaction table.

characters.summary:
Indrechtach an t-Éigse Measceal (IND-rukh-tukh), Céli Dé, looking forty-seven, Fedelmid's apprentice, driven from the monastery at Glendalough because his Gift unsettled the monks. He unsettles most people: fearless, blunt and honest past all tact, he says just what he thinks and will not tell the smallest white lie.

He says the prayers at the Tribunal, and is the one of his covenant other magi meet most: he travels round Hibernia visiting covenants, asking leave to copy books, and lending a hand with humble work most magi would think beneath them.

Tonsured in the Irish manner, in a rough robe and sandals. A Twilight effect crowns his head with a nimbus when he works magic and makes his face glow faintly by moonlight; his sigil, heard in every spell, is a moment of voices singing the Psalms.

characters.name: Cóemgen
